text:
Good morning, everybody. I declare open this hearing of the Senate Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee, looking into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I would like to start by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet, pay my respects to their elders past, present and emerging and extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today.

The committee has set Thursday 5 November as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and Thursday 17 December as the date for the return of answers to those questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Indigenous portfolio agencies, followed by the finance portfolio, as listed on today's program. Under Standing Order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I do remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings, and that is that any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds and estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I do remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth should not be asked to give an opinion on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister.

This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanation of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. The public immunity statement will be incorporated into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

I remind senators their obligation under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. As is my usual practice, I have provided copies of the code in the room for peoples' reference.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I welcome Senator the Hon. Malarndirri McCarthy, Minister for Indigenous Australians; Mr David Knights, Chief Executive Officer of Indigenous Business Australia; Mr Nigel Browne, Chief Executive Officer of Aboriginal Investment NT; and the other officers that you have brought with you to the table. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Good morning, Chair. I'd like to acknowledge that we come together on the lands of the Ngunnawal and Ngambri peoples and pay my respects to elders past, present and emerging and also to the portfolio body members who are here today.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Thank you. Mr Browne, would you like to make an opening statement?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Yes, thank you, Chair.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Please go ahead.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text:
I, too, would like to acknowledge the traditional owners of the land upon which we meet today. Before I start the opening statement, I also wish to, on behalf of the board, management and staff of Aboriginal Investment NT, extend our best wishes to Dr Helen Haines in relation to the tragic events that have befallen her.

Aboriginal Investment NT supports Aboriginal businesses, organisations and communities across the Northern Territory to build economic strength and greater control over their futures. Our Strategic Investment Plan guides our work, supporting business growth, enabling community led development, building long-term wealth and expanding Aboriginal economic participation. Today, I will briefly outline our delivery, the practical benefits of the work and our priorities ahead. In 2025-26, Aboriginal Investment NT approved 110 grants, totalling $21.3 million. This included 72 business grants, worth $6.4 million, and 17 Community Impact and Innovation Grants, worth $14.6 million. Both programs exceeded their annual approval targets. These grants support commercial enterprise, cultural activity and community services. At Babbarra Women’s Centre in Maningrida, Aboriginal Investment NT funding supported a new nine-metre printing table through a Community Quick Response Grant. Installed in March, it enables artists to produce commercial lengths of fabric and enables several artists to work simultaneously, strengthening an enterprise grounded in Aboriginal women's skill and culture.

We continue to improve grant processing and support the completion and acquittal of earlier projects. Our Collective Impact Initiatives supports longer term community led development. The first two communities have been selected, with an in-principle allocation of $30 million. In August, we signed our first memorandum of understanding with AAAC for the work at Ginger Porter, or Santa Teresa. Community priorities and governance arrangements are being developed, with the next stage focused on project plans and funding approvals. A second expression of interest is underway. This gives communities a substantive role in setting priorities and shaping the projects we support.

Our nation-building investment activity has also progressed. Establishing the investment and compliance arrangements took longer than anticipated, delaying deployment in 2025-26. Five transactions, however, were approved in the first quarter of 2026-27, totalling approximately $10.5 million. These include finance for Maningrida Progress Association to expand motel accommodation, for Rirratjingu Aboriginal Corporation to support essential-worker housing in East Arnhem and for Tiwi Plantations to acquire forestry equipment. These opportunities show how capital can support Aboriginal business growth while addressing practical constraints on regional development. Our focus is on progressing approvals into funded projects and tracking the benefit as they are delivered.

Our commercial investment portfolio supports both current activity and long-term financial strength. In 2025-26, the Future Fund returned 6.6 per cent, and the Community Ready Fund returned 3.8 per cent. The Future Fund supports wealth for future generations, while the Community Ready Fund provides capital for our grants, community initiatives and investment activity here and now.

Looking ahead, we are strengthening our investment pipeline and working with organisations such as Indigenous Business Australia, Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation, the Australian National University's First Nations portfolio and the North Australian Infrastructure Facility to identify opportunities for complementary finance. We are also developing supplier finance opportunities to help Aboriginal businesses participate in major project supply chains led by Aboriginal Investment NT.

A compact for Aboriginal economic development aims to improve coordination between institutions, strengthen project readiness and connect Aboriginal-led proposals with expertise and capital. Each participating organisation retains its responsibilities and decision-making processes. Our next steps are to agree on practical coordination arrangements and identify initial opportunities for collaboration.

As delivery expands, we are strengthening our governance, organisational capability and measurement of outcomes. Our 2026 2030 corporate plan supports this through improvement to the data collection and a transitional step that strengthens current measures whilst establishing the foundations necessary to support more matured outcomes and impact reporting over time. This includes shifting our reporting from activities and outputs towards outcomes and impact, particularly how our funding contributes to employment, business growth, essential services and stronger Aboriginal organisations. The ANAO issued an unmodified audit opinion for our 2025-26 financial statements. These have been included in the Aboriginal Investment NT Annual Report, which was approved to be tabled on 26 October. Our priority is to put Aboriginal capital to work responsibly, build lasting Aboriginal assets, stronger businesses and greater economic independence. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Thank you very much, Mr Browne. Mr Knights, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text:
I do. I will be brief. Thank you for the opportunity to speak this morning. Firstly, I would like to acknowledge the Ngunnawal and Ngambri people and pay my respects to their elders. I extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today, and on behalf of IBA, we also extend our best wishes for the recovery of Helen Haines.

This has been a foundational year for implementing our IBA strategy towards 2030 and positioning us to respond to the growing demand for finance and investment across the First Nation's economy. Since releasing the strategy, we have seen significant interest from First Nations organisations seeking capital for larger and more complex projects. This highlights both the scale of the economic opportunity and the importance of addressing IBAs current capital constraints. We are working closely with government, including NIAA and the central agencies, to implement legislative reforms, finalise our borrowing rules and establish an appropriate borrowing framework.

Partnerships continue to be central to our approach. We have strengthened our relationships across government, the banking sector, global Indigenous capital partners and industry to increase the availability of culturally responsive finance and unlock the opportunities for First Nations businesses and communities. Our investment portfolio has grown to $578 million, with 49 per cent of it held alongside First Nations co-investors. This portfolio continues to perform strongly, delivering average returns of 7.2 per cent over five years and 9 per cent over three years. Last financial year we delivered $80 million in lending through our business finance activities. We also continued to invest in capability building, supporting entrepreneurs and businesses to grow, create jobs and participate in new economic opportunities. In response to changing economic and environmental conditions, we strengthened our hardship support measures to assist customers experiencing financial pressures. This ensured First Nations businesses had access to practical advice, tailored support and flexible repayment arrangements.

Demand for our homeownership program remains very strong. During the year we provided $349 million in home loans, supporting approximately 1,465 First Nations people into housing. This included $16 million in shared equity assistance for 90 families. Homeownership remains a cornerstone of IBA's purpose because it creates financial security and builds prosperity for generations of Indigenous families to come. It provides a platform for broader social and economic outcomes. We continue to deepen our understanding of intergenerational impact with our fifth impact report. This report focuses on the aspirations and experiences of First Nations young people and examines how we can better support their financial and economic aspirations. We will be launching the report later this week.

Our enabling legislation requires us to manage and grow a capital base for the benefit of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. I'm pleased to report that our total assets are now around $2.4 billion. Including revolving finance business products, IBA deployed $498 million to the Indigenous economy in 2026. Importantly, IBA continues to operate on a highly sustainable basis, funding 91 per cent of our operations through lending and investment activities. Across housing, business, investment and economic development, we continue to see strong ambition, capability and opportunity through the First Nations economy. Our focus is ensuring that IBA has the capital, capability and partnerships required to meet the opportunity and deliver long-lasting economic impact. I'm confident that the strategic foundations established over the past year position IBA strongly for the years ahead. We look forward to discussing our performance and priorities with the committee.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Thank you, Mr Knights. We will start with questions, and we'll start with Senator Sharma.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for your appearance here today. Can I start with you, Mr Browne. Can I understand the nature of your capitalisation? It was started with $680 million in 2022. I understand the Future Fund that you mentioned in your statement—is that a portion of the $680 million and how is that structured?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you for the question. The original corpus of $680 million makes up a $500 million Future Fund. The board was minded to be a bit guarded in how they invested in that total. But now they've divided it up into eight separate tranches.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The future fund's $500 million is divided into eight separate tranches?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: And now that's fully invested. That's now locked in for a 10-year period earning a return for the future prosperity of the Aboriginal Investment NT and the Aboriginal people of the Northern Territory. The remaining 180 goes towards the Community Ready Fund. That is the fund which essentially funds everything else from our grants, our smaller investments and our activity here and now.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: When was the Future Fund established? The $500 million fund.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The Future Fund was established in December 2024. And at that time, as Mr Browne said, we, the board, decided to invest in eight tranches over a two-year period. It's now fully invested as of September 2026. The $500 million is now invested in the Aboriginal Investment NT trust.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: So it was the board's decision to set up the Future Fund? I just want to understand that.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Correct. The Strategic Investment Plan was developed by the Aboriginal Investment NT board and tabled in parliament in August 2024. In that it lays out the establishment of the Future Fund for maintaining that funding for future generations of Aboriginal Territorians.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Minister, did you need to approve the creation of the Future Fund or was this just a board decision entirely?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Board decision.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: You said the $500 million is now fully invested in eight tranches. Could I just get on notice what those investments are? You don't need to provide it here in the room. I saw in your opening statement you said that that fund returned 6.6 per cent in 2025-26.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: That's correct.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: What's the target return rate for that fund?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The target return rate for that fund is CPI plus three per cent.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Do you have a time horizon on that fund as well? Was it 10 years?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: 10 years.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The decisions about what this fund was invested in, those are decisions taken by the board?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: We have an investment committee, a subcommittee of the Aboriginal Investment NT board, where the chair of that is one of our independent directors, and they're delegated to make the asset allocations and investment decisions.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Thank you. I don't want you to give me an entire breakdown, but what are some sample investments for that $500 million fund? In particular, I'm interested in privately owned Indigenous businesses that a fund would have invested in directly.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: We have a investment manager, JANA. We invest in multiple products that JANA investments holds, but we can definitely take that on notice to give you a breakdown of the different types of funds that are there.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: So you mainly direct through fund managers, then?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Correct.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Do you have something to add, Mr Tilly?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The Future Fund doesn't have any individual direct investments in underlying entities. It's all through other funds, as advised by JANA and the investment committee.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Have these other funds got a domestic mandate or a global mandate? Are they listed or unlisted?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: It's a combination of all—it's structured similarly to how a typical super fund would be structured. There's a combination of local and international equities, private markets, debt, private credit and commercial properties. It's a diversified portfolio invested in other funds, globally and locally.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Is there an investment strategy that's publicly available?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: There is an investment strategy.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: If you could provide that on notice, as well as the breakdowns, that would be helpful. I'll turn now to Indigenous Business Australia and Mr Knights. I'm conscious we're short of time, so I'll be quick about this. I understand that IBA has got a new capital raising model, which, I think, you touched on a little in your opening statement—talking about finalising borrowing rules and establishing an appropriate borrowing framework. What will be the maximum amount the IBA will be permitted to borrow under that new framework?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: We have an ambition that's on a page of our strategy. We have set up a risk appetite statement, which has been approved by our board. We do not intend to borrow out of line with normal financial institutions in terms of debt leverage ratios and so forth. We have a balance sheet, at the moment, with almost no liabilities, so we're at almost 100 per cent equity—

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: You said your total assets are $2.4 billion?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Yes. To give you a perspective, the main banking system runs on a circa 93 or 94 per cent liability-to-asset ratio, with tier 1 equity at about 6 per cent. We'll be running under that, and we'll be under strict management and controls, not only by the IBA board but by the central departments as well.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Okay. What will govern that? Who will put in place the investment rules?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The investment rules or borrowing rules?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Investment rules and borrowing rules. Have those been settled yet?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The borrowing rules haven't been settled yet, but they will be given to IBA via the centrals. In fact, they're being drafted in OPC at the moment. We understand that that process is well advanced. Those rules will then be tabled in parliament early next year for a period of 15 days. We need to comply with those rules. In terms of our investment rules and policies, they will be governed by the IBA board.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Have those investment rules and policies been developed yet?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: They are all being drafted in parallel. As I said, we've got the risk appetite statement, and we're now working through all of those appropriate covenants.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I understand you've said—I don't know if this was in your opening statement, so it might be somewhere else—that you intend to mobilise between $5 billion and $7 billion over five years. Have I got that right?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: That is our strategic ambition, but that is through a blended finance arrangement. Our intent is very similar to all the specialist investment vehicles. As a government CCE, it's our job to catalyse the investment and crowd in private and corporate investment into projects. Going forward, we'll also be looking at our contribution in a blended investment approach. As Nigel said earlier, we're working with other Indigenous portfolio agencies to collaborate around those opportunities.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I know this figure hasn't been settled yet, but, roughly speaking, how much of that $5 billion to $7 billion will consist of debt borrowed by the IBA, do you think?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I'll need to take that on notice—the end shape—and we can come back on the modelling on it, because it's a combination of debt and equity in terms of financing.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Yes, of course, but is it $1 billion to $2 billion or more or less?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: It would be around that vicinity, yes.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I just wanted a ballpark figure. That's fine.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: To give you perspective, if you look at the other specialist investment vehicles, they run at a ratio of about 25 per cent of the total blended investment.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Being debt?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Yes. It's either debt or equity, but that's the government funded component.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Would you do the debt through a bond? What's the intent there?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: That will be dictated by the borrowing rules, but, most likely, we would be taking similar types of instruments that the specialist investment vehicles would most likely do. In fact, we may end up laterally borrowing from within government to ensure that the overall government debt is minimised.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: And then your security for that debt will be the asset base that you've got?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Correct.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I'm just trying to understand—is any of your debt going to be government-backed debt or is it going to be backed by the assets of the IBA?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: It'll be backed by the asset base of IBA.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Not by the government?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: No. To my knowledge, we are not in a position to get a government guarantee.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: If I could just go back briefly to Aboriginal Investment, if you don't mind, what's the long-term vision, Mr Browne, of Aboriginal Investment? You've got the Future Fund, and you've got the community fund. Is that right?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Community Ready Fund.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: The Future Fund is designed to preserve capital and provide a steady stream of income. You said the Community Ready Fund provides grants as well. Obviously, that will deplete it over time. Is it intended that that will be topped up by growth from the Future Fund?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text:
It will be growth from the Future Fund but also from other investments that we make. In terms of the overall vision, the way that I explain it to people that come and work for AINT is that we're reinjecting equity into Aboriginal communities across the Northern Territory that, for a very long time, have not had that opportunity, like a lot of other communities. That's the very basic model. We are working not only to the mandate that we have in relation to self-sufficiency and self-management, which are fairly dry descriptors, but we're also wanting to build—or help build, rather—Aboriginal-led infrastructure and other projects that help communities self-determine whatever they choose to.

The Collective Impact grant is the largest grant that we now have. We've got two communities that we're working with at the moment and the EOI are out for the other two now. They're really, I suppose, the pinnacle of what we're trying to achieve in terms of working with communities on community led projects or whatever it may be, over a number of years, to allow them to create their own opportunities, their own business models and their own industries to, hopefully, one day get to the point where there's no distinction between a remote Aboriginal community and Bendigo or another regional town somewhere, where people have no barriers in front of them to be able to live life as they determine it.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Have you got any specific investments in the Community Ready Fund, or grants, that you hold out as a showpiece for the fund and what it can achieve?

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: It's very early days for the Collective Impact grants. Santa Teresa, or Ltyentye Apurte, in the central region, and Marthakal Homelands, in the Top End, are the first two cabs off the rank, so to speak. They're still very much in the planning stages. In relation to our Community Impact and Innovation Grants, there are a number of different projects across the Territory that we have backed. They're in relation to a range of different things—aquaculture being one of them, agriculture. We're looking into the mining and resource sector, which is another reason we also established an MOU with Tivan recently, and we're looking to establish partnerships with other resource and rare earth mining operations in the Territory. In a lot of places, those commercial projects are the only options for remote areas, so we're wanting to try to not only look at the financial side but also help Aboriginal businesses win contracts and engage in their own economic activity.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: I saw you mentioned in your opening statement helping Aboriginal businesses participate in major project supply chains. In the interest of time, I'm happy to leave it there. Thanks for your time and appearance today.

agency: Aboriginal Investment NT Indigenous Business Australia
text: Thank you so much for appearing this morning. It's always really fascinating to hear where you're up to with the really, really important work that you're doing, so thank you so much. We do really appreciate your time.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Welcome, Ms Stroud and Mr Borg. Ms Stroud, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Good morning. I do have an opening statement that I've tabled. For the sake of time, I'll take it as read.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Okay, entirely up to you. Mr Borg, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Good morning, Chair. We also have tabled our opening statement already. We're happy to take questions this morning with it already tabled.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Okay, no worries. We're happy if you wanted to give us highlights but also happy we do have them in front of us. Senator Sharma.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I haven't read your opening statement yet, so please forgive me if I ask some things that are in there, but feel free to refer it to me. I was interested to discuss the Low-cost Essentials Subsidy scheme. Under that scheme, as I understand it, Outback Stores operates as a retailer as well as a wholesaler. Would someone just help enlighten me a little bit there. Is that you, Mr Borg?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes, we're a service provider that provides services for remote communities from a retail environment, but over the last year we have been working on improved ways to procure goods to service remote communities, not only for the subsidy scheme but for Outback Stores in general. We service 60 stores across the Northern Territory and Western Australia, a couple in South Australia, one in North Queensland and two in New South Wales. We've been working for some time on real ways to impact and improve affordability in communities, noting that traditionally we've been focused on food security, good governance and good retail standards. Post COVID we've seen a wave of inflationary pressures, as we continue to see, and an important part of our strategic direction is to focus heavily on affordability. A large piece of that work was to work on how to open up some supply chain avenues to procure goods at a cheaper cost.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: So you provide you said 60 stores across a number of states. Is that right?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That's correct, the Outback Stores.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: You provide them with the essential categories of goods? I think there's like 30. Are they the household and retail products that you provide them with.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes. I'll provide a bit of detail for you on the subsidy scheme. The subsidy scheme is an excellent initiative by the federal government, which has allowed remote community stores—and I think there are 128 currently listed—to be able to access products to sell for the same prices that corporate retailers, like Coles and Woolworths. Outback Stores is the enabler and was given the task, as a Commonwealth entity, to ensure there's strong governance around the program and to deliver the program over a three to five year period. We, on top of the work we're doing for our own stores, also supply these goods to remote community stores who are participating in the program. We've seen significant benefits around the reduction of sell prices across most of the remote community stores in the north of the country.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I noticed in the post-implementation review that the ACCC expressed some concerns about the scheme. They said they had concerns that it had the effect of reducing the scale and efficiency of grocery distribution to remote communities, which in turn impacts the price, quality and product range of groceries supplied to remote communities that are not included in the scheme. What's your response to the analysis of that ACCC concern?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: There are probably a couple of things there to talk through. Firstly, the government had been exceptional in their controls and governance of the program to ensure that it doesn't expand where it's going to impact other wholesalers across the country, which I thought was a good framework for the government to put in place. There are certainly different views from different wholesalers in relation to the program. They've shared some of those views with the ACCC. But in general—

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: When you say different views, Mr Borg, it sounds a little euphemistic. Do you mean that they're not supportive of the scheme?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Well, wholesalers have probably lost some volume out of their own system, so there may be a level of frustration from their own commercial benefits. I think what's important here is to remember that remote communities are, from a retail point of view, are very disadvantaged, and any work that can be done to assist in this space should be done, like it has been. Then we probably should put to one side the commercial impacts to multinational companies around the country.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'm just wondering, Mr Borg, maybe you've done some work on this, but if you're a competing wholesaler, and you're no longer competitive in the 30 subsidised product lines that Outback Stores is delivering, don't you then just push up your prices in the other categories of goods to protect your margin? Is it not the situation where you have consumers going to a store, and they might be paying less for some things like the 30 subsidised categories of goods, but they're paying more for the other stuff that you don't provide. Have you done any analysis of whether this is having a diversionary impact, rather than a beneficial impact?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: No, that's definitely not the case. The way the scheme is set up is that the products that are listed on the subsidy scheme meet a general practice of a 35 per cent gross profit. The share of the 30 products might be 15 per cent roughly of the retail sales, so it's not like it's a significant amount of volume being taken away from other wholesalers or other components of the market. I can talk for Outback stores. We're aggressively chasing improved cost of goods to continually drive down lines outside of the subsidy scheme as well. We've got a couple of other programs in place at Outback Stores where value and affordability are absolutely our focus. Holding a generalised gross profit return to stores and consistency are also key. Certainly, there's no evidence of anyone putting up prices to offset the subsidy scheme or to make more money. I think the lines that rely on this subsidy scheme return a fairly healthy gross profit for stores for them not to have to worry about playing with margins and other products.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Outback Stores has 60 retail outlets in remote areas, right?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: We don't own any retail outlets. We're a service provider, and we partner with Aboriginal corporations. Of them, most need some support from a retail point of view, a lot of them from a commercial point of view, and/or governance.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: But, under the scheme itself, you've also got responsibility for running the wholesaler or distribution aspect for a larger number of stores. Is that right?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Just so we're clear, we execute the program for the subsidy scheme for the federal government. We've had funding aligned to us and a set of obligations that we need to deliver, and we manage the scheme on behalf of the Commonwealth government as well as service our own stores for other products.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I see. Putting your own stores to one side, how many other stores are you supplying or administering the scheme for?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The scheme has 128 stores aligned to it at the moment, which is exceptional, Senator.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Does that include your 60 or not include your 60?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That includes our 60.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Does that mean that about half of the stores in those categories are not participating? Is that right?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'll share some more information with you, Senator. There are probably about 150 to 160 rural retail stores in remote communities across our country. Most stores are signed up to the scheme, which is excellent. There is certainly some more work to be done with some homelands and smaller stores to bring them online to the scheme, which I think will occur over the coming months. But, in general, there are three large groups that manage community stores: Outback Stores; ALPA, who work closely up in Arnhem Land; and another company called CEQ, across in North Queensland. Really, those three companies are the base of the majority of remote community stores across the country. As I said before, the 128 stores in total are aligned currently to the scheme.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'm not entirely sure where this figure is from, but I thought the independent review said that, of 88 eligible independent stores—maybe that's a subcategory—only 15 are participating in the scheme. Is that correct?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I think it's maybe 17 now, and mostly they're larger stores. There are some independent stores that haven't signed up for the scheme. Just to be clear: there's a fair list of requirements to be able to get onto the scheme. Once again, the government have done a good job of setting up the scheme to ensure strong governance. There are some social and some commercial requirements that you need to meet to even be able to apply for the scheme. It's not like everyone can just get on the scheme, apply to Outback Stores and get delivered stock.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Give me a situation where a store would not be eligible to participate in the scheme. What would it have failed to meet in terms of your requirements? What are some of the requirements that these stores that aren't participating have not been able to meet?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: It's probably a question for NIAA. They developed the scheme, but I—

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Sorry, Mr Borg. I can jump in there, if you like, to assist. We don't have NIAA at the table, but I can give some assistance. Thank you, Senator Sharma, for the question. These stores are remote stores. One of the difficulties that we've certainly found is that stores who are in regional areas have wanted to sign up, but we've focused specifically on the remote for now. We're hoping to roll out to at least 150 stores. But it's completely voluntary, and those stores can put their hands up for applying to the scheme with NIAA. So far, my understanding is there are around 120 stores that have signed up so that there could be those 30 essential items that are at 50 per cent of the price in the nearest Woolies or Coles in whatever region or city is closest to them.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Minister—because my colleagues have—have you had independent retailers and wholesalers come to you or your office and say they're being squeezed out of the market because of this scheme?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: There certainly has been an issue raised in Central Australia. We had a review conducted—that review is now available—so that I could understand what some of the issues are and have that with me. This is the first time we've ever done a policy like this, so it's all completely new, so of course there will be things that we have to learn throughout the process. It was important at the outset, Senator, that I had the ACCC give guidance as to how we rolled this policy out, conscious of the competitive nature of the business and conscious that there are businesses who are there to make a profit. But the call from communities was that they needed these stores to be cheaper, and that's why we've rolled this policy out.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'm unclear—the review. Is that the review done by Yaran Business Services, as on the NIAA website?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That's correct.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Will the government be providing a response to that independent review? Obviously, there are a number of—I think, eight—key challenges it outlined.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Sure. We've accepted all eight recommendations, and we're committed to strengthening the delivery of this scheme.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Thanks, Minister. I'm happy to cede the call, Chair.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Senator Thorpe.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Thank you for appearing today. I have lots of questions—firstly, ATLA. ATLA has been under special administration since 26 March 2020. It's a long time. I believe that it's now the longest special administration ever conducted under the C(ATSI) Act. Is that correct?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes, Senator, I can confirm that the ATLA special administration is to date the longest special administration under the C(ATSI) Act.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: What specific problems identified with ATLA that placed it in administration in March 2020 remain unresolved today?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: There are a number of outstanding matters that remain with ATLA which, unfortunately, are largely caused by an ongoing legal dispute between ATLA, as the native title body for Adnyamathanha common-law holders, and its trustee, which is Rangelea Holdings Pty Ltd. We have a commitment under special administration to return a corporation back to member control when it has strong, sustainable governance and financial security and where there are no administrative, legal or financial burdens on the corporation. It is my view that to hand ATLA back to members and to common-law holders with a lengthy and complex legal battle afoot would be unethical and irresponsible—to leave a corporation with that burden.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: You said that it's important to have strong governance structures before handing it back. Did the examination that led to special administration identify fraud, theft, misappropriation of funds or criminal wrongdoing by ATLA directors?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The examination found significant serious and systemic breaches of the CATSI Act and the corporation's rule book, many of those governance failings, but fundamentally the greatest failing of the corporation was its financial management practices. As to whether there were criminal matters found, the most I can say is that the fact that there has been no ORIC investigation and criminal prosecution or civil prosecution would tell you that there was not sufficient evidence to meet a threshold to pursue prosecution of individuals. But the fact that the corporation did end in special administration largely because of its financial management practices and that that's on the public register tells the public that the manner in which the board at the time, the directors at the time, were managing the finances of the corporation was poor and there was a significant failing in directors' duties.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: What measurable criteria must ATLA satisfy before the registrar would return the corporation to its members? Surely after six years matters should be able to be resolved. I mean, how much does the administrator cost? Over six years, who's paying for that?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text:
ORIC is paying for the special administrator. I'd have to take on notice how much the total cost of that is. I think it would be important to lay out that during special administration it's my practice to attend the corporation AGMs and information meetings. The next one will be towards the end of November. With the ATLA AGMs, I and my colleagues and the special administrator ensure that someone is at each of the three locations that members attend. It is quite common for me to receive requests and be approached at AGMs with a request to maintain special administration until the legal matter is resolved. There is evidence of general fear amongst the members and the broader common law holder group that if the legal matters which go to the common law holders' rights to transparency and accountability of how their native title money is spent—until that matter is resolved and the outcome achieved for common law holders, there is genuine fear amongst the ATLA members that ORIC would be, in their words, abandoning them by ending special administration.

The other point that I think is probably important to outlay is that, while it's not required under the CATSI Act, it is our practice to establish what we call a corporation advisory group, which, for want of a better term, is a quasi-board. Adnyamathanha people have members on the corporation advisory group. The special administrator engages regularly and conducts those advisory group meetings as if they were a board. They are heavily consulted and, at the same time, building their knowledge and skills to become the incoming board when the corporation is returned to members.

We're hopeful that by the end of this year, from the inspector that was appointed by the courts, the final inspector's reports into the Rangelea Holdings Pty Ltd accounts and how Adnyamathanha native title moneys have been distributed over the years will be made public. Once that's made public, common law holders will have a meeting. They will make their own decision as to whether Rangelea has been responsible or otherwise in the management and distribution of their native title money. Once that is dealt with and common law holders have made their own informed decision and the legal matter is dealt with, we think it would be responsible to hand the corporation back to the members then.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: A bit of mission management here, I think. If we talk about self-determination, six years under mission management flies in the face of self-determination. How many native title decisions have been made by or through ATLA since the elected board was removed in March 2020?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'd have to take that on notice, but it's important to note that, whether the corporation is under member control with a board of directors or under special administration, the native title requirements under the PBC regs remain. The special administrator acts as the board, but he is still bound by the same native title requirements to consult and get native title consent for any native title decisions. I'd have to take on notice how many decisions have been made.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That would be great, thank you. If you don't know how many decisions this mission manager is making on behalf of the people whose land it is, are there any decisions—I've been told there have been—that are related to mining, exploration, uranium mining, heritage, land access agreements, ILUAs, compensation or other development proposals? How much are they trying to suck out of the people and the land and the resources in the six years that they've been there, basically, is my question.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I know that there have been native title meetings held. Again, I can assure the committee that the special administrator is bound by the same requirements as a board would be in terms of proper consultation and the securing of consent from common law holders before any native title decisions are made. I think the fact that a special administrator really just replaces directors but is bound by the same level of member engagement and common law holder engagement would probably put us at odds in terms of our definition of a special administrator. I don't think we or the many Adnyamathanha people that have asked us to stay there and need our support would describe that special administrator as a mission manager.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Well, I have different mob talking to me from there. I'm hearing different, and I'm hearing that common law holders have not been consulted or required to consent to any of the native title decisions made in the last six years. I understand administrators. I know all about them: how they fly in, control the community, make their money and then fly out. They don't consult. They don't do the right thing. Lake Tyers Mission had an administrator. They didn't talk to no-one. So, whilst they've got rules, they don't abide by them. Can you explain how all of these people that have come to me have not had FPIC applied or even spoken about as common law holders?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I would, again, have to take on notice how many native title meetings and consultations have been held. I can't answer as to people that are aggrieved that they haven't been consulted. The only thing I would add is that, of the reports of concern that ORIC receives generally, across corporations, a significant number of those are related to native title matters. It is not uncommon in native title space, whether a PBC is member controlled or under special administration, for ORIC to receive complaints from common law holders that they are not being consulted or engaged or that a native title decision has been made not to their liking. They're not matters regulated under the CATSI Act. If common law holders are aggrieved about a native title decision or a native title process, regardless of whether the corporation is in special admin or not, they're native title matters that they would need to take to the Native Title Tribunal.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Are you responsible for the administrator?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I appoint the special administrator. We set out terms of—
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Who's in charge of the administrator?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I appoint the special administrator. He sets out terms and references, but the expectation is that they are independent. They are engaged as the board, if you like, and their sole responsibility is the interests of the corporation. They're not directed or influenced by ORIC.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Has ORIC ever audited ATLA's consultation in decision-making processes during special administration to determine whether they provide genuine informed consent?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: No, because I wouldn't do that for a PBC not in special administration, either. Again, they're native title matters.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: If the administrator is not talking to the mob about doing a dirty deal with a mining company—if they haven't consulted at all—then that's not your problem. He's your administrator, but it's not your problem because he's independent. What do you do when they're not doing the job properly?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'd have to take that on notice, but I am not aware of one native title complaint we've received regarding ATLA. If I was to receive a complaint about a native title matter with ATLA, largely, it would not be a matter that I would regulate. The aggrieved native title holder would be directed to the National Native Title Tribunal. But, yes, in terms of the quality, integrity and performance of a special administrator, naturally, I would ask the special administrator to provide advice about their native title processes. I'd have to take that on notice, but given the fact I haven't asked the special administrator that, I would be fairly confident that we've not received a native title complaint from a native title holder.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: They're coming to me, so there's clearly a problem. What person or body can independently examine the merits of the continuing decision to keep ATLA under special administration?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Special administration is a reviewable decision. That means that, under the CATSI Act, an interested party can seek a review of a decision to appoint a special administrator or seek a registrar review or an internal review. If they're not happy with that, they can seek a review at the Administrative Review Tribunal, and, if they're unhappy with that, they can, naturally, seek a judicial review. We have, over the times, received internal reviews of the decisions to extend the special administrator. I'd have to take that on notice, but I'm happy to give you a brief on which special administration decisions relating to appointment and extensions have been subject to a review.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Is the continuation or repeated extension of a special administration subject to mandatory independent merits review?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Sorry, I missed that?
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: This person's obviously on a gravy train here—six years in a community being the mission manager. Is the continuation or repeated extension of a special administration subject to mandatory independent merits review?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: In terms of who the special administrator is?
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: No. Obviously, someone's making a decision: 'Oh, yes. Stay there for another year. You're right. The mining companies are happy. Everyone's happy.' Is the making of those constant extensions subject to a mandatory independent merits review?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text:
Yes. As I laid out, the appointment of a special administrator and the extension of a special administrator are reviewable decisions. The last time that ATLA's special administration was extended, any interested party could have sought an internal review or an Administrative Review Tribunal review or, if they really wanted, a judicial review, which they didn't.

In addition to that, ORIC has a complaints handling policy. Members and interested parties of a corporation in special administration can lodge complaints about a special administrator. And then, I guess, above all, that is a complaint to the ombudsman. If there is a complaint about the special administrator, that can be lodged with me. There are no active complaints or recent complaints about the ATLA special administrator. If people are aggrieved that special administration was extended, they had a period of time after the extension. They could have sought a review. They didn't do that. There is also the avenue that if people are aggrieved about a native title decision or action taken by ATLA, they could instigate a process with the national native tribunal, which I'm not aware of any. I'm mindful that the special administrator's engagement with members and native title holders is done with the advice, the guidance and in support of the community advisory group, which is made up of Adnyamathanha representatives.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Do I need to share because I've got another topic? I want to ask about the Noongar Charitable Trust misuse.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Please go right ahead.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: In 2023, the Noongar Charitable Trust was referred by the WA ombudsman to the Charitable Trusts Commission and found that Equity Trustees breached its duties as trustee of the Noongar Charitable Trust. The trustees owed to the Noongar people the obligation of examining a proposal to purchase several properties in some depth. But this obligation was not met. The loss and damage to the Noongar people is estimated at $22 million. Throughout the commission's investigation, various concerns have been raised by community members and on information at hand about the conduct of current and former office holders of the South West Aboriginal Land and Sea Council, which established the trust. The commission referred these matters to ORIC for investigation. This was over a year ago, and we haven't heard anything from ORIC. Has ORIC concluded its investigation?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: People don't usually hear of an outcome or action taken by ORIC until it is placed on the public register and that is important to maintain the integrity of our regulatory considerations or an investigation. I can confirm that on 13 August 2025, the commission referred certain information to my office for consideration. This was the referral that was publicly disclosed. I acknowledged receipt of that the following day. We undertook an assessment of the report referred to us and based on the limited information in that report determined that there was no further action required under the C(ATSI) Act. But we did seek additional information from the Western Australian Charitable Trusts Commission. To this date we have not received any further information from the commission that would give us reason to further assess and determine if there are matters they identified that fall in the remit of the C(ATSI) Act. But we remain open to any further information that they might have.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: How come there's no investigation? The Charitable Trusts Commission specifically stated in its report in August last year that it was referring the matter to ORIC given that information obtained during its investigation warranted a proactive referral to ORIC.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Again, the information provided was vague. There was no detailed specific information or evidence that would give us sufficient information to assess whether it warranted an investigation. Again, we've provided an invitation to provide us with further information. If I am completely honest with this committee, the public notice that a referral has been made to ORIC with a vague description that there are matters that might fall within ORIC's remit is not the manner in which we conduct referrals. We would neither make a public announcement nor make an assumption that matters fall into another regulator's remit. The matters raised didn't fall within our remit, and there was not enough evidence for us to even make an assessment as to whether the matter would be investigated. At the moment, it is on the charitable trust to provide that information so that we might make a determination as to whether it warrants a formal investigation.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The commission's investigation showed various concerns have been raised by community members about the conduct of current and former office holders of SWALSC. SWALSC is regulated by you. Do you agree that, as the regulator, it is your role to ensure that corporations registered under the C(ATSI) Act comply with the law?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I do agree. It is my responsibility to investigate director duties that go to breaches of the C(ATSI) Act, but, to do so, I need sufficient information or evidence to make grounds for an investigation, noting that an investigation is undertaken where there is enough evidence to provide a likely acceptance of a referral by CDPP—that it meets the CDPP prosecution policy—and that there are chances of a successful prosecution. Even if we receive enough information and enough evidence to warrant an investigation, there is still not always a guarantee that an investigation will result in the evidence brief being accepted by CDPP and a successful prosecution. Again, that is for offences under the C(ATSI) Act. The referral from the charitable commission lacked enough information or evidence to even give us grounds for an investigation.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: In Mount Isa, given our people were kicked out of their homes and no-one came to their aid—elders with disabilities and 15 families—a developer went in and bought 12 of those homes. So, for those families, thanks for nothing. Under section 487-5 of the C(ATSI) Act, you, as a registrar for ORIC, can place a corporation under administration if a corporation has failed to comply with the C(ATSI) Act, failed to comply with internal governance or failed to comply with reporting obligations. Do you agree that each of these applied in the first half of this year in the case of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders Corporation for Welfare Services?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I do agree that those grounds were met in order to appoint a special administrator. However, the reason a special administrator wasn't appointed to the corporation this year, noting that the corporation had previously been in special administration, was that the corporation was, or was very likely to be, insolvent. Directors of corporations carry duties to not trade while insolvent. They also carry legal obligations and liabilities for trading whilst insolvent or conducting business activities that might be considered creditor-defeating. When a special administrator is appointed, that person, as I set out before, replaces the board. They then carry the same director responsibilities and liabilities—
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I know. We went through that before.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: so a special administrator, in this instance, would have been appointed to a corporation that was, or was very likely to be, insolvent and would have then carried those duties. A special administrator would have then been required to apply to the courts to have the corporation wound up and a liquidator appointed, which is what I myself have done. A perception out there in the community or hope, at the time, that a special administrator would have prevented the sale of the properties is not the case. A special administrator does not suppress creditors' rights. It does not suppress the statutory rights of the council to sell those properties. So the properties would have still been sold even with a special administrator appointed.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Really?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Even though there was $600,000 of rates overdue because the dodgy corporation didn't pay it, you're saying to me that having an administrator appointed wouldn't have sorted that out way back then, and we got to a situation where people are homeless.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The debt on the houses was in the vicinity of $1 million, and it was already—
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Initially it was, but it wasn't in the end, because I checked with the Mount Isa Council myself and I have a letter. They said that, if the rates were paid, people could stay. I even asked the Brisbane Broncos for the money.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The council's correct. If the rates had been paid, the houses wouldn't have been sold. But I wouldn't describe the corporation as dodgy. But most certainly the corporation failed its tenants. Regulatory—
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The person running it was very unwell and doing the wrong thing with the money. Let's face it.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'm sorry?
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The person running it was doing the wrong thing with the money because they were not well. So, that's dodgy, when you're using the money for your own purposes and not paying the rates.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That's a separate matter, and I'm not at liberty to talk about that specific matter today. Essentially, a corporation has been abandoned by its members and its directors, and, in doing so, has failed those people that it serves. There's the matter of the outstanding rates. The only way that those houses were not going to be sold was for the rates to be paid. The corporation at the time the growing rates debt became known by my office and others had $8,000 in the bank. The corporation itself had no capacity to pay those debts. The CATSI Act is not—well, actually, no corporate regulatory framework is designed so that a corporate regulator assumes responsibility for debts that a corporation has incurred.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: That's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that, if ORIC had have intervened earlier, when the red flags were waving at you, it could have gone in then and saved 15 homes for our people. But that didn't happen in this case, did it?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: No. I think that my view and my application of the CATSI Act would differ to that public narrative that ORIC could have prevented this. ORIC became aware of this situation when the council alerted people in March that it was going to sell properties. Despite the public narrative that ORIC was advised and knew of the red flags, I can confirm that from 2019 until 2026 ORIC received one phone call about the corporation, and that was an anonymous phone call about a matter that was not within the CATSI Act remit. So, unfortunately, like many others, ORIC didn't become aware of this debt until March. And, again, I would assert that, by that time, there was nothing that the special administrator could have done to have prevented the sale of those properties, because the special administrator would have been dealing with an insolvent corporation. The corporation didn't have the money to pay the debts.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes. I get that.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The only way the council was going to stop the sales was with the debt paid.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes, I said that before.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
