text: The CATSI Act does not suppress the council's right to sell those assets. So, without $1 million, the special administrator would have had no way of keeping the corporation solvent and preventing the sale of the houses.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: You're skiting up the special administrator that you put into the last community and couldn't put one in here. Aren't the special administrators big-shot accountants that come from big accounting firms and know how to just fix stuff? Isn't that what their role is?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The difference between Mount Isa and ATLA is that ATLA wasn't insolvent when a special administrator was appointed. As skilled, committed and professional as a special administrator might be, they, like directors, carry legal obligations around trading insolvency.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes, I get that. I know that—

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: A special administrator was not going to be appointed and be able to change the fact that the corporation was insolvent or very likely to be insolvent.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Did you take them to court last year for failure of governance and lack of reporting?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes. They were prosecuted for failing to lodge their annual reports.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Were there red flags for you then—that 15 houses were about to be taken again from our people? Did you go into that level?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Certainly, there were concerns with the corporation—the fact that it hadn't been lodging its reports and had been prosecuted—but, noting that, even if the corporation had been lodging its annual reports, the corporation is not required to report to ORIC about its tenancy management services nor about the state of its houses. The CATSI Act and ORIC do not regulate tenancy management.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I have one last question. It's really disappointing to hear this, because you've got the minister, you've got ORIC, and you've got all these deadly departments in NIAA, and you couldn't all just get together to save 15 homes for our people. You couldn't do that. And it was less than a million dollars. It was more like $600. No doubt there were a number of people or agencies who could have taken some action to avoid the loss of homes under the management of this corporation. Can you suggest any better place than you to have taken action earlier this year? With all the departments that you work with, couldn't you have done anything?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: The unfortunate and sad circumstances here go to the heart of corporations registered under the CATSI Act. The corporation is member controlled. Unfortunately, in this instance, members and directors who carry obligations as well as rights failed the corporation. They abandoned the corporation, and, as a result, those people served by the corporation were abandoned.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Yes, 15 families were abandoned, and some could be still homeless. So well done guys. Well done. I'm handing over.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: We'll go to Senator Collins.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text:
I want to read from the ANAO report that was handed down in June. They said:

Compliance with annual reporting—a key requirement under the CATSI Act—is declining for small, medium and large-sized corporations and was less than 30 per cent overall for 2024-25 financial year. To some extent, this is attributed to a decision not to deregister non-compliant and disengaged corporations that hold assets because this is resource intensive.

The ANAO is saying that compliance is poor, and that's been made worse by your enforcement approach. Do you think that's appropriate for a regulator?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Thank you for the question. The compliance rates that were cited by the ANAO and the concerns are ones that we share also. Just recently we deregistered 494 corporations, and 469 of those were small corporations. There are an additional 162 corporations that have avoided deregistration for the time being but have been referred for other regulatory action. Those corporations are corporations that hold assets. There are a number of reasons why we don't deregister corporations that hold assets as quickly as we do others. And, yes, one is because of the resource-intensive nature of managing those properties that are then vested with the registrar when a corporation is deregistered. But the other probably goes to some of the points I just made earlier; regulatory action does not remove debt incurred by corporations. If a corporation with assets is deregistered, the debts and the costs on those assets are still incurred. The CATSI Act does not require that ORIC pays those debts and those holding costs. Often it is not just a resource-intensive exercise; it is also not in the best interests in terms of retaining assets of those corporations. That's why we will exhaust absolutely every other avenue before deregistering those corporations. And, as I said, there are 169 of those currently on our caseload to work through.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Okay. The ANAO said this about the effects. Just give me a sense—how many corporations are we talking about, here? You said 494 had been deregistered, and you're looking at 162. How many more corporations are there?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Following the deregistration of the 494, there are now 2,956 corporations registered under the CATSI Act; 162 of those are in the deferred deregistration caseload, if you like, because they're corporations that, if not for having assets, would be automatically deregistered.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text:
The ANAO said this about the effects of your decision:

Non-compliance with annual reporting impedes ORIC's ability to use data to understand the drivers of non-compliance. Due to a lack of evaluation, ORIC does not have a full understanding of the drivers of and harm caused by non-compliance. Without this full understanding, ORIC cannot be certain planned regulatory activity is responding to the greatest risks and harms.

In effect, they're saying that, because of your decision about these, you don't know why Indigenous corporations aren't complying, and you don't know what harm this is causing. You don't know whether you're being effective as a regulator. Would you assess that as a fair summary?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: They're two separate matters, in terms of the findings of the ANAO. But you're correct; the ANAO did make a conclusion that we don't conduct an evaluation of corporations that are not lodging reports and that we don't undertake an assessment as to the drivers for why corporations don't lodge reports. Roughly 75 per cent of corporations that haven't lodged reports are small corporations, so they're corporations with under $100,000 consolidated income and assets and are under five staff. We haven't done an evaluation. We have agreed to the recommendation of the ANAO audit report to conduct an evaluation program. But I think it would be reasonable to assume that non-reporting for small corporations with under $100,000 and few if any staff is largely down to capability and capacity. But I have no doubt there is a level of apathy. We have recently built into our system prepopulated general reports, remembering that small corporations that are the bulk of the non-compliant are only required to lodge a general report. We've now introduced prepopulation. We've been conducting online workshops for people to step them through and help them do general reports, and we hope to see an uplift in that. But, yes, the audit report is correct. We don't do a formal evaluation program, but we will commence one having accepted that recommendation.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Senator Collins, how are you going here? Your colleague has advised me that you guys had one question. I'm just trying to manage our time and our next witnesses. How much longer do you think you need with these witnesses?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I could just round it off with one final question—so that I can get a bit of clarity. You decided not to stop enforcing government standards by deregistering non-compliant, disengaged Indigenous corporations. The ANAO report has been handed down, but you haven't reversed that decision. Instead, you are taking a recommendation to conduct evaluation. Why have you not reversed the decision and instead are going down the evaluation path? That's how I understand it.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text:
Not deregistering a corporation for failing to lodge reports doesn't mean that the responsibilities on the corporations have been forgiven, if you like. Even those 169 corporations are still required to lodge reports. They still have other regulatory action that could be taken, including prosecution. But, yes, the automatic deregistration of those is something that we've not shifted to, but it has certainly not been ruled out, and it will be considered after we have exhausted all other avenues to get those 169 corporations compliant.

The other ground for deregistering a corporation is that the corporation is, in our view, not conducting business. Not lodging annual reports is only one ground for the deregistration of a corporation. They must have also not lodged anything with ORIC in an 18-month period and also, in our view, not be conducting business—not be contactable, not be responsive to anything.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: You mentioned prosecutions there as a potential avenue. At what point do you refer corporations to be prosecuted, and how often would you do that?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: We resumed the prosecution of corporations for failing to lodge reports in 2023. Our practice is to do that when they have outstanding reports for two years. We had been not referring small corporations for prosecution, noting that they have minimal funds and typically don't get government funding—so in terms of the public interest factor. But we have made a public statement that we now will consider referring small corporations for prosecution for failing to lodge reports.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Does that public statement have the threshold under which you would refer for prosecution?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I'd have to take on notice whether our website and public information explicitly says two years.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: But a threshold is established?

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: I would have to take that on notice. That's an internal policy—two years. Under the CATSI Act we could prosecute sooner than that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations
witness_position: Registrar of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Corporations

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Thank you very much. Thank you for your time.

agency: Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations Outback Stores Pty Ltd
text: Thank you so much for your time, to the Outback Stores and to ORIC. We appreciate you spending time with us this morning and answering our questions. We will now let you go. As people may notice, we are running a little bit behind. We will go directly to our next session, which is the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation and the Office of Township Leasing.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text:
We have limited questions for these two witnesses because a couple of the key senators who requested you, unfortunately, due to other circumstances, are not able to attend this morning. So it will be a short session, but please don't interpret that as any less interest in your work at all.

Welcome, Mr Morrison from the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation, and from the Office of Township Leasing we have Mr Beven. Would either of you like to make an opening statement? We'll start with Mr Beven.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: I do not, Chair, but I'd like to acknowledge the traditional owners on the land we're meeting on and particularly pay respect to the traditional owners we work with in the Northern Territory, particularly where our township leases are on the Tiwi Islands and in Mutitjulu in Central Australia.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Thank you very much. Mr Morrison, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: I do not, Chair, but, again, I would like to acknowledge the traditional owners of the land and waters that this meeting is taking place on.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Lovely. Thank you so much. We will go directly to questions, and we'll go to Senator Sharma.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Good morning. Thank you for joining us today. Mr Beven, if we could start with you, I just wanted to ask a basic question. We know that town camps originally sprang out of discriminatory laws. We know—in the evidence, it's become quite clear over the last 12 months in particular—that there are widespread problems within town camps. From the perspective of the Office of Township Leasing, in the long-term should town camps continue to exist?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: In relation to your question, Senator, that's a matter for government. That's a matter for the housing associations that hold the special purpose leases and Crown leases for the Alice Springs town camps. Our role is to ensure secure tenure for government investment in town camps. But, in terms the policy decisions around whether they should continue, that's a matter for government and, more importantly, for the Aboriginal housing associations that hold those leases.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Minister, since you're here and are part of the government, could I ask for your view on that? Should town camps continue to exist?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Absolutely. There are presidents and boards of each of these town camps, especially in Central Australia. In Alice Springs we're talking about 16 town camps. I think it would be a pretty bad position to be in to say to get rid of them when we have governance groups arrangements in these town camps. Like all things under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, it's about working with Aboriginal people and Aboriginal organisations, and that's precisely what we're doing. It is really up to those presidents and the members of those town camps to determine what their future is, alongside of governments. This is what we're trying to do.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Mr Beven, How many families have become homeowners through the township leasing system? Do you have the figures on that?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: In total, we've had 15 people move to homeownership.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Fifteen over how many years?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Since 2007.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: That's almost 20 years. What's the eligible population, if you like, who could have moved and who are potentially eligible to become homeowners?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: In terms of the township leases that we manage, we have four township leases: three on the Tiwi Islands and one in Mutitjulu in Central Australia. The 15 families that have moved to homeownership were all on the Tiwi Islands. In terms of our approach, we make that option available through the secure tenure that township leasing does provide. But it's voluntary. So, in terms of whether families want to take that up, that's obviously a matter of being able to access capital for the purchase of the home and the maintenance of the home, and most of the families that we do deal with don't have large disposable incomes that would be able to secure or service a mortgage for homeownership. The aim is to—and we want to—make that available to families, but there hasn't been a large uptake since township leasing was introduced.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: It still seems a very low figure. Is there a benchmark figure? You said 'the aim'. I presume the aim is for there to be a higher number of people who become homeowners.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: We don't have an aim or a target. What we want to do is provide the mechanism for those people that do want to move to homeownership. But it's voluntary. We don't have a target that we're moving towards or aiming for. We just want to have the mechanism in place for families that do want to take up that option.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: What are the main obstacles, though—because 15 is a very low number. Anecdotally or otherwise, what are the obstacles you've heard that prevented people from—

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: As I said, poverty, disadvantage—all of the issues that we're all trying to address in terms of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, like improving employment outcomes. Target 9a and 9b is about improving housing options and availability. But all of the issues that are covered off in the National Agreement on Closing the Gap are the factors that are inhibiting people moving to homeownership in remote communities. But what we're trying to do is resolve the tenure issue on those township leases that has prevented people moving to homeownership. But, in terms of the other factors, there are many factors that contribute to a low take-up in homeownership.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Can you just expand on that point 'resolving the tenure issue'? Just explain to me what that means.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: For instance, in the Alice Springs town camps, homeownership is not possible largely because the legislation that the town camps were established under—
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Is that the Aboriginal land rights act?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: No, it's Northern Territory legislation. It's the Special Purposes Leases Act and the Crown leases act, which are Northern Territory legislation.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Okay. Sorry, I interrupted you.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: In terms of the township leases, the underlying tenure is Aboriginal land, which is communally held. So the township leases provide a mechanism where my office takes a long-term lease from the land trust, and that enables us—just like here in Canberra, where there's no freehold title; it's long-term leases. So we provide that secure tenure that enables businesses to have long-term tenure and homeownership to be a potential option, and it addresses the issue of Aboriginal community tenure.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Are there any issues with federal legislation that would help you resolve some of these tenure issues and make it easier to basically deal in and dispose of lease land?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: The minister may jump in. The minister has announced a review of my office, and so one of the things that may come up in relation to that may be legislative reform. But, at this stage, we don't see any major hurdles other than, as I said, the underlying issues around the National Agreement on Closing the Gap and improving and uplifting Aboriginal people in terms of employment, education, economic development, housing and health—all those things—so that they're in a position to take up homeownership if that's something that they would like to advance.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Of the 15 who have become homeowners, when did the 15th party become a homeowner?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Would it be in the last year or five years ago?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: I'm not certain.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Okay. Could you take that on notice. I'd be interested in the time distribution of the 15 who have become homeowners since 2007. Were they all in the 2010s or—

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: My understanding is they were fairly close together, but I'll take that on notice and give you the exact dates.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions. I do thank the Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation; we might put in some questions on notice, in the interests of keeping us on time.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Thank you. We'll go to Senator Collins.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Mr Beven, congratulations on your recent appointment.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Thank you.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: What's the tenure of your appointment?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Twelve months.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: This change occurred recently. Minister, I might direct this question to you. Was there a formal recruitment process that was undertaken to fill this role?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: We certainly identified a number of applicants for this particular role. We wanted to have a review of the executive office over the next 12 months, so what we've done is appoint Mr Anthony Beven as the acting executive director in parallel with the review that's going on in terms of township leasing.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: So it's a temporary role.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Well, 12 months.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Okay, 12 months. And you invited a few people for interview—or did you just appoint? What was the process?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: We have appointed Mr Anthony Beven as the acting executive director.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: There was no interview process. It was just—

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: A direct appointment.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Does that mean that over the next 12 months there will be a formal recruitment process?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: At this particular point in time, we are focused on the review.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: A review of what?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: The review of the township leasing, in terms of across the countries, as Senator Sharma has pointed out, looking at the role of the EDTL and what kind of success or otherwise we've had, and also in consultation with the land councils.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: How many people did you have on the list for potential people for the role?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Mr Beven was directly approached.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Would this be a usual process? I understand it's a temporary appointment and you're focused on the review, but, in 12 months time—when were you appointed?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: On 30 September.
witness_position: Acting Executive Director of Township Leasing

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: By September next year—I mean, it would take a long time to do a formal recruitment process, I would have thought. How long would that usually take for something like the executive director? When would you need to start that?

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: What I've certainly found in the past with general recruitment is ordinarily you'd give three months. It may take longer, but, at this particular point in time, we're not looking at recruitment at this stage. We're very happy to have Mr Beven.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: That's it from me. Thank you very much for your time and congratulations on your appointment.

agency: Indigenous Land and Sea Corporation Office of Township Leasing
text: Thank you very much for coming along this morning. Mr Morrison, I am terribly sorry. Due to some unforeseen circumstances, a couple of the senators who had questions have been unable to attend. Your questions will be placed on notice, but we do very much appreciate you taking the time to join us this morning. So thank you and apologies from the committee, and thank you, Mr Beven. We'll look forward to engaging with you over the duration of your tenure. With that, we will break now for morning tea.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I would like to welcome Senator the Honourable Katy Gallagher Minister for Women, Minister for Government Services, Minister for Finance and Minister for the Public Service. I would also like to welcome Ms Padma Raman, Executive Director of the Office for Women, and the other officers attending with you this morning, and also Ms Christine Castley, Chief Executive Officer of the Workplace Gender Equality Agency, and the officers attending with you. Minister, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Ms Raman, would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We'll go directly to questions then. Senator Kovacic.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for your time today. Since the budget, there continues to be justifiable alarm from small businesses around what they perceive to be the government's attack on their business models. At the last estimates, the Office for Women confirmed that it hadn't considered the impacts of the changes to trusts and CGT on women in business. Since the budget, has the office undertaken any analysis on the number of women expected to be impacted by the CGT changes in the budget?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Can I just start by saying the Office for Women's role is to provide me with advice to support my work through all of the relevant cabinet committees, and they do so. It is not their job to specifically go out and consult on other departments' particular policy areas. That is not their role. So, no, there would have been no update because it is not their role. They do not have responsibility for small business or for tax reform.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: But they do have responsibility for the impacts to women of policy across a portfolio of departments. My question related to—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, hang on—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I get to ask the questions.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The minister gets to answer them. She just wants to make a point.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Just to be clear, their job is to support me in my role as Minister for Women, support my decision-making across government and support other departments in the policy work that they do. But they do not have responsibility for it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: As the minister, you haven't directed them to undertake research on the impacts of these tax changes on women?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Okay.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I don't direct them. That is not the way I operate. I discuss with the Office for Women policies that the government's considering, and they provide advice to me to support my role.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm not suggesting that the Office for Women should be responsible for developing tax policy. I'm not suggesting that. But the office describes itself as the central gender equality institution within the Australian Public Service. Am I correct in that? Surely part of that responsibility is understanding how significant government policy decisions affect women, particularly when women themselves have publicly raised concerns about those impacts.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes. I'm not talking about the specific advice that the Office for Women provide me, but they provide—when making decisions about changes, reforms or policy, I draw on the advice of the Office for Women and that could include impacts on women who work in particular enterprises but also the benefits that certain reforms may bring for women. It's all encompassing is what I'd say in the advice that I'm provided.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sure. Did you draw on them for advice in relation to the impacts on small-business women in relation to the tax changes?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I certainly drew on them in relation to tax reform, but I'm not going into the specifics of the advice. I think the other thing I'd draw your attention to is the Office for Women have been working with Treasury about the tax expenditure and insight statement—I think it's called—to get a better understanding of how particular tax settings affect women. And I think if you look at that, overall, not necessarily talking about individual women operating in particular parts of the economy—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm not asking about individual women. I'm asking about women in small business. That is a sector. It is a large cohort. It is the cohort that will be most impacted by the tax changes. I'm not expecting you to be seeking guidance on how a pay-as-you-go worker will be impacted by CGT changes or discretionary trust changes. I expect that those questions would be related to small-business women. My question to the Office for Women then is: has the minister at any time asked for your guidance in relation to the impacts of the tax changes on women owned businesses or small-business women?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The responsibility for that—I'm trying to be helpful.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: It's a yes or no answer. Either you did or not.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm not going to go into the advice that the Office for Women provide me. They provide me advice—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Respectfully, I think that's our purpose here to understand.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm not talking about the specific nature of advice. I am telling you that the Office for Women brief me on issues around gender equality across a full range of portfolio areas. But the questions that you raised specifically are matters for the Treasury.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I appreciate you're not going to disclose the specifics of advice provided through the budget process, and I'm not asking for that. I would really like to direct my questions to the Office for Women officials now, if possible. Ms Leahy, since the budget was handed down, has the Office for Women undertaken any work or been asked for guidance to establish how many Australian women are likely to be affected by the capital gains tax changes?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I will have to take the details of that one on notice. Certainly, we are not running a large project in relation to women in small business, but there may have been some small pieces of advice that we have provided.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think, in budget submissions online, there are a number of women's organisations who have provided advice that we draw upon. Many organisations draw out the fact that often tax concessions across the board predominantly positively benefit more men than women. That's the nature of higher incomes and the benefits that tax concessions draw, as you go up the income scale.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I have another question related to that, so I have some clarity here on process. Did the Office for Women provide advice to you, Minister—or the question to the office to the minister—on the policy in preparation for cabinet and ERC consideration of the policy, particularly as it would impact small-business women or women-owned businesses?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That would go to the advice that I get to support my role as a cabinet minister. I can confirm that the Office for Women regularly brief me on matters on the agenda discussed through those committees. They do. That is a very useful part of the Office for Women in their support of me.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: My specific question relates to the impacts on small-business women or businesses owned by women and whether there was any specific consultation or impact done in relation to these tax changes or not. I'm not asking more broadly or about the broad consultation. I'm asking about whether or not there was any analysis, or whether you sought any guidance or advice, about how these tax changes would specifically impact women who owned and ran small businesses.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I am not going to the nature of the advice that the Office for Women provides me. I am answering it in the sense that I have regularly received advice, as you would expect, around taxation arrangements and its impact on women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The office is responsible for coordinating the implementation of the government's Working for Women Strategy, which specifically identifies women's economic equality and security as a priority. Have I understood that correctly?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So how can the office monitor progress against that objective if it doesn't establish the gender impacts of significant government policy decisions like this one? How is that possible?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, I don't accept that we don't consider the specific gender impacts, so I don't accept that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: But you don't assess it or seek advice on it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That is not the evidence I have given this morning. That is not the evidence.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: In terms of gendered impacts, as the minister inferred before, the Office for Women is the sort of steward of the gender-responsive budgeting system, under which and as outlined in the BPORs, portfolios responsible for the policies being developed are required to undertake their own gender analysis, and, if certain criteria are met, undertake gender impact assessment.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Let me put it a different way: how many formal consultations has the Office for Women undertaken since 2022, specifically with women in small business—startups, entrepreneurial sectors, the whole scope? Are you able to provide us a list of those engagements so we actually have an understanding of the scale?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We can certainly take that on notice.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Would you be able to give me a rough estimate?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Since 2022?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Probably not.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We do a lot of consultation and engagement with a range of stakeholders on a range of issues.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm aware.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: In relation to formal consultations, certainly—I will have to check—there was consultation undertaken to inform Working for Women, the strategy. It was very significant widespread consultation. That is a formal process that that we have undertaken. We can confirm through that process and through some of the other processes we've run subsequently.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
That question was asked by Senator Cash on 27 May this year. It was also taken on notice. I'll read to you the answer that we received on notice:

OFW also engages regularly with a range of stakeholders, including the National Women's Alliances, to ensure the lived experience of women and experts informs implementation of Working for Women.

We weren't told how many. We were given a general answer in relation to general consultation, general discussion, with stakeholders.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That time period would also take in the Women's Economic Equality Taskforce, where there was substantial consultation with a range of stakeholders. If you want the numbers from that and from Working for Women, we'd be very happy to provide that on notice.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What I'm really trying to understand is what, if anything, informed decision-making of government as to the impact of the budgetary changes on women, specifically on businesses owned by women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Can I just repeat here, the Office for Women is not responsible for that policy. That is the Department of the Treasury. It's the Treasurer. The questions around small business would be for the small business minister. The Office for Women is not responsible for those policy decisions. In fact, we have spent a long time trying to get the message across government that gender equality is everyone's responsibility. Forty-five people, or thereabouts, are in the Office for Women and that is not the place where this work gets done. It gets done in the Treasury. The Office for Women will work with the Treasury in that instance, in this scenario, and provide advice to me.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I understand that, Minister, and you've said that before, but what I have also said is that this office's role is to specifically identify women's economic equality and security as a priority, and they provide that advice to you. The government made changes in the budget that specifically impact small businesses. They specifically impact women in small businesses. Entrepreneurial women have indicated that this is a big impact to them. I'm curious, then, as to why you do not seek the guidance of the agency that is effectively charged with assisting the economic participation and equality of women—the Office for Women—to give you guidance on the impacts to women of that government policy.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I've already answered that I do get advice from the Office for Women and that does inform the positions and the discussions I have at the table. Just because I'm trying to say that tax reform is not the Office for Women's responsibility does not mean that they don't brief me on aspects of the tax system as to its impacts on women. They do. They get involved with the work that other departments do. The tax expenditure statement is one example of that, where the Office for Women is involved. In fact, we've tried hard in that statement to explore the differential impacts of those tax concession arrangements on women, and now we report that in that statement. That is because the Office for Women has done that job and worked with the Treasury. What that shows is that, overall, tax concessions tend to benefit higher income households or individuals who, disproportionately, tend to be men.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: In this case, many of them are women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Kovacic, we'll rotate the call, if you want to wind up that one question.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, if I can just finish this one, if I get an opportunity to ask.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I can tell you that I did have a number of submissions from the Working With Women Alliance and the National Foundation for Australian Women. There are a number of organisations that have provided submissions to the government supporting tax reform because of the gendered nature of tax concession arrangements.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: None of those were small-business women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: They're organisations working for women in alliance. Don't dismiss—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: My question relates to women who own and run small businesses.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, but we're talking around the gendered impacts, and we have organisations that have expertise in that area. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that there are quite a number of organisations that support the reforms because of the gendered nature of the beneficiaries of tax concessions.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Chair, we have limited time. I would appreciate the opportunity—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No-one is curtailing your time, Senator Kovacic, but we will maintain some behaviours here that are respectful and we will allow—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I've been nothing but respectful today.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Kovacic, don't start talking over me now, because that is just proving the point. If we could all just have some respect and give each other enough time—I will give you as much time as you need to ask your questions, but the minister will also have the time she needs to answer them. So, if you would like to complete your line of questioning, we will then rotate the call, because there are other senators in the room. That is not to say we will not come back to you, but that is the manner in which we will proceed.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I will proceed, Chair. If I may make a point: I do nothing but conduct myself respectfully in this environment. If we are going to call me out for speaking over someone, perhaps that same should occur for others. I am here asking questions. I should have the opportunity to ask those questions and for those questions to be answered and for me to have the opportunity to complete my questions as well.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No-one is stopping you from completing your questions, as I've said. I did not just refer to you; I referred to the room. We will conduct this hearing in a fashion that respects everyone's opportunity to correct the record, say whatever they feel they need to say, ask their questions and answer them. Senator Kovacic, if you would like to finish up this block of questions, that would be lovely.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Did the Office for Women review a gender impact analysis on the legislation which creates a minimum tax of 30 per cent on discretionary trusts?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sorry, but can you just repeat that? Did the Office for Women—?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Did the Office for Women review a gender impact analysis on the legislation which creates a minimum tax of 30 per cent on discretionary trusts?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I tried to deal with this in the earlier questions. It's a similar set of questions. We don't talk about the advice that's provided to government.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: It's a specific question, if I could ask the agency.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Again, the agency isn't responsible for doing the gender analysis of another department's policy. It's not the Office for Women that does that. The department or agency bringing the submission is required to undertake, depending on the nature of the policy being developed or the decision being taken, a gender impact analysis—or just a gender analysis. Sorry, I just don't have that in front of me. But, depending on the size and scale of the change, the departments themselves are responsible for that. It's not the Office for Women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And again, respectfully, I didn't ask that again.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You asked if they undertook a gender impact analysis.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No. And I asked the question twice. If they could perhaps answer the question, it might be different. I asked whether they reviewed a gender impact analysis. I know it is not their job to do the gender impact analysis. I want to know whether the Office for Women reviewed a gender impact analysis on the legislation that creates a minimum tax of 30 per cent on discretionary trusts, and that is the third time I've asked that same question.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And I'm trying to—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Not whether they wrote it or whether they have responsibility for it, but whether they were provided with one by the agency that was responsible and whether they reviewed that document to give you advice as to what the economic impacts on women of that tax change in the budget would be.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator, I know it's frustrating, but we do not discuss advice that we give towards the ERC or cabinet processes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: But, going back to my earlier advice, on tax reform in general, yes, they do provide advice to me as the Minister for Women and have done so during my time in that role. Your question relates specifically to a piece of legislation. In relation to the decision we made around trusts; that was a budget decision, and I was appropriately briefed for those discussions at budget time.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you. Just to clarify again to the Office for Women: I'm not asking you to tell me what advice you gave to the minister or the government. I simply want to know whether you were asked to review such a document in giving any advice. I'm not asking you to tell me what you said or what the detail of it was. Simply, were you asked to review a gender impact analysis in relation to the impact of the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think that would still go not to the content of the advice, but to the nature of the advice that was presented to cabinet or the ERC in the context of budget deliberations. The minister mentioned before the Tax Expenditures and Insights Statement, which does contain public information on the benefits of a range of tax subsidies and expenditures, including trusts, capital gains and negative gearing.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So the government's Working for Women strategy acknowledges that access to capital remains a significant barrier for women led businesses, and that's commonly known through industry as well. I'm trying to ask these questions and get the answers to get an understanding of what work was done and if advice was sought as part of your—you have a women's economic policy branch. Is that correct? Right. Have they undertaken any work since the budget to assess whether the tax reforms could affect women's abilities to establish, finance, grow or sell their businesses? Noting you can't tell me what advice you gave before, and you can't even tell me whether you've reviewed a particular type of document, can you then tell me what you've done afterwards and if that economic branch has been charged with doing any of that additional work?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'll just say again, Senator Kovacic, we do need to share the call.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What I can say is certainly we have engaged with the tax reforms, including tax reforms made through the most recent budget, and considered their impacts for women writ large rather than, I guess, just specifically focusing on women as small-business owners. Certainly we are very interested and engaged in policy around tax and a number of other economic matters.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We'll go to Senator Whitten.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We've recently seen the Minns Labor government in New South Wales walk back language used in a parliamentary breastfeeding policy that used gender-neutral terms like 'lactating parent'. Premier Minns said the use of that language was strange and not what the public expects. Minister, do you agree with your state counterpart that biological difference between people who are born male and people who are born female must be referenced in law?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think some of these issues were traversed last night, which is the appropriate committee for that to happen. The approach I bring to the role I play as Minister for Women is one of respect. I just try to be respectful to all individuals regardless of how they identify. I think some of the debates that people try to draw into are difficult, divisive and harmful. So I prefer to have a more inclusive way of operating. That language doesn't bother me.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I also try and be respectful, but I have a mother, I have a sister, I have a wife, I've got two daughters and I've got a granddaughter, and they expect me to ask questions like this.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Entirely reasonable.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I don't think it's being disrespectful to anybody.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I don't either.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Just because I like apples doesn't mean I hate oranges.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Whitten, you might want to take a breath. The minister said nothing along those lines.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I wasn't casting any aspersion on you, Senator Whitten.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: She really didn't.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You were talking about having respectful conversations, so I'm just making sure—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You asked me about what I thought. I was just explaining how I choose to engage on this. I think for many people it can be a very difficult and traumatic discussion, and I just try to bring a sense of treating everybody as they wish to be treated.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We should be able to have the discussion respectfully.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, I agree, and I think we are right now.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Good. Premier Minns's comments stand in stark contrast to the Gillard-era changes that remain in law, which repealed the statutory definitions of men and women and has been used in recent months to ensure that biological men can access female-only spaces. Does the federal government agree with the New South Wales Labor government's assessment that the public expects that 'male' and 'female' take on their ordinary use in law?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Again, that's not really a question for me as Minister for Women. That's a question for the Attorney, and that was dealt with. The relevant officials appeared last night, as I understand it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Is the Minns Labor government in breach of the Sex Discrimination Act by not being inclusive of other genders or lactating men in its policies?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That's, again, not a matter for the Office for Women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: How are we going with an office for men?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, we've had the appointment of the member for Hunter—is that the right seat?—Mr Repacholi, from the other place, which has been the first appointment in a federal government with a specific policy focus on men, and he's doing an amazing job.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And how are we going for an office for men?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The government has recognised the specific policy area, in this instance men's health, that we want to work on specifically in relation to men. That is the first time this has happened. I think it is proving that it is needed and the work that Dan is doing—supported and working very closely, I would say, with Ged Kearney, who's working in the women's policy space—is needed. But there has not been a decision to have a specific office for men.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think that men's problems and men's issues are growing by the day and they would be worthy of an office for men, because it would actually make women's lives better if we had better men.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Kovacic.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Last Monday, Four Corners aired a program called 'The Pregnancy Penalty' exposing allegations of pregnancy discrimination across Australian workplaces, including the public sector. Are you familiar with that program? Has the Office for Women briefed the minister on these allegations, or has the minister requested any advice from you more broadly about those allegations?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We would definitely have talked about issues around this. I also talk about issues with the APSC, the Public Service Commission, in relation to our responsibilities as an employer.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: There was an example of both the private sector and the Public Service in that show. The example from the Public Service was from the Department of Home Affairs. This woman in particular was denied flexible work arrangements when she returned from maternity leave. Have you reviewed this particular matter or consulted with the Department of Home Affairs since the program aired in relation to that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
I'm not here to comment on individual employment matters. They are appropriately dealt with by the minister, the Minister for Home Affairs in that case. My job as—it crosses over—Minister for Women and Minister for the Public Service is making sure that our employment arrangements, which don't allow for discrimination now, are followed and enforced. It's very clear that no woman should face discrimination because she's pregnant, taken parental leave or having caring responsibilities.

I know about and I've had raised anecdotally examples which are difficult to grab hold of, in a sense, in the public and private sectors, where you just don't get the promotion or there's a restructure. There are stories like that that I hear. For me—and we're currently in bargaining with our employees at the moment—it's doing what we can to make sure that, as much as possible, we are implementing policies which very clearly set the standard around that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What I'm trying to understand here is the scale of the issue. I note the specific responsibilities in relation to particular cases. I'm trying to get an understanding of whether you've consulted with the Department of Home Affairs since the program aired, given your overlap with your ministerial portfolios, as well, and the work that the Office for Women does.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I haven't specifically spoken to the Minister for Home Affairs about it. It's the responsibility of those individual ministers if they've got a complaint or are dealing with a particular issue that they know about. I don't know if the minister was made aware of that case or if a complaint was lodged. I have been dealing more with what we can do to make sure, on some of those harder-to-grab-your-hands-around issues, that we are looking to minimise opportunity for that. One thing I'm interested in is why women find it hard to move up the EL ladder. I always get it wrong—is an EL1 more than an EL2, or the other way around? Is EL2 more than EL1?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: EL2 is higher than EL1.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I always get it wrong. I always think that because you're No. 1 you're at the top, and I have to flip it. I have been spoken to about how the opportunities to move from, say, an EL1 to an EL2 are difficult, particularly when you have caring responsibilities. Part of that is around a perception that there aren't as many part-time opportunities at that level—that you have to be full-time and there is that impact. So they're the kinds of things I'm trying to grapple with about our own employment arrangements. If there are women out there who have been discriminated against based on pregnancy, returning to work or caring responsibilities—or men, for that matter, because we are encouraging more men and more men are taking up those caring opportunities—then I hope that they are finding a way to come forward and let that be known so that we can pursue it, because, in my experience, the issues are harder to grab hold of. You don't not get the promotion because you've got a baby or you're going to have a baby; it's for another reason, but the individual feels that it's because of the pregnancy.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes. Well, this is even worse than the promotion. It's the fact that you don't even have your right to work from home, at whatever rate you had before, when you return from mat leave. So it's a much more basic issue than a promotion.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I guess what I'm trying to understand is whether you have perhaps engaged with the Australian Public Service Commission or other departments about the broader issues raised by the program about pregnancy discrimination, how many cases like this there actually are across the Australian Public Service, and whether any work has been done on that or whether you're seeking to have work done on it by the Office for Women.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm sure the APSC, which will appear next, will be able to go into this in a bit more detail. Part of what we've been trying to do around flexible work arrangements and paid parental leave and all of the issues that are currently on the bargaining table is that the unions and other employee representatives are seeking greater flexibility at work. They're all areas that we are actively engaged with at the moment. I can't recall an individual—well, I'm careful about what I say. But I haven't received complaints around pregnancy discrimination that I can recall post that show, and I'll check with my office about prior to that show.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sure. Have you sought data from across the Public Service to understand the scale of the problem?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, I haven't specifically requested data. I'm not sure—we can ask the Public Service Commission later—how that would be documented and collated across government about the nature of complaints that are being made. The area that I have been trying to focus on is to make sure that we have employment law that sets the standard and then that the policy decisions we take support flexibility for people with caring responsibilities and those who have recently had children.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sure. Because they're fairly serious allegations that were aired on that program, I'm trying to get an understanding of whether, as far as you're aware, those policies are consistently applied across those agencies and, if they aren't, whether that's being reviewed—or whether there is a review, in fact, to ensure that policies are consistently applied to not discriminate against women who are coming back from parental leave.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, they were serious allegations that were raised, and they will be followed up through the work that we already have underway.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I have one last follow-up question in relation to the data. Does the Office for Women have access to data on how often flexible working requests are refused across APS agencies, particularly for women returning from parental leave? Would you be aware of who would collect that type of data?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I suspect that you're better off asking the Public Service Commission on that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: But you don't have any access to that type of data.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, but we have worked with the Sex Discrimination Commissioner on the report that she talked about last night as well.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think either the APSC, at an aggregate sense, as well as individual corporate areas in each department might have more granular data on these issues.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I have one last bit to add to that. I think it was in 2025 that the APS employee census found that about 8.4 per cent of respondents experienced discrimination. I think something like 17.1 per cent cited caring responsibilities. Have you done any work in relation to that or examined those findings to understand the prevalence of pregnancy discrimination across the APS, or have you not drilled down to that at this point?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You're probably better off asking the Public Service Commission about that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I've got a set of questions for the Workplace Gender Equality Agency. Your corporate plan has a series of quantifiable economic KPIs—your scorecard, I guess. These include total remuneration pay gaps; corporate velocity, which the rate at which companies take up a gender equality agenda; and leadership metric, which is the percentage of women in leadership roles. Are these the main KPIs?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts, could you please repeat that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I want to clarify the question. We have the corporate plan, which sets the principles on which our organisation operates. That is to deliver regulatory excellence, to turn world-leading data into action, to accelerate employer action, to lead the national conversation and to aspire to excellence through our ways of working. We then have the national scorecard, which we put out each year. I suppose, in the first instance, I'd like to clarify whether your question relates to the scorecard or the corporate plan.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The scorecard.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The scorecard is basically, as you would know, based on a national picture of data that WGEA collects from employers. We then report on a set of metrics, which I would describe as basically a picture of what is happening on gender equality in workplaces rather than a set of KPIs. What we do is track that data over a period of years. We produce that data each year. It draws from data that employers report to us, and we then use that analysis to provide that information back to those employers and to the nation generally to understand what is happening in gender equality in the workplace and where there are areas to target for action to ensure that we achieve gender equality in the workplace.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So you don't have KPIs, then?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The scorecard is essentially about trying to identify where we're at in terms of workplace gender equality. We set a target of what we think is the correct level, which is a plus or minus five per cent either way. There needs to be a range because we recognise that it's going to be very difficult to achieve zero per cent. That, in a sense, would be a KPI, if you like, that we are working towards in achieving workplace gender equality.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The total remuneration pay gap has fallen from 28.6 per cent to 21.1 per cent since 2013. Are you claiming that reduction was a result of the actions of your agency, in part or in whole?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
We wouldn't say that that is a result of the actions of our agency, because action is the responsibility of employers. What we're trying to do is support and assist the effort by providing data to employers. By providing that national picture of what is happening in individual workplaces and how that extrapolates also to what's happening across industries and occupations nationally, we can understand what is going on with people's representation in the workplace, what roles they're in, and what opportunities they have for promotion and to access flexible work, which impacts on the decisions around their participation in the workforce.

By providing that data based information, putting that out publicly and presenting a national picture, we think we are supporting and assisting employers to understand where they can focus their efforts within their workplaces to actually take action to improve workplace gender equality. As you say, there has been a reduction in the gender pay gap over time. Certainly, we would see ourselves as doing what we can to contribute to that effort that employers are putting in to address gender equality in their workplaces by providing them with data and evidence that will assist them in that role.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You've used the words 'support' and 'assist' quite a few times. What are you doing that a statistics agency like the ABS couldn't do?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
Our data is based on actual employer workforce records data that we collect from employers. It is workforce data, and it's across a large sample. It distils insights across industries and occupations so employers can have a look at what's happening across the industries and occupations. But it also targets a level of detail that's not generally available, for example, to the ABS, around things such as employment arrangements and the part-time/full-time/flexible piece; what's happening in terms of recruitment; what's happening in terms of promotions and resignations; and also what's happening in terms of parental leave.
