There's a set of data that relates to the actual workplace and is available to employers to have a look at in terms of what's happening not just across their organisation but across industries and sectors and what's happening nationally so they can look at patterns which can also inform something around how to take action to address workplace gender equality.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I still can't understand how that data collection couldn't be done by a data collection agency like ABS. What are you adding to support and assist?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The form of reporting that we do is specifically focused on workplace gender equality. It provides that level of nuance and detail that is not generally available in broader datasets. It is around workforce data that employers collect. What we do is collect that data to provide a national dataset that allows us, employers and others who are doing work in this space to understand what's happening in terms of patterns around movements and what is happening in a workplace where there may be areas to target to address the causes of inequalities that might be happening in the workplace.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: From your scorecard, every industry pays men more on average than women. What is the pay rate you're comparing? Is it an hourly or weekly base or base plus overtime and allowance?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: It's the average full-time remuneration that we're having a look at.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Full-time remuneration not including overtime or allowances?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: It does include overtime and allowances. It's total remuneration.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Total pay? Gross pay?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Looking at mining, for example, does your comparison compare the salary of an office worker in a mining company in an air conditioned office in Perth with a labourer in the heat of the Pilbara? What adjustment have you made to compare apples with apples in this comparison?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
What we do is collect that data and identify the occupation that the person is—it's de-identified data, but we certainly see the individual employed in a particular role within the organisation, which also is the data that's reported, which may be an office job, and the data of the remuneration of an individual onsite on a mining site. It allows you to distil that data and understand what's happening. Then, what we look at is: in a global sense, within that organisation, what is the representation within those roles and who has access to which pieces?

The data we collect is about telling the story of what is going on in a workforce so that an employer can then understand what is happening in terms of patterns of employment, retention and those sorts of things. It helps them understand whether there is an overrepresentation of women in one part of their business as opposed to another, and it helps them to understand the causes behind that and whether there are things that can be done to enable greater flexibility of movement across the organisation, if that's appropriate. But it's for the employer to use the data that we provide to them, based on the patterns that they see from the data they report to us about what's happening across the industry but within the organisation.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Can I just jump in? WGEA just had its 40th anniversary.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Who has?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: WGEA, the Workplace Gender Equality Agency. It just had its 40th anniversary. Going back through the history of that organisation and its establishment and beyond, it has been a partnership with business. Business has been there. When it started, it was businesses that put their hand up and said, 'We want to be part of this,' and that's how it's grown over time. Even at the panel that we had, business was represented, talking about the benefits that come. I think the issue that we're all thinking about is: how do we make it easier for business to provide that data? Timeliness, efficiency and making sure it's not onerous—all of those things—are legitimate policy discussions that we are having now, as is how they use the data to improve their own organisation with the support of WGEA.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts, we will look to rotate the call, if you'd like to finish up your line of questioning.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Okay. Where was corporate velocity when you first started measuring it and where is that now?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Could I seek some clarification of what you mean by 'corporate philosophy'?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That's your agency's term, I think—the rate at which companies take up the gender equality agenda.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That is not a metric that we ask agencies, employers or organisations to report on.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Have you or your agency made comments about it?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: On what—on corporate philosophy?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: On corporate velocity.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I personally have not. I can go back and check this, but certainly not as far as I'm aware. But I'm happy to take that on notice to check if the agency has made any comment on corporate philosophy.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you. We'll continue later.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I just want to follow up on some of those questions, specifically those around WGEA's submission to the Productivity Commission inquiry into business reporting. WGEA stated that they—you—consistently engage with employers to identify areas of complexity and consider how it can be made clearer and easier to navigate without compromising data integrity. What does the engagement with businesses look like?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That happens on a number of different levels. As you would be aware, agencies report to us every year. That reporting period starts 1 April, and then there's a closing period. Once the reporting is closing, we actually do a survey of reporting agencies every year, and we do get a very good response in terms of the experience, and we use that—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What's a 'very good response' percentage-wise?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'll have to take that on notice, but my memory of it this year is that, in terms of the response, it was somewhere between 80 and 90 per cent, but please don't hold me to that; I'd like to check.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No. That's alright. Take it on notice.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
It was a high rate of response. Certainly, we use that feedback to then inform us in looking at the reporting system. That would be technical issues with the actual reporting system and also things like numbers of reporting hours. What we look to do is to then improve that experience. In regard to what we've put in place this year, we've tried to improve what we call our case management approach, which is the response to assisting people who are reporting. When they contact us, we see what we can do to ensure that they only do a report once—for example, they don't submit a report and have to go through iterations of correcting it—and we're correcting technical glitches which support and provide information and guidance. We regularly review the guidance that we provide to employers. So that's the mechanics and the technical support in reporting. I should say we're very cognisant of the design of the reporting system, which is very much geared towards using data which employers already have systems in place to report on. Certainly, that's a piece that's in there.

Finally, I suppose, at a broader level—certainly since coming into the role—I have made a deliberate effort to go out there and speak to employers from a range of sectors and industries of a range of different sizes to actually get a sense of what their thoughts are on the regulatory impact and to ensure that we can actually identify opportunities to make the experience as seamless as possible. I'm very, very committed to doing that and continuing to do that and continuing to both engage at the peak body level across different sectors and speak to a good sample of employers who report to us.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I want to follow up on the issue that you raised there, particularly around Single Touch Payroll data and using that. Obviously the 2021 review recommended exploring the use of the data that's already provided to government. Using, particularly, Single Touch Payroll was highlighted as well as other digital solutions to extract that information from employers' existing systems. The government committed to implementing the review's recommendation in August 2022. I want to understand what work WGEA has undertaken to implement that specific recommendation.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
At this stage, the Single Touch Payroll and other ways of trying to tap into existing datasets that we could use are something that I would describe as an ongoing conversation. There are some real challenges here because the workforce data that employers provide to us is de-identified data. We can manage that in the sense that that minimises your privacy and confidentiality issues. I'm flagging this as one of those issues that we need to think about in terms of accessing, for example, payroll data to make sure that those confidentiality and privacy obligations are met. That's one issue that we have to work through.

There are also mechanical issues around having systems speak to each other but also issues around whether, in fact, the data that would become available from STP, Single Touch Payroll data, will actually ensure we can have a consistent dataset so that we're getting the same information. The benefit of our system, I think, is that longitudinal piece—that we're collecting data over a number of years. We also ensure, I suppose, that we minimise the regulatory burden for employers by ensuring that we're continuing to not shift and change the reporting system too much because organisations within themselves have reporting systems in place. Many of them have had that now in place for more than 10 years. We're very conscious that any shift and change can sometimes impose a burden in terms of having to shift and change something that's become automated.

I suppose what I'm trying to say here is there are a range of things—we're actively looking at the issue—to be worked through and we want to be careful to make sure we get it right not just to ensure that we can continue to do WGEA's function but also to make sure that we're not compromising individuals' privacy, confidentiality and all those issues and to make sure that we're also thinking through the consequent pieces. So, certainly, it's an ongoing piece. It's taking us a while because we want to make sure we get it right, and it's not a simple piece either.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm acutely conscious that there are lots of submissions to that inquiry from people like the BCA and Master Builders suggesting that there could be some productivity gains for them making greater use of existing employers' data and that this should be part of the 'tell us once' approach, which I know that the government is committed to. The coalition committed to it in opposition as well. Is this part of that 'tell us once' plan, Minister?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, essentially—looking at non-financial reporting as well. It's part of a bigger piece of work, which I know is underway, but, definitely, we would like to make things easier and for data to be more useful to everybody across the board. I think WGEA has done a great job. I get a lot of feedback about a lot of reporting. I don't get too much about WGEA in terms of people's engagement, and that's because, I think, of all of the work WGEA's put in over the years in having those good partnerships with businesses that they cover.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So the use of Single Touch Payroll data is something that the government supports WGEA exploring further?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I haven't seen the work come back about the best way to ensure the most efficient and effective reporting from business into government and for government systems to support that. So I have an open mind about how we achieve that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Is it something that WGEA has looked at on a field-by-field basis—what could be reused from Single Touch Payroll reporting in what it is that you collect?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: That is part of the process that we're looking at in terms of the broader bit. In fact, that would be an important part of making sure that we're actually getting that congruence and that consistency. I suppose you'd appreciate that, when systems are set up separately, they don't necessarily always align. That's part of the issue of trying to work through what we'll do versus what won't work. But, certainly, we are very open to looking at minimising the reporting burden for employers and are actively engaged in that process. We see minimising that regulatory impact as an important part of our responsibility, so we're very open to being engaged in that process. As you will appreciate, Single Touch Payroll data sits with the ATO. It's their dataset. It comes down to what's made available to us. As part of our continuous improvement process, we're very open to looking at all options going forward.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm conscious of the fact that this was a recommendation in August 2022. It's four years ago now. That you're open to it is terrific, but it seems to be taking a long time to progress. It is ATO's data, but conversations must have been had about sharing that data and accessing that data in the last four years.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: My sense, having come into the role in the last five months, is certainly that it is an active, ongoing conversation that we're being engaged in.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What's the timetable, from here on in, to try and minimise duplication of reporting, to try and have that 'tell us once' mentality and to reduce the regulatory burden on businesses?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think it's probably a question for Finance later on in the day, because they've got regulatory reform responsibilities that WGEA would be feeding into but is not the decision-maker of.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And WGEA is not the only one. I think there are a number of regulatory agencies that are involved in this process. Again, I would imagine it would be about where you would have best impact in terms of where regulatory burdens are and in terms of how you would prioritise the agencies you would share information with.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Do you have a work plan and a timetable for further reducing duplication and improving efficiency? Is that something that you can share?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I would describe the work that we do as ongoing rather than a single project. It fits within our cycle each year. What we do each reporting cycle before we go live is look at what's come out of the previous year. For example, based on those survey results that I spoke about and on the information that our reporting team have gathered in speaking to employers, we then look at how we improve the process for the following year. I would see it as an ongoing, continuous business process rather than a single project that we would have a project plan around—more as an ongoing process piece.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What's improved in the last 12 months?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We've managed to retain data. The only reason I'm hesitating is that I know we do have numbers, so I might take that on notice—but, for example, between the previous year and this year, the number of hours that employers reported to us has significantly reduced. We've also got some metrics on the numbers of errors which caused the return, as I talked about, to that turnback process. We do certainly have some of those numbers, which I'm happy to share with you, if I can take that on notice. It will give you a sense of there having been, even between last year and this year, a significant reduction in the number of reporting hours. Again, if I can be a bit vague, it is around 40-something reporting hours versus 25-something reporting hours. I think that's a material impact in terms of reporting. It's a mix of—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Obviously, not every business would have 40 reporting hours. Do you scale that for the size of business and number of employees?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
Yes. I'll have to check to see whether we have that scale of the responses we've had across how we collect that data. We collect it at a higher level. There's significant work. We've got close to 10,000 entities reporting to us, so that's a big set to have a look at. But what we're looking at is: on average, are we seeing a consistent improvement in the experience? I like to call it almost the client experience or the user experience. That's certainly our goal in terms of what we're looking at.

If you think about who reports to us, the scale can be quite significant in terms of looking at it. While you might get some very, very large organisations, they will also have the resources to have that assistance in place, and therefore the impact is minimal on them versus on others which are smaller and potentially have fewer resources. But, again, the design of the system says that it's really only businesses with 100 or more employees who report to us, so it manages the regulatory impact in that sense.

We're conscious at all times about trying to think about how we can manage that reporting experience in the best way we possibly can, and we're also conscious about how, through the insights and the analysis and the work that we do—and through putting the data out, publishing the data, as well—we're returning value for the impact of reporting to us. That's certainly very much an underpinning driver for how we do our work.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'd be very interested—on notice, obviously; you wouldn't have this with you now—in getting a sense of the hours it takes to report to WGEA.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I can take that question on notice.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, perhaps for businesses of three different sizes, of the ones that you assess that are over a certain number of employees. I don't mind how it is that you measure it, whatever you call large businesses, medium businesses or relatively small businesses even if they have got more than 100 employees. But it would be interesting to know whether those hours that it takes to report to WGEA have reduced in a consistent way across business sizes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm happy to take that on notice to see what we can do with the information that we have.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
Chair, can I jump in. I'm following up from Senator Kovacic's questions. I want to correct the record: the Office for Women's ASL is 53.4, so I lowballed it. My apologies to the Office for Women for that.

In relation to the questions about pregnancy discrimination, I did receive some correspondence from an individual prior to the ABC show, which I have responded to. That individual did not want me to share that information with their department/agency, but the information feeds into the work we're doing and looking at through current employment arrangements. That's the way we have responded there. We have had some correspondence since the ABC show, but none of that was about the APS, so all correspondence has been referred to Minister Rishworth for handling.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you. Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Continuing on, this is a quote from your report: 'Even in highly feminised industries like health care and social assistance, where women make up 78 per cent of the total workforce, men are disproportionately fast-tracked into leadership, holding 49 per cent of the CEO and head of business roles.'

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, we do see that in feminised industries: where there are men, there are more of them in the senior roles.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So you've got 51 per cent in senior roles being women and 49 per cent being men. Let's call it 50-50—mission accomplished.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Not compared to the size of the overall workforce.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So the target is not 50-50?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: It's feminised industries. In relation to that comment, it sounds like—I don't have the annual report with me—it's making a comment about how even in the industries where women dominate as a percentage of the workforce, we don't see that replicated at senior management. Where they're 79 per cent of the workforce, they are not 79 per cent of the management. It's just a statement of fact, no other view about that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The report also talks about the pedestal effect: men are fast-tracked into leadership more quickly than women in general, supposedly. Have you done any research on the pedestal effect?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
Yes. I assume you're referring to the joint report that we released a couple of weeks ago with the Bankwest Curtin Economic Centre at Curtin University. That report actually was where I think the issue was raised around the male pedestal effect having an impact on what happens particularly in female dominated industries. It basically joined up a set of data from not just our data but also ASX data that they hold and also HILDA, which I can never remember what the acronym stands for, to actually understand what is going on. It's simply saying the male pedestal effect, again, is a comment that, even in female industries, there seems to be bias that uplifts people as much as potentially bias in some other areas which might basically constrain people's progression. It simply highlights this as an issue to be looked at, and we provide data that tells that story. It's then for others to look at that story to see what is happening in workplaces.

The point here being that, in female dominated industries, as the minister has already said, even where you have equal participation or probably greater female participation, there is something happening at the management levels. That's, I suppose, a factor of the work that we're looking at to say, 'Let's have a look at what is happening in the patterns of remuneration, employment and retention in an organisation to say, "Where do there seem to be things that give rise to questions to ask about what's happening," so that employers in organisations and industries can then have a look at that to see if there are things that can be done for them to then basically put in place the best possible workforce participation arrangements that we can have for Australia.'

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Do you look at the root causes, the reasons, for this claimed pedestal effect? For example, is it physical? Is it behavioural? Are there family constraints? Because I believe women and men should have equal opportunity, but they're not equal. If I were to line up against Maria Kovacic as a candidate to be in a basketball team, she'd win—no doubt.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm a really good volleyballer too!

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I bet you are. So are you looking at the reasons rather than just saying there's a pedestal effect—giving a name to something—and just saying there it is?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The data that employers report to us gives us information on pay, on who's in which roles, the employment arrangements—whether they're part time or in other flexible arrangements—recruitment and promotions—so what's happening in terms of movements. Then we put that data out there for employers to look at, and I think that is a key benefit of what we do. That information is made available to employers and publicly—and also information across industries, which helps them to understand the patterns of what's going on to then try to understand the causes. We leave it to employers because employers are best placed to make decisions about the operational arrangements for their businesses to take that action. We don't make any judgement. We simply collect the data, and we put it out there and allow it to tell the story that it tells.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: A pedestal would tend to be judgemental, surely?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Those were words that came out in the BCEC report. It is an academically researched phenomenon which they have certainly done work on and which they put in that report. It was a joint report. What we try to do is provide our data and use that data to then work in partnership with a whole range of other organisations and peak bodies, as well as research entities like BCEC, to develop some insights and some thinking. Our input into that report was to provide the data. Their input, because they have the research capability and the analysis capability, was to overlay that data with commentary and a description of what is happening in the workplace.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Your research suggests, apparently, a lack of flexibility in child care or parenting as a major restriction on women in senior management. Yet the ABS shows the number of women currently aged over 40 who will not have children is 22 per cent, which is up from 11 per cent 20 years ago. Have you tested your theory by surveying how many women in these roles are childless and how many women self-report having been passed over who had children, which would prove your hypothesis? How much empirical evidence is behind this?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We don't collect that data, because it doesn't align with our functions and the objective of the act. Our role is basically to collect workforce data which shows us the movements and the patterns within those workforces and to then provide that national dataset, which is then tiered at a number of different levels to look at what the patterns are so that others, such as employers, can then understand the root causes of those patterns and what's happening.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Can we move on to the Office for Women?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We're here jointly.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The Office for Women's website states: 'Women face greater impacts from climate change. In Australia women are more likely to live in housing unable to cope with extreme temperature and experience higher rates of ill health and death as a result, especially older women.' These questions are from a female constituent. Of the 122,494 people experiencing homelessness at the 2021 census, 55.9 per cent were male. Men account for around 66 per cent of people sleeping rough—the cohort most exposed to extreme heat. And 65 per cent of homeless people aged 65 to 74 are male. Given these figures, why does the office frame heat vulnerability as a women's issue rather than as an issue affecting multiple vulnerable groups, including men, older Australians, people in North Queensland, Aboriginals, Torres Strait Islander people and veterans? Why do you frame it as a gender issue?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm not sure exactly what part of the website you are referring to. But, more broadly, there is good evidence that shows that men and women have different experiences of climate change and related issues like natural disasters. Certainly, there are a range of other factors as well—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Could you explain about men and women having a different range of experiences with regard to disasters?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Certainly—matters like women being on lower incomes and the financial pressures that interact with natural disasters. We know that there are increased rates of family and domestic violence following natural disasters and in the context of natural disasters, and women are more likely to experience family and domestic violence. Caring responsibilities become more acute or heightened in the context of natural disasters. They're just some examples of the different or the particularly gendered experiences that women may have as a result of natural disasters. This is not at all to take away from the experiences that men have or the experiences that other cohorts of people have, based on location or indigeneity or cultural background. But we do know that about the kind of aggregate gendered experience of natural disasters.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Data for 2023 to 2024 from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare shows the most common reasons people sought homelessness support were accommodation issues, at 55 per cent; financial difficulties, at 41 per cent; and the housing crisis, at 37 per cent. Where is the research identifying climate change rather than income and housing costs as a cause of women entering poor housing?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Again, I'm not entirely clear on which part of the website you're referring to.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No, that's data from the Australian—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You're putting together the AIHW data—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: With the website.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: and then challenging some things around—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And asking where's the evidence for climate.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think there's a lot of international evidence that is not contested about the impacts of climate change on women and girls for the reasons—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Could we have some samples?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sorry?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Could we have some samples—hard references?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I'm very happy to provide them to you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: If you could on notice, please.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: UN Women have done a huge amount of work in this space, as have a number of international organisations. Poverty, hunger or food insecurity, having to care for children, not being able to relocate, sometimes because of those reasons about care but also around cultural reasons—there is a lot of evidence, Senator Roberts. You may not agree with it, but there is certainly a lot of literature written about it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I look forward to your answers.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts, I'm going to need to rotate the call.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Can I have one more question?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: One more, did you say? Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Australia has always experienced hot summers and cold winters, and cold contributes to more temperature related deaths than heat for most causes. That has been throughout human history. And it's a marked difference. Whether a woman or a man is harmed depends on whether their home is adequate and whether they can afford to heat or cool it. Housing quality and energy affordability can be addressed directly. So why is this Labor government trying to make climate change a scapegoat? These questions are from a woman constituent.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We're not trying to make climate change a scapegoat. We're trying to deal with the real-life impacts of climate change. Again, if you talk to anyone—I know that NEMA is appearing now, the National Emergency Management Agency. If you look at any of the analysis about the impending weather season, experts in the field universally accept that the number, the frequency and the intensity of natural disasters as a result of climate change is affecting this country, and we are responding to that, Senator Roberts. I accept you do not agree with that, but we are the ones that have to take responsibility for it because we're in government.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Even the UN's climate body is now walking it back.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The advice to government is very clear that we are going to have to continue to respond to high-risk weather seasons that disproportionately affect certain parts of the country and that that is as a direct result of the effects of climate change.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We'll rotate the call, and we'll go to Senator Kovacic.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I have some questions around the AusAlert system. Was the Office for Women consulted by NEMA during the design process of the AusAlert system?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I don't believe so, but I would like to confirm that.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Minister, do you know whether there was any consultation sought by your office in relation to the AusAlert system with the Office for Women?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I would have to check. I was certainly involved in discussions around AusAlert, as you would expect, including in the lead-up to the deployment.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Did you provide any guidance to them in relation to that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Many people, particularly victim-survivors of family and domestic violence rely on concealed mobile phones, as we know, and other devices. The AusAlert system overrides the do-not-disturb and silent-phone settings, and it plays a loud siren. Was this issue raised at any point by the Office for Women or by yourself, Minister, to NEMA about this design feature of the AusAlert system?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: There was consultation around this. It falls under the direct portfolio responsibility of Minister Plibersek, who deals with women's safety. I was certainly part of discussions on that. Across our offices there was extensive consultation, and I recall at least one discussion I had with the relevant minister.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: In conjunction with that—and I note the earlier question being taken on notice—was any guidance provided to NEMA by the Office for Women in relation to an awareness campaign around the AusAlert system being tested and what that would mean for individuals with concealed devices?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: DSS had carriage of that side of things under Minister Plibersek's portfolio. I can see if I can get an update. They appear later in the week, but I'll see if there's anything further I can provide about that. I'm aware I spoke to a couple of community organisations that were advising on how to appropriately respond to that trial, that test run.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Shadow Minister McIntosh and I wrote to Minister McBain in relation to this as well. We were quite concerned some time out about the risk. So I was curious whether either you or the office provided any feedback in relation to that or whether any of those concerns were expressed.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: The answer to that is yes. I'm just looking at a note. There was a lot of engagement with the safety sector on how to manage and how to communicate the trial safely, especially through frontline services through the DSS networks.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: What did they say in response in terms of their concerns around how to run the testing and the impacts then on women with concealed devices? Was it an approach that said, 'This is the only way to do this, and we will need to have an awareness campaign so that people know,' or was there any other sort of thought process put into it or feedback from them that said what was the best way to deal with the test to ensure that it didn't impact people?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I think that's one that we have to refer to DSS because they were dealing with that side. But I think I'm appearing with them later in the week.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Okay. Finally then, following the AusAlert test on 27 July, did the Office for Women request any information or briefings from NEMA or any other departments about the test impact on victim-survivors of domestic and family violence? Was there an uptick in reporting? Are you aware of any effects?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Across office levels, we had been involved. I was not briefed on any problematic outcomes after that trial. But, again, I think we'll just leave it—I'm sure Minister Plibersek and her department will be able to go through if there were any additional concerns raised.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: And the Office for Women meets with that part of DSS with great frequency, and those issues were not raised with us.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I note your interest in this space, because you're running the systems abuse audit. Is that right?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Did that flag any concerns for you, in relation to that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: One of the things that we are doing through the systems abuse audit is trying to embed safety-by-design principles in the design of new systems but also—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes—hence my question.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes. So we certainly are looking at safety by design in different systems and encouraging other agencies to build that into the design and upgrade of their systems.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Did your office request any data to establish whether there was an increase in reported domestic and family violence incidents after the test?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Minister Plibersek and I have a pretty clear delineation of responsibilities. She has responsibility for women's safety. We work across that, as we do. But that would be more appropriate a question for DSS.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Sure. I note that, and I accept elements of that. But it was more about the data piece, given the courage of work in relation to the abuse audit.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: As Ms Leahy said earlier, we haven't been told, and we do work with them on a weekly basis, so the questions are probably better put to them in terms of whether they have any data. Certainly, they haven't alerted us to the fact that there was an increase.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text:
In an answer to QON 861 from last estimates, the Department of the PM&C expressly identified the following—and I'll quote—as work led by the Office for Women:

• leading coordination and publication of regular updates on the progress of the audit of Australian Government systems,

and guidance on applying safety by design principles across the Australian Public Service.

Just to have clarity in my own mind, if the office coordinates work to identify and prevent government systems being weaponised by perpetrators of domestic violence, is there an inverse role of identifying the risks associated with the AusAlert as well—how that would actually expose someone who was trying to protect themselves?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I absolutely take your point, and I think it's a very good one. We were aware of a range of activity happening in the lead-up to the AusAlert test, including by the women's safety sector, ensuring that women were aware of what the impact would be on devices that were set to silent or 'do not disturb'. The scope of the audit is largely focused on how perpetrators of family and domestic violence are actively engaging with systems to weaponize them against victim-survivors. The work that has been underway to date has been particularly focused in the last 12 months on the child support system as well as closing financial abuse loopholes, particularly through coerced directorships and perpetrator access to superannuation. But certainly there is broader work as well happening across the Australian public service in relation to embedding safety by design in systems so that those systems aren't able to be weaponised.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Have you requested any of that data in relation to whether there was an increase in incidents post the testing?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We meet on a reasonably regular basis. There are a couple of governance mechanisms that sit under the system's abuse audit, including the Department of Home Affairs, Department of Social Services and a range of other departments related to this particular. Through that convening and governance, this matter hasn't been raised in that kind of formal setting where we're explicitly looking at systems abuse, which is a good forum in which to explore these sorts of issues. But then there are also our informal engagements, from which that hasn't emerged.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Just to clarify: I note you said that it wasn't raised, but you haven't specifically sought any data in relation to any spikes in incidents after that test?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: No. The expectation would be that, if there was, it would be an issue that would be raised through those forums.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: As a matter of course, it wouldn't need to be asked about.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, it would be that area's responsibility to raise it, and that hasn't occurred. But the government will be working through. I don't know if Minister McBain's areas of emergency management have dealt with this today, but obviously lessons learnt from the AusAlert trial will be considered as well if there are—I mean, it was a particular set of circumstances in that there was a national trial of this system, as opposed to more localised utilisation of it, that I think elevated the concerns around women's safety.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I do have an updated piece of information, which is that the team in the Office for Women responsible for the systems abuse audit did reach out to NEMA ahead of the trial and share with them safety-by-design guidance.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Great. Thank you very much.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts, over to you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Your website references the Women's Agenda 2023 report titled The climate load, a report whose only original data is an online poll of 600 of the publication's own readers. Are you aware that even this very limited report found that 27 per cent of women surveyed expected difficulty paying their energy bills within the next three months, that insurance premiums are rising around 10 to 11 per cent annually due to inflation and weather related risks and that being able to afford air conditioning is a major factor in coping with heat? Aren't these cost-of-living issues?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes. Weather related risk is associated with some of those you just read out yourself. That is exactly why we are putting in place—the huge transition that's underway now is to deal with these things. I accept that you're in a position where you can not agree, but government is different. We have to respond to the issues that we are facing right now. The fact is we are replacing and essentially rebuilding an energy system in this country because of ageing infrastructure that is breaking down. Those investments are about building an energy system that works and has the most affordable energy on offer, which is the shift to renewables. I accept you don't agree with it.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I go by data from around the world. But anyway—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, you go with selective data. I've sat in front of you—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: How dare you say that?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, I've sat in front of you for a number of years, and I would say you use certain data and not all data.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: If the driver of women's poor housing is income, housing supply and family violence, what does linking them to the climate change agenda achieve for those women that tackling those issues directly would not? Why don't you attack the real issues?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: In relation to specifically—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Housing—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We are. If you actually look at all of the things that we have done in trying to improve and support women, whether it's in women's safety, whether it's in women's wages, whether it's in women's health, whether it's in housing that's appropriate for women, whether it's in ensuring that they get the jobs and training that they need, whether it's making the childcare system work for women—all of those things are dealing with the real life issues that women face across the economy. The fact is that we are also responding to a change in climate and rebuilding an energy system in this country. Those things are all happening together.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Do you understand the difference between natural variability, cyclical variability and process change statistically?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Well, I agree that we disagree on the science around the climate.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: We have 24,000 data sets from around the world that show not one physical attribute of climate is changing. They're just varying naturally and cyclically. So let's move on. If we woke up tomorrow and the world had completely forgotten about the two words 'climate change', these problems would still exist. Telling Australians that weather affects women more than men doesn't house a single woman or pay a single power bill. Is the Office for Women advocating for women or using women to advocate for the government's climate agenda?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: If you look at the work that we have done since coming to government—and it's outlined in our Working for Women strategy, which has a focus on economic equality, women's health, the role that care plays in the economy and ending gender based violence, which is the major issue affecting women economically and socially in this country—that is the focus of the work that we have been doing. The interaction of gender policy and climate policy, I would argue, is real, but the focus has been on those other areas that I've just talked about and outlined through the Working for Women strategy.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I must say I'm a little perplexed by the approach taken by the Office of Women when it supports non-biological women, trans women, biological males, and seems to ignore the calls for women-only spaces for privacy and safety by straight and lesbian biological women. When those women are in conflict over access to women's spaces, which groups do you support? English correctional facilities have resolved this by placing trans women offenders, biological males, in men's prisons. I've not heard of a trans male, a biological female, being violated in a women's prison. Concerns have been raised with me by women—and remember, this is coming from a woman—that, if a trans woman were to be placed within the female population of a women's prison, it would be an issue of safety of the other residents. There are certainly reports of violence by trans women towards biological women. One would think that the Office of Women would stand up for the protection of biological women. This is happening in English correctional facilities, which have woken up to their mistakes. Has common sense returned and prevailed in the UK? Why do you support trans women rather than women?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: You would understand that corrections is a matter for states and territories.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Why do you support it though?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: I don't support—we don't have a role in making corrections policy.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: So is your office really the 'Office for Trans Women'?

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: A lot of these questions were dealt with last night through the Attorney-General's portfolio. I can be very clear to you about the issues that the Office for Women works on. It is those areas of housing, health, the role of care, how women get good jobs, how they get paid well in jobs—

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Safety.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Yes, I was getting to women's safety—and women's safety, which impacts on all of those other areas that I just talked about. That is the work of the Office for Women. They and we are focused on dealing with the practical solutions to the problems faced by women in this country.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet Workplace Gender Equality Agency
text: Senator Roberts, on that point, we are going to move on. Office for Women and WGEA, thank you so much for your time. We do really appreciate you coming and spending time with us and answering our questions this morning. We will now release you from the program.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Welcome to Ms Curtis, Australian Public Service Commissioner, and other officers who are appearing here with you, and also the Australian government consulting officers. Thank you all for attending. Do you have an opening statement, Ms Curtis?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
I would like to make an opening statement; thank you for the opportunity. Before I begin, though, I would just like to join my colleagues in wishing the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, strength and every support in her recovery following the tragic attack in Wangaratta last Monday. As you're aware, this is my first appearance before the committee as the Australian Public Service Commissioner, having commenced in the role in early June, on 9 June, this year. I would like to acknowledge and thank Dr Subho Banerjee for acting as the commissioner before my commencement, including representing the commission at this Senate hearing on a previous appearance.

My immediate focus as the new commissioner has been on three things: planning for the future of the APS, building our people and capability, and keeping integrity at the centre of how we work and deliver. The government has been very clear about its ambition for the APS to be a model employer, and the current APS-wide bargaining round is an important part of delivering on that ambition. It is about a sustainable employment offer that helps the APS to attract, retain and develop the people and capabilities that it needs. That ambition extends to how we plan for and invest in our workforce. We are building on the strong foundations of APS reform work already undertaken, focusing on core public service skills and practical support to help agencies prepare for the workforce of the future. That includes preparing the APS to use emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence responsibly and effectively.

Capability, as we know, goes hand in hand with integrity. The APS has strong integrity foundations, and my focus is on keeping integrity at the centre of our work, embedding it in everyday decisions, behaviours and workplace culture. Where matters do warrant further investigation, the commission will continue its statutory responsibilities and undertake them appropriately, proportionately and with impartiality. I look forward to discussing the work of the APS Commission with the committee today and at future hearings. Thank you.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thanks very much and welcome to estimates in general. We will start with Senator Hume.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you, Ms Curtis. First of all, I want to ask a question of the minister here—I think you had questions about it earlier today—about the Four Corners reporting last weekend of widespread discrimination of pregnant public servants and public servants returning from maternity leave. I suppose I want to ask first when you first became aware or were approached for comment. Were you approached for comment prior to the publication of that Four Corners episode?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'd have to check that. I don't recall being approached. I wasn't asked to participate. I will check with the media team on that. I think I just became aware when they promoted the show ahead of normal programming. I think it's usually on the morning of the evening that that goes to air.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The report showed that 24 public servants have made the extraordinary step to go to the media with claims of being demoted, denied flexibility, turned down for promotion, refused a comfortable place to breastfeed, or being made redundant or let go after they fell pregnant or took parental leave. I'm interested to know whether this is something that the Public Service takes seriously—is it the tip of the iceberg?—and whether the APSC is aware of this systemic issue across the Public Service.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I will just draw on some of my colleagues to help with this answer. I think we have a couple of colleagues here that can give you some data and give you some indication of what the evidence we have about this issue is. It is spread across the commission, so I might just throw to Ms Jo Talbot first, who can give you some broad data, and then we have Dr Nicole Steele, who looks after our APSC database. We do have some things that are relevant to the conversation that might give you an indication of the issue at hand and how prolific or otherwise we think this is.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. Thanks.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As the APS Commissioner has said, we do actually collect data relating to complaints that might be made. Dr Steele will be able to give you some data in relation to gender and caring, which is how we actually break down that information. I might just get her to do that. But what I would say is that, in response to that promotion of Four Corners, I did ask Dr Steele to have a look at our data, to see whether we were aware of any particular complaints, but also our ethics advisory service, to see whether anyone had come forward. I'll just get Dr Steele to go through that information.
witness_position: First Assistant Commissioner, Workforce, Tribunals and Inclusion

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Every year we collect data on the reported complaints of discrimination—as reported to an agency's HR system—and we report on that every year in the State of the Service report. I have the most recent information, which is from the last financial year, 2025-26. We break down the complaints of discrimination into several categories. Of most relevance would be the number of complaints for caring responsibilities—that's eight complaints—and the number of complaints on gender discrimination, and that's 10 complaints.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Over what period of time, did you say?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: 2025-26—the financial year.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Just in the last financial year?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Just in the last financial year.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. I'm assuming this is information that you've reported back to the minister.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. And we publish it as well.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: [inaudible] always publish data.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. So what was your response when you saw that data?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's data that's reported every year. This has been something we've been working on and don't stop working on, really. It's why we've been looking at how we can provide better flexibility through our enterprise agreements. It's why we're extending paid parental leave, including to the second parent. It has informed a lot of our thinking about employment conditions at work. We don't individually—those complaints are not complaints that we seek to resolve, but they inform our thinking, and we want to see no complaints. We've got no tolerance for discrimination on matters of care or pregnancy across the board in the APS.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I might just add to the minister's comments. The minister said earlier, and the previous officers that were here from different departments, that we are looking at what's happening in bargaining, and I can say that some of the issues that are raised around conditions for parents returning to the workplace are being addressed in the current bargaining round. We do actually have our chief negotiator here today that can talk about some of those things that have been put forward as initial proposals on the table, but obviously we are still in bargaining. I would say, looking back over the data, though, that we don't see a really significant trend towards this that's come through in our data. That's not to say there aren't issues in the workplace, but the provisions that are in our enterprise agreements and in legislation really do, I would say, put agencies in a very strong position to be able to manage their workforces effectively, and most agencies have very strong mechanisms for people to speak up if they do feel that they're discriminated against.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I suppose, in that context, then, the Four Corners episode must have come as something of a surprise. Did either you as the APSC or you as the minister seek to find out the veracity of the claims that were reported in that Four Corners episode, or find out whether there was some correlation between that data and the data that you've collated yourselves?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Jo Talbot, my colleague, did actually speak to the Department of Home Affairs. She might be able to give you a little bit more information on that space.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When I saw the promotion of that episode, I actually reached out to Ms Blight, who is the chief people officer at the Department of Home Affairs, to understand a little bit more in and around that. As I mentioned earlier, I also went to have a look at what our data holdings were, given, as you have indicated, the inference was that there were 24 public servants. But the data that we've got is obviously only over the last number of years, and it doesn't break down into the matters that the Four Corners episode went into, but—
witness_position: First Assistant Commissioner, Workforce, Tribunals and Inclusion

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So it's not necessarily inconsistent?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: There are very low numbers in our actual data. What I would say is that we have a range of legislation that we operate under—the Fair Work Act, the maternity leave act and the Sex Discrimination Act. We do a lot of work to ensure that APS agencies and departments are aware of their obligations. We also have our APS Gender Equality Strategy. There are a range of supports and things that are in place. As the APS Commissioner has said, these are the matters are around flexibility and parental leave and other arrangements that underpin the enterprise agreements.
witness_position: First Assistant Commissioner, Workforce, Tribunals and Inclusion

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Certainly, I think, the number of complaints does not depict a systemic problem across the APS when you consider the size of the workforce and the number of people who take up parental leave and issues like that. The thing I am worried about, which will be dealt with partly in some of the bargaining—it's also how we do our work—is the people who aren't raising complaints. What are the things that we can remove or amend to ensure, as much as we can, that the flexibility in the arrangements for returning to work with young children after a period of leave, which seems to be one of the pressure points, is the best that it can be. The issue that's been raised with me—I haven't got an answer for it yet, but it is one we talked about in the earlier session—is that, as you move up the levels in the APS, it seems to become harder to balance those two roles, and that is because there's a belief that, if you're moving into the EL2 category or into the SES, part-time and flexible working arrangements should not apply and that they are full-time in-the-office roles. We've had discussions about that in estimates. That seems to be a particular area of pressure.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Hume, we're going to need to rotate the call. Obviously, we're going to come back to the APSC after lunch, but we have promised Senator Pocock a quick block before the lunch break.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Sure. I will have some more questions on this issue.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Welcome, Ms Curtis. It's great to hear about your commitment to integrity in the service and that that's going to be a real priority for you. I have some questions about a complaint letter lodged by Mr Michael O'Neill, former CEO of the Tax Practitioners Board, during the investigation of PwC in relation to the tax leaks scandal. The complaint letter was lodged with the ATO on 1 September 2025 and referred to the APSC on 5 December. I table the complaint letter and an email from Mr O'Neill giving consent for the tabling of the document. I have some questions about the role of the APSC in relation to this matter.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I confirm that this has also been referred to the Economics Legislation Committee.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's right. My questions relate to the APSC role.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm sure that will proceed independently. I will make sure you receive a copy of that document. Mr O'Neill makes a number of allegations in his complaint email with reference to, firstly, breaches of the APS Code of Conduct; then evidence provided at parliamentary hearings and responses to questions on notice which go to questions of privilege, which are being picked up at the economics committee; the ongoing bullying, harassment and threats against him as the TPB CEO and secretary, as he was at the time of the PwC matter; then a whole range of issues related to the independence of the TPB, the Tax Practitioners Board; and the TPB's investigations in relation to PwC and Mr Peter John Collins. I start by asking: what was the process undertaken by APSC in the investigation of the matter?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm going to have to ask my colleague Dr Tracey to come to the table because, as you would be aware, I was working at the tax office prior to this role. But Dr Tracey has dealt with this matter since he's been at the commission, which is also a slightly shorter time than me. But he also has representatives here from the department that can speak to the issue.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Hello, Senator. Lovely to speak to you today. I can speak in broad terms to the commission's handling of procedures as you've articulated there. I would say at the outset that the commission's ordinary practice is not to speak about individual matters, but I appreciate you've tabled documentation. I haven't had a chance to read that, but I will speak in general terms to the commission's processes.

Concerns raised by Mr O'Neill were proactively referred by the tax commissioner to the APSC. At that time, the former commissioner of the Public Service Commission delegated decision-making authority in relation to considering the matters that had been referred to us to an independent delegate—to someone outside of the commission.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I just clarify, Dr Tracey. You're referring to this document in your comments here, are you—because you received this in December last year at the APSC.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't have a copy of that in front of me, unfortunately, and so I'm not able to verify.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: A copy will be provided to you. It is the document provided—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

To come back to your point around process, though, as I said, upon referral by the tax office to the commission, the former commissioner appointed an independent delegate to carefully and thoroughly consider the matters that were referred to us, and that independent decision-maker has assessed very carefully all of the matters that were raised, and the matter is now concluded.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

text: I'm mindful again of the fact that, when we talk about individual inquiries conducted exercising the commissioner's statutory functions, we operate in this space where the information we obtain is confidential information and protected information under the Public Service Act. So it's not usually the level of detail we would speak to in these matters.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Which of the allegations made by Mr O'Neill were investigated by the APSC, remembering the investigations were breaches of the code of conduct and bullying accusations against him?
