Which of those accusations were pursued by the APSC to investigate?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Again, without going to the detail of what concerns may or may not have been referred to the commission for consideration, what I would say is that our ordinary practice with any integrity related referral is to carefully consider all of the concerns that are raised to us by anyone who comes through. What we do with any integrity intelligence that comes to us through different channels is that we assess the nature of any concerns raised against the information that the commission has to hand and we map that, effectively, to what the commissioner's statutory functions are under the Public Service Act and a delegate of the commissioner makes a decision about appropriate action. I appreciate that your question goes to specifics—again, I think we're straying into territory where the commission is very mindful of the confidentiality that applies to this information. But, in general terms, we assess the entirety of information that's referred to us by anyone who wishes to reach out to raise concerns of any nature.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: There are very specifically different categories of complaint here. Did you pursue the bullying, harassment and adverse action complaint that Mr O'Neill has made?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Pocock, can I just jump in here, because I think—we've had this discussion before about what information the commission is able to discuss in relation to code of conduct matters, as allowed or required under the Public Service Act. It is very constrained. I'm not sure about whether there's another way, perhaps with Mr O'Neill giving certain permissions to you, that this can be done, for you to get the information that you need. They are constrained, by law, about what can be discussed publicly, specifically in relation to individual complaints. I think Dr Tracey has been trying to say that, at a general level, we look at all the issues that are referred to us, but I'm not sure we can go one by one through Mr O'Neill's complaint. We considered this at length during the robodebt code of conduct inquiries and some of the constraints on the commission at that time. The code of conduct investigations have offered protections to people involved in it so that we don't head down legalistic—it's really been a pathway to assess and investigate employment related concerns in a non-legalistic way. The minute we open that up into a broader discussion about individual complaints—I think that that will see the commission lose the ability to actually undertake these very important investigations. I'm not trying to frustrate. I just wonder if there is a different way that we can get you the information other than a public hearing.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, Dr Tracey and I had a chat about that in the break—about the tabling of it and some of our concerns over that. I'm just going to throw to Dr Tracey, who will explain those to the committee so that you can see where we stand on this issue and what you would like to do about it.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

So we would ask the committee, on your indulgence, to have regard to those matters in the disclosure of any information that's in this document, particularly in circumstances where information that's referred to the commission may be the subject of future processes as well. What we're mindful of is how that interacts with, or might inadvertently impact, how future matters are handled. agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I just want to follow up on some of the questions that I was asking before about the Four Corners episode last week that reported widespread discrimination against pregnant public servants and public servants returning from maternity leave. My understanding is that it was Minister Rishworth who responded to those claims, but, Minister, as Minister for Women and Minister for the Public Service, did you make a response?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, and I checked over the break. A Four Corners journalist asked if I, or a relevant government minister, could sit down and do an interview on their story, but I don't think it was specific that it was about the APS, so it was referred to Minister Rishworth to deal with under her portfolio responsibilities.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Having seen the show now and knowing that it was about the APS, is the Minister for the Public Service going to formally respond?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The response is in the work that we're doing.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Alright, well, that's actually a good question. Can you tell me what steps you've taken to ensure the Commonwealth meets its basic employer obligations?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Through the work that the APSC does all the time. We're not responsible for individual complaints within agencies, but we do have a broad responsibility across the APS to ensure that agencies understand their responsibilities under law. In addition, issues being ventilated through bargaining, of which this is one, around flexibility at work are being considered.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Sorry, I just want to understand whether you have taken any specific actions in response to the Four Corners episode.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
This is a piece of ongoing work. We've done a lot of reform in the APS to ensure that there are good conditions of employment for everyone who works here. That's why we've extended parental leave, including to the other parent—the second parent, the non-birth parent. It's why we've included flexibility arrangements in the EBA, which I know others in this place have criticised over time. That is in direct response to ensuring that we are supporting people with different caring responsibilities in the workplace, and that work will continue.

There is zero tolerance for not following the law. Pregnancy discrimination is unlawful and should not occur anywhere, and the APS should lead the way. It's a model employer. It has to set the standard, and that is a very clear instruction from the APSC and from me. I think it's well understood across government. If we received an example or a complaint, we would pursue it. I urge women to come forward if that has been their experience.

More often than not, as I was saying to you before lunch, the thing I worry about most is that people don't make a complaint and how to deal with that—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, but that it might be systemic.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: How do you make SES and EL2 jobs more available on a part-time basis? That's a big issue in the APS. I hear that from women. We're considering that as part of both the culture and the bargaining that's under way.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
The Department of Home Affairs responded to the Four Corners episode by stating, and I'm quoting:

Any expenditure of resources, including the engagement of staff, must be considered within the department's budget and in accordance with its obligations under the Public Governance Performance and Accountability Act

You're the minister responsible for the PGPA Act. I don't know of anywhere where it says in that act that it can somehow be used as a shield for discriminatory practices against women.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, it can't.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay, so is that an inadequate response from—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And the act, though I have responsibility for it, actually devolves the responsibility to agencies for the decisions they take. That's what the PGPA Act actually establishes. You are the accountable authority for the purposes of your budget. I haven't seen that full quote—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It does sound, though, like an inadequate response from Home Affairs, surely?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think they're separate issues. How you live within budget and whether you discriminate on the grounds of pregnancy are two different things.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator, I might just let you know that the commission has actually followed up with Home Affairs. One of our officers has checked the circumstances of this matter. Just as the minister says, we can only look at issues that are brought to our attention. This has now been brought to our attention, and we are looking into the matter. I understand that Home Affairs will be prepared to answer some questions on this issue when they appear.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When you say that you're looking into this now, what does that mean?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: One of our officers has spoken to Home Affairs, as Ms Talbot said earlier in the hearing today. We have sought to understand the circumstances with their chief people officer. I understand there may have been further circumstances that they may not have put in the response you've just read out.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I want to turn to the termination of those that might be holding the position of secretary and how that might work, the process questions. I suppose I want to get an understanding of what role the APSC has in providing advice or support to government when a departmental secretary is terminated.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I might need to take this particular circumstance on notice because I haven't, to date, had to actually be in a position to provide any advice. I understand that I do get consulted, as the Public Service Commissioner, on these issues. To the extent of my knowledge, it is a consultation to see whether that is an appropriate course of action, as I understand that. I might check with Dr Tracey to see if there's anything further in the legislation that could expand on the answer for me. Otherwise, we'll take it on notice.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The short answer is that that is the thrust of it. It's a consultation provision. It is, effectively, given effect under section 59 of the Public Service Act.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Section 59, in my understanding, mandates that the Prime Minister has to receive a report from the Secretary of PM&C prior to the termination of a departmental secretary, and the report requires prior consultation with the APS commissioner. Have I missed anything?

text: Explain to me on what grounds the termination of a departmental secretary can occur.

text: What I want to understand is: when a termination occurs, would the Public Service Commissioner be required to provide a report in writing, or can the advice be verbal?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I want to go to the ANAO audit of the strategic commissioning framework. I have some questions about the way the framework works. What are the differences in the roles and responsibilities of the APSC, compared to the Department of Finance, on the strategic commissioning framework.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Firstly, we work very closely with our colleagues at the Department of Finance because many of these matters do traverse the responsibilities of the APSC and the Department of Finance. That's because, in the strategic commissioning framework, we were looking at aspects of external contractors and consultants in different ways, and that external spend issue is a vital interest of the Department of Finance, and they have responsibility for a range of reporting and other measures in that space.

In terms of the strategic commissioning framework itself, the APSC was the lead agency for the strategic commissioning framework, which looked specifically at this issue of core work. Because it was looking specifically at the issue of core work, it was looking at matters that particularly pertained to integrity and capability of core government functions. That was seen as an APSC responsibility, and so that's why it sat with us directly. Aspects that went to external expenditure are primarily a matter for the Department of Finance. Now, as I say, we work very closely with them, so when we were looking at the reporting, when we were looking at the implementation of the framework and throughout the framework we worked closely with Finance. But the primary distinction is that we're responsible—the APSC is responsible—for the strategic commissioning framework. The Department of Finance is responsible for the broader policies around external spend and the broader accounting standards in government—how they are reported and how that is put together—as well as a number of other measures that go to reducing the external spend. They're all matters for the Department of Finance.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The ANAO found that agencies could meet targets for reducing reliance on external labour while increasing overall external workforce expenditure. Minister, do you consider the framework to have been successful in meeting its central objectives, given these very contradictory outcomes?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, I do, and I disagree with the analysis by the ANAO.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. Tell us about that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Because the strategic commissioning framework was about a particular subset of work across the APS—the pieces of work that we've been very clear should be done by public servants. It was to deal with a particular issue when we came to government—what we saw as core Public Service work being outsourced, essentially. It was consultants sitting on management committees of departments, consultants writing cabinet submissions and things like that. That was the problem we were trying to fix. It was not to use the framework to cover every circumstance of Public Service work where external labour, whether it's contractors, consultants or labour hire, might be used. It was about a subset of work. I think the ANAO's view of what constitutes core Public Service work—maybe they have a different view on that than what the strategic commissioning framework was originally intended to deal with.

We've got two different things going on. We've got the strategic commissioning framework and then we've got another piece of work, which is about looking at how we reduce expenditure on consultants and contractors and labour hire. If you look at the conversions from labour hire to permanent public servant jobs—about 14,000 of those, I think, from memory. That's happening outside the strategic commissioning framework. That's part of a broader piece of work. But we've never said that the strategic commissioning framework would result in departments not being able to use consultants or contractors. There are two different things going on, and I'm not sure that was the interpretation that the ANAO took.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Are you saying the strategic commissioning framework is not about reducing spending on external consultants, labour hire—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It is part of it, but it's not the only thing.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So it's part of it.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
If you go back and have a look at the strategic commissioning framework, there are core functions. There's APS-wide core work: developing cabinet submissions, drafting legislation and regulation, leading policy formulations and roles that are on an agency's executive team. And then there were other core APS functions that should be brought back in house as a priority, noting that they may need some time to adjust because people might have been in longer term arrangements: undertaking procurement, managing contracts, cost-benefit analysis and some of the work around grants. So I think we were pretty clear about what the strategic commissioning framework was intended for.

The other thing I would say—because this has turned into an assessment of whether agencies are doing the right thing or not, for those that don't want to see a use of consultants or contractors in the public service—is that the big uplift occurred in a relatively short period of time. So, with this issue of target setting, where you don't set a target now because you've insourced all that work and you've changed those arrangements, it's hard to then set a target to do something you've already done. In that sense, the strategic commissioning framework doesn't reflect that.

I'm giving some thinking, while I look at the ANAO report, to how we deal with that challenge. Services Australia brought a lot of people in through labour hire before they had to report under the strategic commissioning framework. So they did the right thing, because we'd asked them to insource jobs that had been outsourced. But then, because they'd done that, in the first reporting year, they looked like they weren't making a big effort, because they'd already made the big effort and it wasn't captured. So there are some issues there that I think we have to turn our mind to, about how the strategic commissioning framework applies over the longer term. Perhaps, the target setting should have been for a time limited period before moving into just accepting that 'this is the definition of APS core work and you're not to outsource it, and that's the way things are.'

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The ANAO found that 12 of the 22 sampled entities increased their spending on external labour in 2024-25. What is this telling us about the effectiveness of the framework? They aren't all agencies that had a massive cut in the year or two beforehand. There really is a problem, is there not, that we aren't seeing the reduction in consultants and contractors that this is meant to be driving?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Again, I think this really goes to the scope question. The ANAO, through that report, puzzlingly keep going back to the full spend on all of the consultant/contractor outsourced providers—everything that is an external spend. Within that, they then say a small percentage—and the rough approximation they use is about three per cent—is covered by the strategic commissioning framework. The strategic commissioning framework, for what it was considered to do, in the report itself is shown to be successful. The targets were met. We've discussed previously that the targets came substantially from two agencies. But there were a number of other agencies that also reported. For those other agencies, they reported getting to about 82 per cent of their target requirements as well. So, while the bulk was in these two agencies, it was widespread. There was good-faith engagement all the way across.

The fact that you just quoted that through your question—that is, the 12 of the 22—is on the basis, again, of the full external spend. There was never any suggestion and there was never any implication that the strategic commissioning framework would cover the whole of the external spend. So the idea that it has gone up in 12 of the 22 entities is a completely different matter. It's a different piece of work. When the ANAO looked specifically at the targets in the strategic commissioning framework itself, it found that those targets were met overall. It found that there was engagement across all the entities that were within scope. And it found, as the minister had said, that there was actually substantial effort in the first two years, to the point where a large number of agencies, the majority of agencies, got to a point where they no longer felt like they were outsourcing core work.

This definition of 'core work', as I said, is fundamentally an integrity question—things that should have been done by public servants being done by public servants. It's a good thing that agencies have had a really serious look at that, they've brought that in and they can now declare through their annual report that that has now been done. On that three per cent, that was three per cent where there were integrity or capability questions of a very acute nature.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Isn't it the case that there are very diverse definitions of 'core work' across agencies? I talked to the ANAO about that yesterday. Isn't that a problem?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: During the design, we set out—the minister actually read out the section in the framework document—some functions that it seemed clear to us would be core work on an APS-wide basis, such as drafting cabinet submissions, the work in the executive board and other things like that. In the consultations, it was very clear to us that, across the range of agencies that would be in scope—and it's over 100 agencies—how each would think about core work is inevitably very different in different types of agencies. It depends on the type of work that you're doing. For example, in those 100 agencies, there are some relatively small agencies. They might well do some quite technical work, only occasionally, to support a particular project or to support a budget bid or to support something like that. That piece of work, for them, might not be core compared to their other delivery responsibilities, but, in an analytical policy agency, that similar piece of work might be core. So that consideration of exactly what is core really does depend on the agency context. Consistent with the devolved nature of the financial framework, accountable authorities are responsible for making sure that this is done in a responsible way. The reporting is through the annual reports, and they need to assess against the framework, which is very clear, around the expectation that core work will be done in-house.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Given the differences between your perception and the ANAO report, did you go back and forward with them to negotiate, and what changed?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We talked to them extensively through the process, and, in the report itself, as is customary, they reproduced the letter that the APSC also put at the end of the process. In that letter, we make it clear, again, that we think that the scope was not the scope that was originally the policy intent. The framework document itself literally starts with 'core work needs to be done in-house by APS employees'. That is a position that we put consistently to the ANAO. Of course, it's the prerogative of the ANAO to publish the report in full.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: How does the APSC plan to improve the framework looking ahead?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As we said in the report, there are still things to improve in the framework, particularly in the implementation of the framework. One of the things that agencies had said to us consistently is that, when we were thinking about core work, because it was trying to get to this policy and public admin concept of what the things are that have to be done in-house and what poses an integrity risk in-house—that's different to an accounting concept. There wasn't really a natural fit from accounting systems or a natural form of reporting for that. So we've been thinking really carefully about how to get that information in a reliable and authoritative way and in a way that doesn't put too much further reporting burden on agencies. We're working with our Department of Finance colleagues on that. That's been raised with us over time, and we've got further work to do.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If we zoom out and reflect on change over time, there was $20 billion in external spending in the last year of the Morrison government. We're back to about that level now. What does this say about the effort of this government on this really important priority of rebuilding the public sector and reducing reliance on external contractors, consultants and so on? That's the bottom line here, isn't it? Are we getting this down? The figures suggest to me that we are not.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Would I like to see more? Yes, I would. But we're also doing a lot more. This is ongoing work for me. We've got a much busier Public Service in a whole range of areas. If you look at some of those departments where you've seen an increase in spending on some consultants, they are in those really technical areas. DCCEEW was one of them, I think. We'd seen a big increase in the use of consultants and contractors, which was not unusual, I would think, in the energy transition, where you're getting specialist advice at times. And there are some other areas. We've got an enhanced effort in the Pacific and in our local region, so you can see DFAT has increased expenditure in the area. What I'm trying to do is work out what is reasonable and what is work that can and should be done by the extra public servants that we've employed across the APS. It's an ongoing piece of work. How the strategic commissioning framework sits within that and how we deal—we will look at what the ANAO report says and the views it has. But I'm not going to have a framework that sets unreal tests or tests for agencies that are hard to meet. I'd prefer something that was just very clear on what is core public service work and can't be outsourced where accountable authorities are responsible for the decisions they take outside of that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm going to follow up on a couple of Senator Pocock's questions. On that issue around the ANAO finding that agencies are able to create their own definition of core work and that there wasn't a consistent APS-wide definition, how many agencies that defined their own definition of core work then revised their definition between 2024-25 and 2025-26?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It was a matter for agencies in each of the years to look at what they thought was core work.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Do they do that prospectively or do they do that retrospectively?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: They do that prospectively. In the first two years, those that had work that was covered by the SCF set a target, and for that they had to specify on what basis they set that target. But the overall accountability requirement remains that accountable authorities have to report back through the established processes, including through annual reports and now through corporate plans as well. These are serious accountability requirements. The idea that they have to then test against a set of principles about what constitutes core work for themselves is a judgement that they need to make, and we have absolutely no evidence that that is not a judgement that's being taken in good faith.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: On notice, can you provide me a list of agencies that revised their definition of core work between the years 2024-25 and 2025-26? I'm also interested in knowing how many agencies have set no target number for insourcing in that 2025-26 year. Have you got a list of those?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'll ask Ms Sedgwick to help with the second part. With the first part—and perhaps I wasn't sufficiently clear—each year, if we take an individual agency, they had to think about what constituted core work.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, but surely it's not going to change from year to year on a regular basis. You know what your core work is.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You might get some changes at the margin as they're thinking about exactly where the functions of the department are, what the work of the department is and what the prioritisation is. But each year each agency did that exercise. In a sense, the answer to your question is that—
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: All of them.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: every agency that was covered thought about what constituted core work each year.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: They've changed their own definition of core work each and every year.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It depends on what you mean by definition there, because they assessed against the same set of principles but they looked at what constituted core work or not. It is a requirement for accountable authorities to make sure that that is done in good faith in the proper way in terms of public management. The number of agencies that haven't set targets for this year—
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We published an update around this time in 2025 setting out agency targets for the 2025-26 financial year. I think it was about 40 agencies that set a target. The bulk of the other agencies reported that they were operating in line with the framework and were not required to set a target. Which agencies did and didn't set a target is in the public update, but we can table that information if it's helpful.
witness_position: Assistant Commissioner, Organisational and Workforce Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: If you could, that would be helpful. My understanding is that basically all of the reported savings under the framework came from Defence and the ATO. How did Defence and the ATO define their core work?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We can look to communicate with those two agencies to follow up as to how they have specified core work themselves. But, as I said before, there was full engagement from all agencies that were in scope. The numbers were larger in two of the larger agencies, partly recognising the circumstances of those two agencies. But overall all agencies that were in scope that had set targets—agencies got to about 82 per cent overall in terms of the achievement of those targets, excising those two large agencies.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So, for the two biggest agencies that make up the bulk of the claims of savings, you can't actually verify their claims. Is that right?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As I've explained, I think, the decision about core work, the analysis of core work and the assessment of core work is an agency matter, so it was never intended that there would be some sort of central assessment of each and every agency and how they reported. There was a set of principles enunciated. Agency heads were responsible for thinking about what constituted core work against that. Agencies, to the best of our knowledge, have done that in a responsible and good-faith manner. We engaged very closely with agencies through the implementation process. There was very close interest and engagement in how to think about core work across the working group, and, as far as we are aware, that is something that has been taken seriously all the way across the scope of the framework.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It may have been taken seriously, but, to be honest, if the ANAO has given a rather scathing report that clearly the framework is ineffectual and the APSC has given ministerial approval to remove the formal reduction targets and the public progress updates for 2026-27, doesn't this essentially say that the work has ended?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
That's not our view. The ANAO report, as was canvassed in estimates last night, gave its findings overall. For the framework overall, they found that it was partly effective against that scope that we've been discussing now, which is a scope that for some reason was considered across the total external spend rather than against the commissioning framework itself. In the commissioning framework itself, in the report itself, it makes the point that the targets have been met and exceeded. Indeed the report itself says that the APSC was largely effective in the implementation of the framework.

There was clearly a further conversation about what the scope is. We've looked to draw that out through this conversation here today and more broadly, as I've said to Senator Pocock, through the engagement with the ANAO. They have audited against a much, much larger scope than the framework itself. As I mentioned to Senator Pocock, the Strategic Commissioning Framework targets came to about three per cent of that total spend. If the audit scope is somehow the larger scope, then that's a different matter. But, when they have comments within the report itself about the framework, they're clear that the targets were met and that the implementation was largely effective.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
The report says:

Better clarity on scope could have assisted the APSC in ensuring the Framework would be effective at achieving all aspects of the policy intent. The APSC's scope for the Framework was an unclearly defined and small part of all government external workforce spending. As 'core work' is not a clearly established and consistently applied APS concept, the APSC does not have an estimate of what 'core work' represents across APS supplier or external workforce expenditure … .

The ANAO just yesterday said, 'Our language of a partly effective conclusion is a negative conclusion.' I think that itself is something of concern.

Let me be very clear about what it is that I would like from you on notice. That is a list of agencies who revised their definition of what their core work is between 2024-25 and 2025-26. You've said that that's all of them. If that is all of them, that's fine, but I do want a list. I also want to understand exactly how many agencies set no target for insourcing in the 2025-26 year, so I want a list of those. I'd also like an understanding of what the annual cost was of collecting, checking and publishing framework data since inception, because there must be millions of taxpayer dollars that have been spent not achieving what this framework was supposed to achieve.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I disagree. It has achieved what the framework set out to do.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I ask then—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Agencies reach their targets. We've been clear about what core work is with the ability for agencies to add or revise based on their needs.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I must have missed something then because my understanding is that the framework was designed to contribute to the successive budget measures that collectively projected about 14—in fact, I think it was—$14.8 billion in external labour savings from 2022-23 to 2029-30. The whole point of the framework—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: was to—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No!

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: and external labour hires.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I just went through this with Senator Pocock. No, it wasn't. It's a subset responding to the government that you served in that had consultants writing cabinet submissions, writing legislation and sitting on management committees.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But they're still doing that according to Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, they are not.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: She reckons that there's still exactly the same amount of money being spent on external consultants—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, they are not. That is a different point that she is making. That is a different point. There are not consultants sitting on management committees of agencies writing cabinet submissions or writing legislation. We have been very clear on that. This is the disagreement that I have around how the strategic commissioning framework is being interpreted. It was to establish a set of core work principles which agencies could refine for their own operational reasons if they wanted to. It was never the avenue to deliver all of those savings. Never. Not once have I said that—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: What was the avenue to deliver those savings?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And in fact, the target that was set in the first year was $527 million from memory. And I think we got close to 550. But the problem we're in now is that, as you say, Defence, ATO and I think the NDIA all did the heavy lifting because they had a lot of outsourced core work. Services Australia also did, but they did it before the strategic commissioning framework came in. Now we're in a position where the framework is being used as a way of saying 'you're not doing what you said you would do' because the big areas of reform have happened. They've brought that work back in.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The claim was a $14.8 billion saving from external labour.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Is there any other reporting mechanism other than this framework where you are tracking the efforts to achieve what is nearly $15 billion in savings?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We go through this in finance. We take that money off agencies. It's gone. That's the tracking of it. It's gone. It's not provided to agencies.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But there's exactly the same amount of money that's being spent on external labour now as there was when that claim was made.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
The 14.8 has been achieved. We have removed that from agency appropriations. It's a budget decision. It happens at budget time. That has happened. Running alongside that, there is the strategic commissioning framework, which is doing a different job, which is saying we do not want these particular tasks outsourced. It is core public service work. The targets that were set under that were in the order of over $500 million in one year, the first year of target setting. That has been achieved and reported against.

The point I'm making now is because that has been done, ongoing reporting of targets is difficult because the agencies have brought that work back in. If Defence did the heavy lifting and brought about $300 million in, they're not going to have another $300 million to bring in the next year because they've already made that decision. And that's the issue, I think, that we're wrestling with now that the strategic commissioning framework is in place.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It sounds to me like you claimed the savings of the $14.8 billion by simply cutting off those appropriations, but you've just shoved it elsewhere.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The same amount is being spent on external labour but just in different departments for different reasons.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We've taken the savings, and agencies have been given their appropriations and have to live within their appropriations that they are provided.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The ANAO highlighted that reductions in supplier expenditure under the framework were not a saving because agencies would have related employee costs.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. Most of them were conversions from contractors to permanent public service work. So that was the point.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So was there a $14.8 billion saving?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, because you're muddling two different things. We have removed the 14.8. It's gone. Agencies have had their agency budgets reduced by that amount. That is how we got that money back. We said, 'That is to come from reducing your reliance on consultants and contractors, labour hire, travelling'—a whole range of things. There were a whole range of things in that $14.8 billion. Then, separately to that, we've made sure that conversions—you've criticised us for expanding the size of the Public Service, and I know you were out there again saying you're going to sack thousands of people again but—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When have I said that?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The coalition have said—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

But, of that increase in public servants, about 14,000 are from converting labour hire into permanent Public Service jobs. So, yes, it is a reduced cost. There was a saving for agencies in that conversion because they're not paying the pass-through person; they're not paying the labour hire company. agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So is it a net saving?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The reduction, the $14.8 billion, is a saving. There is a net save. I don't know if I've got the figure with me.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So the insourcing compared to—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Insourcing has been cheaper than the expensive labour hire arrangements that were in place when we came to government.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'll see if I can provide you with the figure.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That is very helpful.
