agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have a few lines of questioning to go. A Canberra Times article published in July of this year reports that the federal government has removed the targets for reducing outsourcing of core work; is that true?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: This is the ground we've just been covering. After two years of the Strategic Commissioning Framework, we got to the point where a substantial number, over 60 agencies, had said to us that they were not going to set targets on the basis that they had minimal or no core work outstanding. This is the point the minister has just been making. Having put a lot of effort into the first two years, particularly around this core work issue where there might be integrity or capability concerns—you would expect agencies to move quickly on that—our assessment is that they did indeed move quickly. And, at that point, our assessment then was that targets were no longer as an effective measure for trying to drive this process forward.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Will you have any oversight of core work? How will you know what's happening?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Agencies are required to still put their plans in their corporate plan, to set out exactly what they're going to do, and then report against their progress in the annual report. The annual report, of course, is a report to parliament. Accountable authorities are required to put in that what action they are taking.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: How will the APSC ensure that an improved framework will measure and result in a sustained reduction in reliance, not just on consultants but on contractors and labour hire, rather than just a narrow expenditure target?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As we've been covering over the last conversation, in terms of integrity concern, in terms of ensuring that public servants are doing roles that only public servants can do, it's very important that accountable authorities are thinking about that against the principles in the Strategic Commissioning Framework. That is not principally a matter of targets. That's not principally a matter of dollar value. Some of the examples that the minister gave before were really not necessarily large amounts of dollar value. They were about the appropriateness of the role and that a public servant should have been doing that role. The accountability measure for that is through the corporate plan and through the annual report. The Strategic Commissioning Framework remains in force, and accountable authorities are clear about that requirement—that core work must be done by public servants. That is the principal measure for making sure that this integrity measure continues.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And do you expect then—is it a requirement—that corporate plans and annual reports will make specific reporting on the use of consultants, labour hire and external agencies in relation to core work?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: As it pertains to core work, yes, in those two—
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Only in relation to core work?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's the requirement under the strategic commissioning framework.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So, Minister, if I can come to you, why does the Commonwealth still lack a consistent and comparable reporting framework or mechanism—some way in which we can see a comparable report on the use of consultants, contractors and labour hire?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I believe the work we've done is appropriate for the role that the APSC plays in this. I have a disagreement with the ANAO's interpretation of what we're trying to do here.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Do you think the current devolved approach to financial reporting gives us enough visibility for you to manage the external workforce across the APS as a whole?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We can talk about this when Finance get here, but that's the way the PGPA Act has established the accountabilities for the public service. Secretaries are the accountable authorities for decisions made around their financial arrangements and how they work within budget. Would I like more central control with some of this? You're asking a minister from a central agency. I think that would be contested. But what we're trying to do is the role that Finance and APSC can bring to this, which is to give as much guidance as we can centrally and then ensure that the accountable authorities understand that and are doing what they need to do. But it would be contested, I would imagine, even at ministerial level.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Perhaps, we will return to that when Finance are in the room. I want to go to the KPMG ethics contract. It's contract No. CN4030135. It's worth $1.27 million. It provided training on ethics and leadership for the top public servants, 300 of them through the APSC via KPMG. I've raised concerns about this contract in previous estimates, and, in the middle of the year, I wrote to you, Minister, demanding or suggesting—requesting—that the contracts cease. It didn't stand up to any kind of pub test I can think of to have a multibillion-dollar operation clearly shown in the public square to be in breach of ethics requirements, engaging in cover-ups and unable to manage whistleblowers with anything like a decent response. I understand the contract's AusTender page was updated in August to say the contract ended on 31 July this year, not in December as originally planned. Can you confirm that this contract has ceased and that KPMG is no longer delivering it?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, we can confirm that that contract has ceased.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's good to know. Can you give us some information about the circumstances and the timing of the termination?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The contract ceased on 31 July.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Do you want to tell me why you ended it?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It is common in these contracts, particularly when we're thinking about capability development or leadership, to have specified personnel—people that are particularly qualified and that are assessed at the time of the tender process to be particularly suitable for the delivery of these programs in association with the APSC. We were notified that there were going to be some changes in the specified personnel in the KPMG contract. At that time, we reassessed because, as we in fact canvassed previously at this committee, KPMG had previously been using people that were very well qualified, including in the APS—that is, previous APS senior staff. When we were notified that the specified personnel were about to change, we reassessed our position at that time. This is common; when specified personnel change, that's a reasonable time for the government—in this case, the department—to think about whether or not it provides approval for different specified personnel. At that time, given the broader context, we made the decision that we would cease the contract. We were in a position where the remaining deliveries of that program were able to be handled in house. As I've covered with you previously, we had been in a co-facilitation arrangement around the program in any case, and we were able to assess that we would be able to handle the remaining months in house from there.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And have you contracted a new provider?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We have not.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Are you going to?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, we're intending to go to market. As I said previously, for the leadership programs, we—it's a longstanding practice and common to the way these sorts of leadership programs are done, in the private sector and in the public sector in different places, to partner with external experts to get external perspectives about leadership, about different sectors, about different approaches. That is a model that we have found to be very successful in the past. We've mentioned before that we've partnered with a range of different external organisations—universities, expert bodies, ANZSOG, other partners like that. We still think that is a good model, so we would intend to go to market.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Have you got any other contracts at the moment with KPMG?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: There is a technical contract on the finance side with KPMG.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And is that continuing?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'll ask Dr Tracey to provide some more information on that.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Before Dr Tracey answers that, though, I just want to comment on the course that you've been asking about and some of our other courses. I've spoken to the academy staff about what we will be doing, and our approach, going forward, is going to be trying to use subject matter experts from within the Public Service to help with the delivery of programs and to partner with agencies who've the expertise to be able to help us in this space. So, whilst we still will use partnerships with external providers, we are looking to reduce that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Anything that builds internal capability—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Pocock, I'm going to need to rotate the call.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes, sure, if I can just hear about any other sides of the—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Absolutely, yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Certainly, Senator, I can be succinct. The one other contract that the commission has with KPMG is to the value of $86,000. It's for technical IT assistance with one of the financial systems in the back end of the commission's IT.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Has there been any extension to that contract in recent times?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Not that I'm aware of, but I can take that on notice.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you. Let me know if you—thank you.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm going to take the opportunity to encourage senators to consider the questions that they need to ask, which is totally fine, and any questions they may have a burning desire to place on notice, given where we're at in the schedule. I'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have got some questions that I'll put on notice, but I do want to just clear up two things. First of all, I want to understand the process that the APSC has established to act on the agreed ANAO recommendations to improve the framework.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The recommendation that was agreed was particularly about reporting implementation, trying to streamline how agencies can report on strategic commissioning matters. We're working with the Department of Finance, as I mentioned in one of the previous answers, to just think about what the easiest way to do that is, given that it doesn't necessarily come through the existing finance accounting classifications.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Is there a timeframe on that?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That work will be ongoing with the Department of Finance.
witness_position: Assistant Commissioner, Organisational and Workforce Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Minister, you just said that you fundamentally disagree with the ANAO on this. How can we have any faith—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But I've also said—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: that the ANAO's recommendations are going to be acted on, if the relevant minister doesn't agree with the findings?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The recommendations and status have already been agreed. I've also said twice that we would consider the audit report in our thinking about next steps, essentially. So it will inform our thinking. But I don't want to set up a process where agencies are essentially punished or fail to reach targets because we've got a framework that might not, after the first couple of years, adequately reflect where we're at with core work. I just want the core work done in the APS. That's all I want. I don't want it outsourced. Core work should be done by public servants for the Public Service in the public interest, and that's what I want to make sure whatever we have surrounding that does.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I just want to be very clear. Finance only noted that recommendation; it didn't agree to it. Why didn't your department agree?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: To what recommendations in particular?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The first recommendation was a recommendation for the Australian government. It's conventional, when there's a recommendation to the government rather than to a department, that that recommendation is 'noted' rather than 'agreed'. The second recommendation was to the APSC, and we agreed that, again, it's conventional for a response that is directed to an agency or a department to be 'agreed' or 'not agreed'.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That won't preclude the APSC from working with the Department of Finance, even if the Department of Finance only noted the recommendation rather than—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: On recommendation 1. Recommendation 1 is a matter for Finance, and they're about to follow us. On recommendation 2, which was sent to the APSC, we've agreed it. There is work to be done on the implementation and streamlining. We will absolutely do that. We're underway in doing that.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Head of APS Academy and Capability

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Minister, can I ask if you still believe that the Public Service is 'appropriately sized'? I know that you've said that a few times and repeated it a few times. It's currently around 217,200 or so for the financial year 2026-27.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't have that number right in front of me, but it's around that, if all in.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And that is 'appropriately sized'?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think it is, for the nature of the work. You can see that, I think, in Budget Paper No. 4, which shows the relatively modest growth of the public sector as a percentage of the population overall. It's smaller now, relatively, than it was in 2006. It's doing a lot more things. I accept that you're going to cut some of those, like all climate policy. Fair enough, but we think supporting the economic transition is important. The NDIS is something that hasn't been done previously. Our expenditure in Defence, the population that Services Australia is servicing and supporting—all of that has changed. It's unrealistic to expect that you can do that and cap growth down at an unreasonable level where services suffer and workloads are unreasonable. We'd get where we got last time, which was core work being outsourced and policy failures like robodebt. We don't want to go back.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can we be clear—it's growing. The Public Service has been growing at 28 people per day since you came to power. It's 28 people per day, so I think your idea of modest growth and your average, everyday citizen's idea of modest growth of the Public Service—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't know where you get that number from, Senator Hume. I have to accept, when these are thrown out in political contests, that we may have a different view to you. But, realistically, what happened under your government was that you suppressed APS numbers and outsourced the work. It often was more expensive, and it was a failure of transparency about what was going on. We have sought to repair that, and we're seeing it in satisfaction with government service numbers, with people getting their payments on time and with work and programs actually being delivered as opposed to being announced and then not delivered. Across the board, we can see the benefits of this, accepting that you disagree. You see it as a cheap political way of making a point and, allegedly, saving money. You weren't saving money; you were just outsourcing it.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Let me just be very clear on the numbers. When the coalition left office, there were 171,938 members of the APS. There are now 217,256. That's 28 people a day, so that's where the mathematics comes from. I want to understand this, though, Minister. Upon the release of the APS-wide bargaining offer of nine per cent over three years, you were quoted as saying that it was 'fair and reasonable in a constrained fiscal environment'. Minister, the Public Service total wages bill in the budget is very fiscally constrained. It's actually got negative growth each year from 2027-28 through to 2029-30—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: This is probably a matter for Finance. We are straying into how agencies report against their financial budgets.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I am interested in finding out how you can square up—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It would be great to move on to Finance at some point.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: we'll get there—a declining wages bill with a public service that's an 'appropriate size' after a nine per cent offer over the same period.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
It'll be done as it's been done under governments of all persuasions. We have not changed the reporting of that or the way we index departments and expect them to make allowances for wage increases. It's the standard way that it's been done, certainly for as long as I can recall. We have not made a single change to that.

In addition, I know you have a view about the size of the Public Service overall. You were spending the money on wages. You just weren't reporting it as Public Service wages, because you were giving it to outsourced labour.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm just trying to make the numbers add up. The independent PBO, in its medium-term budget outlook released in July this year—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: This is a Finance matter.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: highlighted that in the current budget base line ASL it would be 'around 189,000 at the end of the forward estimates and 176,000 at the end of the medium term'. That is what you have budgeted. That's a 41,200 cut to the Public Service in your budget.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We can come back to that, but that is squarely a matter for Finance, and I can deal with that when we get there.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. I hope we will because it's a billion-dollar black hole, for want of a better expression.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Let's get there, and we can find out.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Commissioner, now that the pay offer is out, what are the next steps in that bargaining process, and when do you expect finalisation?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have the chief negotiator here for the enterprise agreement, who can take you through answers to those questions.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We have made substantial progress. It is quite a big process. We have over 1,900 claims from nine unions and over 280 individual bargaining reps. We have listened to all those claims in good faith in the bargaining room. We have tabled 95 per cent of preliminary positions and we're just working through with bargaining parties now, negotiating what the final offer and package will be, and working through feedback from bargaining parties. There have been a number of topics that we've brought back to the bargaining room several times, as we've been receiving feedback and refining. Parental leave was one of those. We've taken it back to the bargaining room twice now after receiving feedback from bargaining parties. We've tabled on our website our meeting dates, which go out to December at this point, but we are working with bargaining parties as quickly as we can, noting that enterprise agreements do have a common expiry date at the end of February next year. We have 108 agencies that are participating that I'm chief negotiator for across the APS and two non-APS agencies as well that are part of that process.
witness_position: APS Chief Negotiator, Workplace Relations and Bargaining Taskforce

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: When you do the bargaining, is there an understanding that the numbers of APS employees will be reduced as part of the pay deal?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I would say we work obviously within appropriations of departments. The agency lead negotiators that I brief every Friday have an understanding that they will need to fund enterprise agreements within their current appropriations.
witness_position: APS Chief Negotiator, Workplace Relations and Bargaining Taskforce

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Which comes with a reduction in numbers.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The answer is no. Indexation arrangements apply to entities, and they are funded for programs and delivery that they've been asked to do by government. This wage offer is not conditional on reducing job numbers.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But job numbers will be reduced.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Dare I say your colleague Minister O'Neil said so this morning on television—that cuts to the Public Service are part of the savings package that you are considering.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I haven't seen her transcript, so I can't comment on that. What I'm saying is—and I have said this a number of times—we think the Public Service is roughly the right size. Up and down in particular agencies there will be movements over time, but it's roughly the right size, resourced appropriately, and the wage offer that we have provided is in line with that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But it doesn't add up.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You are asserting that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Your budget papers assert it.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, they don't—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm looking forward to reconciliation on a nine per cent pay rise and a 217,000-strong APS.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: and we don't agree with the PBO analysis, and we can have that discussion in Finance.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I will move the call. We are trying to get to Finance, so we can keep the Finance questions for Finance and get through the questions for these witnesses so we can let them go. They've been here for a very long time. We are about two hours over the mark, in terms of where we should be. Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: My colleague Senator Shoebridge is about to walk in the door, and I will give over to him. Is a trial of a four-day working week being considered as part of bargaining?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No.
witness_position: APS Chief Negotiator, Workplace Relations and Bargaining Taskforce

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I see some shaking of the head.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We have tabled a preliminary position to those claims. We have not accepted those claims. That is our preliminary position. Staff have access to flexible working arrangements, which include condensed working weeks and part-time arrangements. That's on an individual basis. That's what we've put to the bargaining room, but, obviously, we're still bargaining in good faith on all topics at this point.
witness_position: APS Chief Negotiator, Workplace Relations and Bargaining Taskforce

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you. I've got a bunch of other questions I'll put in on notice. I'll hand over to Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's good to see you all. I'm going to ask you about the submission, which I think you were a part of, to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Parliamentary Standards. It probably doesn't come as a great surprise to you, Commissioner, that I'll be asking you questions about that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's fine.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: What was your role in the creation of that submission?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I am part of the Secretaries Board and there was a discussion, as was talked about last night by Secretary Kennedy and staff from PM&C. At one of the first Secretary Board meetings I attended—I think it was the July meeting—secretaries considered whether they would make a submission. There was agreement that they would. And then PM&C, as they explained last night, took the lead on coordinating that submission. The draft of that was sent out to all secretaries, to me and to the CEO of the NIAA. We were asked for comments back on that. We did provide some comments back from the APSC, and then, as was explained last night, that was circulated again before being finalised and submitted to the committee.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: What was the nature of your comments on it?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: At a high level, we just wanted to clarify what the position of the commissioner was with regard to the board, basically making sure it was clear what that was in any submission that went forward. We also highlighted our obligations under work health and safety laws, and I think there was one other element to this. I think Dr Tracey coordinated the response on our behalf. The third element was—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It just went to some of the examples listed on one of the pages of the submission. And it was effectively a comment, I recall, to the effect of just making sure those examples were clear so that the committee had the benefit of knowing exactly what the submission was drawing attention to.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: And accurate.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Indeed.
witness_position: Chief Operating Officer and First Assistant Commissioner, Integrity and Enabling Services

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You must have had something in your mind when you put your name to it. You must have understood what these various elements of the submission meant. I'm assuming you adopted them and understood them when you put your name to it. Is that right?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Yes, certainly. I think the intent of the submission was we wanted to provide something that would highlight concerns that had been brought forward by us or that we had witnessed ourselves—not that went to the sort of robust discussion, accountability or free-flowing questioning that you would have in a Senate committee or any parliamentary committee—where these issues went to the wellbeing of our officers who are witnesses.

So we put forward some examples of where we had seen this in practice and some concerns, particularly as was canvassed yesterday at the PM&C hearing on this, around the way in which things were communicated that had gone on in proceedings in social media, the fairness and accuracy of those, and the harm that could be caused if those were misrepresented or if tools available on social media,—for example, comments et cetera—were prolific and could cause harm to the officers that were at the estimates committee hearings or in other parliamentary procedures.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: In the course of the meeting with the secretaries, did any secretary identify an instance where they'd raised an issue with a committee chair or raised an issue with a committee and it hadn't been addressed?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Not that I recall.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I ask, then, how it is that a group of secretaries and you, who are used to sitting here, understanding the exchange in committees and respectful treatment of the chair, how you put pen to paper, making these allegations, making these propositions, without ever once doing the due process of raising the issue with the committee chair or raising these concerns? Are you aware of a single instance where that was done?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I am. I don't need to weigh in on the submission. I wasn't aware of the submission before it became public. But I have seen public servants treated appallingly by senators in these hearings. I have seen public servants scared to attend hearings because of the way they've been treated. I have seen public servants essentially called liars by people, and, when they've sought to correct the record—when a public servant has gone to check to make sure that everything was in order in the evidence they gave—and written to the committee, what happens? Nothing. Nothing. Their reputation gets clipped and put on video and sent around the place, and it's all very funny to drive clicks. But their professional reputation has been tarnished, and there is no answer from the Senate committee. So I—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, Minister, I've never—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, Senator Shoebridge. We will allow the minister to finish and then you will have your turn.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So I think there is an issue about how Senate committees operate. Yes, it's robust. Yes, I'm used to it. But public servants turn up here to do the job that we ask them to do, to answer questions, to be treated respectfully, and I don't think that is always the case, Senator Shoebridge. I think it has got to a point where secretaries have raised these concerns—because it's not necessarily about secretaries; it's about the people that they employ and it's about a safe workplace, and I don't think this place offers a safe workplace at all times, and I think that's a legitimate issue to raise.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Minister, I'm not aware of a single instance where a matter has been raised where I'm a member of a committee—concerns have been raised. I'm not aware of a single instance, in my experience. Admittedly, I've only been here since 2022 and, admittedly, I don't sit on every committee. But I'm not aware of a single instance of a committee that I'm involved in where a matter has been brought to the attention of the committee and it has not been treated with seriousness and has not been addressed. Indeed, I'm not aware of an instance, apart from bureaucrats seeking quite reasonably to correct an answer where they think they may have misspoken—I'm not aware of an instance in my experience that in any way accords with your proposition, where a bureaucrat has suggested that they've been, inappropriately, called a liar and there has been no clarification. I'm just saying from my experience, in four years, in the multiple committees I've sat on, I've not seen something that comes even close to that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, I have, repeatedly.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Shoebridge, I have to say that I have too.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Where a committee refused to correct?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Where a particular senator has refused and continued to attack a person. I'm—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: This is quite a different point from what I was raising. I have seen senators behave badly, and I'm not going to deny that, Minister. I've seen it. I think our job is, in the moment, to correct that. But it's a different point that I'm putting to you. Your point is that you're aware of formal processes having gone through, issues being raised and committees not addressing them, and I am unaware of those. In my experience, not only would it be extraordinarily out of character for the committees that I've been a part of, who take their job seriously, and the chairs, who I respect—I've never seen that happen.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have. And the damage is done in the hearing or in the video clip. If a public servant seems to correct or explain or contest a fact that was put to them and deals with that through a letter weeks later, the damage has been done. The damage has been done. I've spent hours here with public servants being treated appallingly, and I try to offer protection and say: 'Hang on a minute. Cool it down. Let's not behave this way.' But the reality is, in the last term in particular, the behaviour of senators in these forums has on occasion, I think, created an unsafe workplace for public servants.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I come back to my question to the commissioner. Did a single secretary identify an instance such as the minister has just said, and are you aware of any instance such as the minister has just said, before this submission was crafted and submitted to a parliamentary committee?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The way in which the submission was formulated was that the secretaries and I and the CEO of the NIAA were asked to provide content and examples back to PM&C, who then coordinated the submission. You asked me about the discussion in the room on that day, and I said that I did not believe that there was somebody that raised that particular issue in the room. There were secretaries who raised issues such as the use of social media and the experience of witnesses in committee hearings, but there was not, as I recall it, anybody who raised that particular issue. Having said that, in some of the content that was provided back to PM&C, my understanding is that there were examples provided, including examples that were raised where senators had actually gone online and then moderated things in the social media clips. So just to pick up your point, where things are raised, I do think there is consideration given to correcting these issues, but, specifically on your issue of somebody going back to a committee and raising an issue, I do not have any examples of that that I can provide to you.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I just jump in there, because it is an important discussion. In the situation where, after you've appeared, someone clips your evidence in a way that tells a different story or tells a story that the person who's doing the clipping wants to tell, what rights do the public servants have then? The damage is done. The most significant issues I have around personal safety are as a result, at times, of clips from Senate estimates that are clipped in a particular way to tell a particular story that sets off clickbait online. What rights do public servants have then, Senator Shoebridge? The damage has been done.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That is one view of it. You call it 'clickbait'.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, when it's—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Let me finish; I let you finish. There is an obligation that I think all of us have when we're communicating these matters online to make sure the communication genuinely represents what happens. That is an agreed position. Well, that's my position.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes. Fair enough.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It may not be your position. I think it's your position, and I'm not trying to put words in your mouth.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: No, I'm saying it's not followed by everybody.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That, I think, is a basic standard we should respect. But I have seen multiple instances where the evidence that's been given has been discursive, indirect and not responsive to the answers, and the frustration that I've felt—I've seen the frustration felt by other senators—is palpable and real. You can feel it in the room—the frustration that direct questions are getting indirect answers and obfuscation. It is quite reasonable to share that with the public, because your wages, my wages and the commissioner's wages are paid for by the public, and, when answers of that nature are given, they will attract criticism. I would suggest that one of the clearest ways to avoid that criticism is for public servants to give direct and unambiguous, to the extent that they can, answers to direct and unambiguous questions.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator, I think the Secretaries Board submission was very clear that our expectation is that witnesses will give full and frank answers, to the best of their knowledge, in committee hearings, and we were in no way suggesting that officers shouldn't be accountable and shouldn't provide that information. The intention of this was to bring to the attention of the committee looking at the behavioural standards and code circumstances and concerns around the wellbeing and safety of our officers appearing and asking for the committee and for parliamentarians to consider that with respect to your own code of behaviour and standards. What you do with that, what the committee does with that and what decisions they make are entirely up to them, but I still stand by this submission, because we have an obligation, as the leaders of the Public Service and, in particular, in my role as the Public Service Commissioner, to be very diligent in making sure that our staff are not exposed to things that can harm their wellbeing. We are not in any way—and I think the submission is very, very clear—trying to prevent witnesses giving full and frank answers in a committee hearing.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, part of your—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator Shoebridge, I'm going to have to pull you up there because we're five minutes over. We have a private meeting, which was to start at four o'clock, to deal with another matter, and then we have a break. We are a solid 2½ hours behind our schedule, so the committee will also consider where we go from here in our agenda. But, on further questions, it's down to the committee to make a decision.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have more questions.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: In which case you're more than welcome to join us for the private meeting. We will break now to enable the committee to conduct a private meeting, and we'll come back to the Australian Public Service Commission about how long you may be required.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Welcome back, everybody. We will have one very short and succinct block of questions from Senator Shoebridge, and then we will let you go.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I don't like being verballed by the chair, but I'll endeavour to—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm merely going on the promises you made to me, Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
Commissioner, I have been asking you questions about this submission. One of the matters from the submission that I might say causes me some unease—and it reads a bit sovereign citizen—is that you say on page 6:

Recognising the evidence provided to a committee is on the public record, these officials have not consented to a subsequent use of their image, or its use by parliamentarians and their political parties for party-political purposes.

Why did you include that in your communication?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I feel that these issues were canvassed last night with Secretary Kennedy. Really, the submission is quite clear as to what our intention was when putting this forward to the committee that's looking at the behavioural standards and the behavioural codes. Yesterday evening these issues were all canvassed with Secretary Kennedy, members of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet and witnesses. The submission speaks for itself. I don't have anything to add that's different to what's in the submission, and I believe that it's now up to the joint committee that's looking at the parliamentary standards and inquiring into the operation and effectiveness of the behavioural codes to look at the submission, take it on its merits and determine what course of action if any and which suggestions if any it would like to take up. I also believe that it's incumbent on all parliamentarians to think about some of the issues we've raised and how they address them personally or implement any of the suggestions that we've put forward here.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Mr Kennedy can give his evidence as one of the signatories of this. I'm asking you for your evidence as one of the signatories of this. That is actually the purpose of this exchange. agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Good. I will continue to ask questions about this until I do get an answer from you about it. Do you understand that this process is a democratic process?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

text: Do you understand that most but not all of the senators engaged in this are members of political parties?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
On what basis were you saying this, and what did you intend to achieve from making this statement:

… these officials have not consented to a subsequent use of their image, or its use by parliamentarians and their political parties for party-political purposes.

What were you hoping to achieve by saying that public officials have not given such consent? What was the purpose of that?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It just goes to the fact that when giving evidence officials are very well aware of their obligations under the witness guidelines, but they are not necessarily consenting to images of themselves or some of the evidence they are giving in committees being framed or shaped in a way that could be used to support a particular political view. That's what the clipping of these recordings and broadcastings is doing in some instances. That's my understanding of the examples that were given. That's my understanding of what we meant by that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Sorry, but this is often a political contest. It's a political contest.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: But not for public servants.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's a political contest about how resources are being used. It's a political contest about how the government is directing resources. It's a political contest about whether issues that are serious for people in their lives are being appropriately addressed. It is not the job of officials to be telling politicians that they can't use the evidence that's being given to address matters of politics. Officials may not be engaged—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I would like to respond.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The phrase here is 'for party-political' purposes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Stop patronising and let her respond.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Please let me respond.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think we've all got your question, Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You've had a sermon and a question.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text:
I have given an answer which is my understanding of what you've asked me. If you disagree with that, that's totally acceptable. That's your prerogative. My interpretation of this is that when officials come to committees or hearings or appear in front of parliamentary committees they need to respond to questions and give evidence that is accurate, clear and transparent. That is the responsibility they have, and they need to abide by the official witness guidelines, which is what they do. In doing that, what can then happen in certain circumstances—which is what we were drawing your attention to—is that that is then broadcast or used to communicate to the public. That is totally acceptable, but the official guidelines for those broadcasting is that it needs to be fair and it needs to be accurate.

What we are saying here is that sometimes the transmissions, whether they are on social media or in other types of media formats, are not fair and accurate. What that can do is potentially mislead people, because things are taken out of context or do not give the full answer to a question, which can then be used to support a particular political view. That's what we were trying to raise. But as I said previously the intent of the Secretaries Board submission was to raise concerns about some of the behaviour in committees that is harming officials either from a mental health perspective or by potentially eroding their confidence to appear at these committees by humiliating them, demeaning them et cetera.

Now, that may not have happened in your committees, Senator Shoebridge, but we've heard evidence here, even today, from other senators that they've witnessed this. We were also raising concerns about the use of social media. As I have said previously, it is incumbent on the Secretaries Board, as the most senior leaders of the public service, to make sure that we are fulfilling our obligations under the Work Health and Safety Act. We are raising these concerns so that our officers are treated respectfully and are given every opportunity to have information that reflects what they have said in a committee hearing transmitted, if that's the word you'd like to use, or communicated in an accurate and fair way. That's the intent of the submission. It does not, by any means, go to us trying to circumvent or stop frank and fearless advice, discussion or answering your questions in these committees.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: None of what you just said would be objected to if it were included in the submission, but your submission went well beyond that. It didn't include those caveats about unfair, misleading or inaccurate use. It simply said, 'These officials have not consented to a subsequent use of their image or its use by parliamentarians and their political parties for party-political purposes.'

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That's one element of the—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Commissioner, what you just gave as an answer is a very different proposition to what's in your submission. How do you explain that?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Senator, I've answered the question. I—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I'm going to intervene here. Senator Shoebridge, I appreciate where you're going. The witness has answered the question a number of times in a very consistent fashion. I've read that document. I appreciate that you're picking one piece out of it. There are a range of things within that document. It is a submission and, as the witness says, it is up to you to either accept it, reject it or whatever. It has been put to a committee who are considering these matters. The committee will weigh up what they believe to be valuable in that submission and will do as they see fit with it.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Look, I don't want to extend this in any way. I don't think it is the role of the chair to make commentary like that, but, if what you're asking for the assistance of the committee to move on, I'm happy to comply.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you very much, Senator Shoebridge. I appreciate that.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I just say that, in the break, I've also remembered further representations, including letters that have been sent to committees—not this one—objecting to behaviour that occurred in committees, to no outcome. So I think letters have been written and issues have been raised. The reality is, Senator Shoebridge, that if what you seek is better engagement in Senate estimates, whatever your criticism might be, I don't think the way they're operating now is going to elicit that, because people are scared. People are leaving the public service because they don't want to come to Senate estimates and, essentially, be bullied, harassed, demeaned and ridiculed by senators.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Any of that is unacceptable. Suggesting that it has in any way been the proposition of any senator that that is acceptable, is, I think, a straw-man argument. For these proceedings to have benefit for the public, which is ultimately what this is meant to be about, I would suggest that the simplest way forward is through clear, direct and accurate answers—as you've characterised them, Commissioner—to make these sessions timely, give the public confidence in the public sector and allow us to do our job as efficiently and respectfully as possible. This is a two-way street, and if we are, at the end of all this, getting to a point where we recognise it's a two-way street, I think that's a very useful advantage.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Thank you, Senator Shoebridge. Senator Hume.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I have a short line of questions following up on a question on notice from the last estimates hearing asked by my colleague Senator Chandler, who is on maternity leave. It's question on notice No. 65, relating to Australian Government Consulting. The question was about the daily charge-out rate for an Australian Government Consulting team member, and the response was $2,260 as at 31 May 2026. To put that in perspective, if a team member was charged out on all working days in a year, assuming 250 working days in a year, that's around $565,000 per annum. That seems quite high to me when compared to average APS, EL or SES salaries. Is there someone who can explain what that $2,260 per day is comprised of?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: It's a lot cheaper than KPMG!

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: ACG's pricing is based on a couple of inputs that drive us to a break-even number. So we're on a cost-recovery basis starting from this financial year. In the past, we've been somewhat subsidised by NPPs. The average figure varies based on the composition of the team. If we have more junior people on a given project, the rate is lower. If we have more senior people, the rate is higher. It's quite common in the consulting industry to have a utilisation figure. In the private sector, that is comprised of a range of metrics that might drive you to not be working 250 days a year on projects. We, similarly, have utilisation rates that mean people might be between projects. They can be working on internal projects to drive intellectual property. One of the features of ACG is that the APS owns the IP from the project. Those are some of the drivers that will cause the calculation that you did—which would be, 'What if there was a day rate for all of the days a week?'—not to be correct. I think that 250 days is also based on 50 weeks a year and five days a week, in your calculation.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I think our annual leave and sick leave and so forth would bring that number down.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Can I ask, then, if you're charging out team members at a rate that is comparable to the private sector—particularly to the private sector consultancy that you're supposed to be displacing?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Yes.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Okay. Can I ask also: that $2,260 a day, am I right in saying that that's not full cost recovery; it's partial cost recovery?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Right. So is that 70 per cent or is that 87?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: That was going to be my next question. What's the updated figure from $2,260 if you are now at full cost recovery?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We worked incredibly hard, Senator.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

text: We have been trying to grow and test the market's willingness to pay since we were established. In our first year we were free.

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: So that hasn't changed since the last estimates.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The budget claims $10 million of savings from AGC due to displacing external consultancies. Last estimates you advised you were tracking a figure close to $11 million, but you've just told me it's now $12.5 million. That's your most recent estimate?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: You said 12.5, and I said that that could have been our displaced spend. And just then—I'm so sorry—I thought you said 11?

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

text: I feel like I'll need to go back to Hansard to check the figures. I can go through each financial year if you'd like. I've got the very total but not the 2025-26. witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

text: spend is 15.5, but you said that your internal government service costs $18.7 million. So at this point you are costing more than you save—is that correct?

text: Okay, I get it. And it's a gross save, not a net save—is that right?

text: Yes. When we look at our value, there are several things that we consider. One of them is: how do we compare how much it would have cost if someone had decided, rather than in-housing, which is what they also might do for a taskforce, say, to go to market? Do the components of value include the fact that we retain the intellectual property for the work that we do, that we are a capability of the APS? witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

text: We maintain a raft of metrics and are held to account by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, which we're housed in, and we regularly discuss those with both our executive board and our advisory group, which contains a set of public servants. witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: How do we manage the scrutiny here, considering this is really the only place that we get to speak to you, without any more than—

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: What would you like to know, Senator?
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Well, I'd like to know what the financial metrics are that you're sharing internally. I think that would be helpful.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: A hundred per cent cost recovery, and then the other two fall out of our scale. The reason why I haven't set a public expectation for what our revenue might look like is that, if we actually find 16 great candidates and bring them on, our revenue would be higher than that target. If we pick up 14 or lose someone, there's too much variability. To ensure that we can be held to account properly, we landed on the client satisfaction figure, otherwise it would be—
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: The whole point of this is that you're supposed to be saving the taxpayer money.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: There are several objectives. One of them is reduction in reliance on consultants and contractors. Another is that we're building a capability for the APS. A third is that we're attracting people to the Public Service that would otherwise not join the Public Service. There are a range of things, including building capability. There are projects where we help set up strategy units and policy teams inside of line agencies that further reduces their reliance on consultants and contractors. Then there's a work stream we have to help the Public Service buy better, so that they get better value from the private sector when they do need to go to market.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: Again, my only concern with all of this is that the metrics that are offered up that are publicly facing—any sort of publicly facing assessments don't exist. The only financial metrics are ones that you use internally, and the only measure that we have that is publicly facing is customer satisfaction at this stage. For the size of the project and the ambition of the project, probably some financial metrics that were more public facing would be helpful.

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: We've tried to reveal those through exactly this conversation. The annual report is but one of the opportunities that the public have to understand AGC's operations in more detail.
witness_position: Chief Consulting Officer, Australian Government Consulting

agency: Australian Public Service Commission Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
text: I would hope that, when we get to the next Senate estimates, maybe we can be a little bit more explicit about some of the numbers in advance so that we have a chance to ask some questions from a position of knowledge, rather than just seeking out that data in advance. text: I want to start with some broad issues around spending. So can you tell me what government spending was as a share of the economy in 2025-26 in the Final Budget Outcome?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Payments were 26.3 per cent—sorry, that's the 2026-27 budget. It's 26.6, I think. Is it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's 26.9 per cent.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, yes. It was slightly up on what was published.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can you tell me from that data, outside of the pandemic, the last time government spending was that big—27 per cent of the economy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We've been through this before. When you look in the back pages of the budget document, you can easily find that out, Senator Hume. I've got the budget book here, but I think you can check that. That's why it's published in the back of the budget papers. But we have brought spending down from almost a third of the economy to where it is now. We found savings, but we are seeing and continuing to see increase, particularly in automatic payment variations: $118.9 billion since coming to government. So there is significant pressure there on those demand driven programs: social security; NDIS; aged care; natural disaster relief, which I think has grown 280 per cent in the time that we've been in government; and veterans compensation payments—almost $16 billion in those, in automatic variations. It is good that veterans are getting $16 billion worth of support, but it obviously has come and impacted the budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you for that extrapolation. I suppose what I want to understand is that, at around 27 per cent of the economy—or just under—if government spending is, as reported, at a 40-year high outside of the pandemic, is there a level of consciousness from the government that this level of spending would keep inflation higher for longer and interest rates higher for longer?

agency: Department of Finance
text:
The Treasury usually answer questions around these types of matters in the macro section of the Treasury appearances. We can answer questions about the cost of programs and where the growth has been. As you know, we have found significant savings, including some that are stuck in the Senate without your support, Senator Hume. I would just draw your attention to that. So I get a lot of feedback about reducing spending, and, when we bring ideas and proposals, they're often a lot harder to get through. Even the NDIS save of $37.4 billion was delayed several months, which had an impact of several hundred million dollars on the budget. The PHI save that we currently have before the Senate that the Senate objects to seats a very modest change to deliver a saving that's then reinvested in an area that's growing rapidly, and the Senate has said no to that.

So we'll just keep on, looking at ways that we can find savings in the budget, but we also have to be realistic that we need to invest in the services that Australians want and need. You see those big movements; you can disagree with them. They're in health, they're in aged care, they're in disability, they're in veterans compensation, they're in disaster relief and they're in defence and managing debt. They're the big areas where we have seen increased pressure on the budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I note that both you and the Treasurer have said that, if there are going to be calls for expenditure reductions, people should come forward with their ideas as to what those reductions should be. Obviously, the coalition has done that and been pretty explicit about that this week. I now understand that after Treasurer Chalmers put the call out to the business community to put their money where their mouth is, they too have come out with some suggestions as to where those cuts might be. Can I understand, from you, though, what was the real spending growth outcome for 2025-26?

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Let me just see if I can get that. I do have it somewhere. I've got a lot of numbers in my head. You would know that the final budget outcome actually came in at $6 billion smaller than forecast at budget. I'm sure you've recalled that. The budget deficit itself is half of what we were left when we came to government. The budget, over four years, is $230 billion better than when we came to office. All of that helps in the fight against inflation. The reality is, improving the bottom line—as we have in every budget update, including in the final budget outcome for 2025-26—has reduced pressure around that.

Sorry, I'm just getting it now. Real spending growth was 4.3 per cent in 2025-26. I think a discussion about spending is really important, because, if you look over the last 20 years at the pressure on the budget, for example, in disability spending—disability spending contributes two per cent to GDP. That wasn't the case 20 years ago. So, if you remove disability spending, spending as a share of the economy would be lower than it was under Howard at the same time. So there has to be some acknowledgement that areas like disability; health, which has grown just over under one per cent; and aged care and pensions, which have also grown just under one per cent, are placing pressure on the budget. That would be the same regardless of who was in government. Those are just facts. When you look at real spending growth over the last four years, it's around two per cent, which is half of what it was under you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That was a very long answer to get to 4.3 per cent real spending growth, but thank you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I answered it at the top. But, also, can we just have some rational debate about this? To pretend that disability spending, as a share of the economy, has not impacted on—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I haven't asked a single question about this.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I know you're going to make a political point. That's fine. I can make those too. I can say that the saves that you've announced in the last day don't even touch the surface of the spending that you've already announced. I can be making those points, or we can have a genuine discussion about some of the areas of pressure on the budget and the fact that government spending and investment has changed over the last 20 years in line with our demographics and with decisions taken from governments of all colours about support that's provided to individuals across the economy.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister, you sound so defensive on the most basic of questions.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not defensive.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I asked you what the real spending growth outcome was. The answer was 4.3 per cent. Can you then confirm for me, please, that that is close to double the growth of the economy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The average of spending growth over the last four years has been two per cent.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The real economic growth in the 2025 budget is 2.4 per cent, and real spending growth is 4.3 per cent.

agency: Department of Finance
text: These are questions, really, for Treasury. They're not questions for this department.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm sorry. Spending growth—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've answered the questions about spending. You're then going and talking about economic growth which are questions that are more properly put to the Department of the Treasury.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not a rule of thumb that you would use what is our spending growth compared to what is economic growth?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've answered the question.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Treasury is on later this week.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Tomorrow.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you have plenty of opportunity, Senator Hume, to get there.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I want to ask about the 2025-26 final budget outcome and the tax-to-GDP ratio.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That is definitely a matter for Treasury, not Finance.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The last time that the tax to GDP ratio hit 24.1 per cent, which is where it is now, was the budget in deficit, or was it in surplus?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's a matter for Treasury.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Again, these are Treasury matters. We're at the 10-minute mark, Senator Hume. Maybe we will rotate the call, and we can come back to you for some finance questions after Senator—

agency: Department of Finance
