text: I can't believe we can't ask questions about expenditure to the Minister for Finance in finance.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You weren't asking—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We were.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You weren't.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I was.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That was not—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Hume, you just asked about tax to GDP. That is not the same as—

agency: Department of Finance
text: If it's a question about the budget bottom line, surely I can ask the Minister for Finance and the Department of Finance. That's kind of what we're talking about, isn't it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The department is here—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I asked about surplus and deficit.

agency: Department of Finance
text: to answer questions about areas of their portfolio responsibility. That is not one of them, Senator Hume, whatever way you want to twist it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Budgeting?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're going to rotate the call.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, that's not what you asked.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not what you answered.

agency: Department of Finance
text: As is always the case, we get further if we ask questions in the relevant portfolios on the relevant days, or we'll just spend all of our time arguing the toss about whether we're in the right spot. We will go to Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've got some questions about Finance's review into KPMG. Last week Finance tabled Dr Ian Watt's independent review into KPMG and your department's response, Minister. Dr Ian Watt's review found, among other things, that KPMG's handling of the whistleblower claim was 'misguided, fragmented, prolonged and, at critical points, lacking clear ownership'. Do you have anything you want to add about this review, Minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: On KPMG?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No. I mean, it was commissioned by the Department of Finance, and it's informed some of the decisions that have been taken since. I think it stands on its own. I engaged with Dr Watt on two occasions. I think he did a very thorough job, and I will work with Finance on how we progress. They've agreed to pause their work until the end of February.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The outcome of Dr Watt's review—I met with him also, thank you; it was useful to engage. Finance has extended the temporary pause on KPMG bidding for new Commonwealth contracts, as I understand it, until 28 February 2027. However, some of Australia's biggest corporate players—Lendlease, Macquarie Group, ANZ—have dumped KPMG as auditors well into the future. Some departments, as we heard yesterday, like PM&C, have ended contracts. For example, the internal audit contract has been ended by PM&C with KPMG. Why have you as the department, Minister—as the leader—left the door open to letting KPMG back in February, given that clear judgement that KPMG's handling of the whistleblower matter was misguided, fragmented, prolonged and lacking clear ownership? Shouldn't you be an exemplar of how to respond when such appalling corporate practice is visited on us as an economy? It's all wrong.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think we have responded and we've responded in a pretty comprehensive way. We've had a review. We've had a pause on procurement, essentially, with them. But I think running government procurement and an individual decision by an individual company are two different things.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do you agree that KPMG misled the parliament?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, I've read the review. I've followed, at a distance, some of the work that you've been doing. I'd wait for the committee to come back once you've finalised your discussions and considerations of that. I haven't been a part of the work that you've been doing. I've been focused on it from this side, in terms of government procurement.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Let me summarise just one event. For example, the whistleblower claims that there were documents—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: confidential audit documents photocopied and kept in a secret locker. That was denied for a very extended period of time by the leaders.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, I have seen the changing evidence.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. That was a deceit, was it not? It was eventually shown that there were such documents.

agency: Department of Finance
text: As I said, I haven't followed it as closely as you've been. I've been looking at it from a different point of view, which is about government procurement. This didn't happen through a government procurement. contract

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's worse, though, isn't it? Isn't polluting our audit system more of a problem than a single misdemeanour in relation to a contract? This is our financial system we're talking about—the integrity of information.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, and there are other ministers involved in that—Minister Mulino and others. I'm focused on it from my point of view, which is being responsible for government procurement. yes, I think the behaviour that's been uncovered is appalling, which is why the department undertook a comprehensive review and has paused, essentially, them getting government work until the end of February, during which time they have to show the steps they've taken to remedy the deficiencies that your work and others have identified, including the whistleblower.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What steps will you take in February as you approach the end of this extension of the pause?

agency: Department of Finance
text: At the end of February, that will be a matter for our department. Over the coming period, KPMG needs to develop an action plan and agree that with us—if you like, the actions that they're taking to deal with their conduct both in the treatment of whistleblowers but also in the events surrounding this enormous failure inside their firm. Once we agree that action plan, they need to show progress against that action plan, and we will review what that means for them in terms of Commonwealth potential to bid at the end of February.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What other mechanisms are available to you, Minister, beyond the pause—options to deal with the misconduct that's been laid bare in this review?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not quite sure what you're getting at. We've taken some decisions based on the review that Dr Watt has completed. There are a range of remedies and suggestions and recommendations in that that we are now working through.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do you have contact with the state and territory governments, some of which have also placed pauses on contracting with KPMG? Do you have any information about how those other governments are reacting? Are you in communication with them about that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I will ask Mr Danks to answer that, because we are in contact with state and territory procurement officials.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We are members of the Australasian Procurement and Construction Council. It comprises the states and territories and New Zealand. When the KPMG issues first started up, we had a regular Thursday meeting with all states and territories to talk about each of the actions we were doing. They were provided a copy of Dr Watt's report before it was made public, because we were doing this together with the states. We are talking to them this Thursday to understand what they are doing with a further pause. I understand some states are considering a further pause, but I don't know their level of detail. I'm happy to take it on notice and provide that information once we talk to the states.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would appreciate that. On the overall work that KPMG has with government, do you have information on all current contracts with KPMG, both total value and quantity? I'm asking if you've got it. And, if you have, could you please provide it on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We can certainly do it on notice. We have lists of contracts entered into during the pause and amended, but we don't have a list of all the contracts that are currently in the system for KPMG. But we can easily provide that on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm also interested in the extensions, which have been quite significant. A sizeable amount of money has gone into extensions of contracts with this firm, which I find rather astonishing. These are, in consultant land, often the sweetest money of all because they're right at the end of a contract. It's very profitable earnings, and KPMG has certainly been making hay on extensions. I've got some more questions about Finance's review into KPMG. Who from Finance has met with who in KPMG on the matter?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We created a small secretariat to assist Dr Watt with the review. That secretariat was headed up by Mr Sebar, who is with us here and who can answer detailed questions. Dr Watt met with KPMG, I think, 10 times. It might be 10 times. The secretary and I met with Mr Sams, the new CEO of KPMG, last week on Tuesday, to take him through and discuss the outcomes of the review, after which I sent a letter detailing what we would like KPMG to agree to. During that time, the secretariat was with Dr Watt speaking not just with Mr Sams but with a range of KPMG officials who the secretariat asked for information and material to assist Dr Watt in the report and the review. Mr Sebar might be able to take you through a bit more detail of exactly who was spoken with and when. He might have that on hand, if that would be helpful.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On page 149 of Dr Watt's report, the relevant appendix sets out who Dr Watt consulted with, throughout the course of the review.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I will go to that, and thank you for saving us time; that's useful. Are you satisfied with how KPMG has responded so far?

agency: Department of Finance
text: KPMG have responded quickly to everything that we have asked them for. My understanding from Dr Watt is that they responded appropriately and quickly to all of the requests. In the response to the letter that I sent and where I asked them, they responded quickly, overnight, and they have agreed to the requests we made to pause bidding for Commonwealth work until the end of February.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I said, just a moment ago, that PM&C had terminated a contract. Clearly, we just heard earlier, that the APSC also terminated its training of senior public servants through KPMG. Do you know of any other contracts across the public sector that have been terminated with KPMG?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not aware of contracts that have been terminated. Those decisions are made by the appropriate accountable authority and departments. We wouldn't necessarily know. I'm not sure that we have that information. I just want to double check that for you—no, we don't.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On notice, could you check and let us know if there have been terminations of contracts, with what departments, the focus of the work and the size of the contract.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm looking to rotate. Is that a useful place to stop?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can stop now, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The Prime Minister, the Treasurer and the minister have consistently claimed $178 billion in savings—and have repeatedly done so. Secretary, as per the budget papers, can you confirm that that number doesn't solely reflect savings? It also reflects reprioritisation. The decision is taken that the money will in fact be spent, not just saved. It's on different expenditure; it's not saving. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We've been clear. I say it in almost every press conference that I give that it's about savings and reprioritisation within agencies and across the Public Service.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Over what timeframe is that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Since the 2022 pre-election economic fiscal outlook, which was the final publication before the election where Prime Minister Albanese formed government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's $178 billion that's been banked. Is it just in the past? What about in the future? Is it also forecasts and projections?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll check with my colleagues, but I believe it would reflect the forward estimates value, which has evolved since that time. Paul?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That includes, effectively, the eight years since the 2022 PEFO. So it includes both the forward estimates from now—

agency: Department of Finance
text: And the medium term.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, sorry, not the medium term but as in the actual results.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The forward estimates covered in each of those updates.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Right.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You add an extra year each year.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So it goes out to what year now that $178 billion?

agency: Department of Finance
text: To 2029-30, the end of the forward estimates published in the 2026-27 budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: For the savings that are estimated over the next four years, do they largely come from NDIS savings that haven't occurred yet?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, it would include the $37.8 billion. That would be a component of that $178 billion.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, can you say that again, Minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The budget saving—I think that was prior to the delay, so it might move around a little bit—was $37.8 billion over the forwards from this budget year, 2026-27; the forward estimates period for that. It forms a sizeable component of the $178 billion.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Page 95 of budget paper 1, colloquially known as the table of truth—can I just get a better sense from you of how much the spending decisions actually worsened the budget here.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll see if I can get it. There are different components. There's spending as a result of decisions, and then there are obviously those other significant areas, which are the demand driven programs. I'm just trying to find the right number for you. It's about $118.9 billion in automatic payment variations.

agency: Department of Finance
text: How much were the payment decisions?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm just seeing if I can find that. I'd have to go back and see if we can find that total number for you. I can't see it in front of me right now.

agency: Department of Finance
text: From what I can see, the net spending decisions are actually negative $535 million in the table of truth. Is that right?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Oh, so you're looking over—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Page 95.

agency: Department of Finance
text: in this budget. In this budget alone? Let me just get my right documents, because I've got the final budget outcome, and that's the budget. I've just got to work from different documents. In this budget—is that what you're after?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On page 95, that's right.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So net spending decisions are negative $535 million over the four years. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, according to that table.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, according to the budget. When inflation is high and interest rates are high, you're spending an additional $535 million over four years. So it's not a net save at all. It's a spend.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's for the payments line only. If you wanted to compare what has been the overall impact of the budget, you'd need to go to the bold line that shows how the underlying cash balance is better than it was at MYEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's from higher taxes; not from spending, not from saving.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If you look on table 3.2 as well, yes, there's the interaction between receipts and payments, but there are also provisions—policy decisions including previously made provisions as well.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But I just want to be clear, Secretary. This is from higher taxes, yes—the number you were pointing to?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, that's your language, Senator Hume. There's an interaction.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Well, higher revenue.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I know it's convenient to look at one section, but the budget overall takes into consideration receipts and payments.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's exactly what I'm trying to get to—receipts and payments—and payments have grown. They are a negative. Spending decisions are negative in that table of truth—a reconciliation.

agency: Department of Finance
text: As you say, there's the $535 million over the budget—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Over the forward estimates.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Over the forward estimates. But, if you look in particular at the 2026-27 year, you can see the restraint, essentially, that's been shown there. We have done the hard work to deliver the savings that are needed and the reforms that are needed to reduce areas in those fast-growing programs. In all of them, we are doing the work.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I understand that that's the message, but clearly what's been decided in this budget is to spend an additional $8.7 billion in 2026-27. Is that right?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, what are you saying?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The decision has been to spend an additional $8.7 billion in 2026-27. I understand that you can say that there are spending pressures, interest repayments, defence, NDIS and all of those things.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. Well, that is the real world.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, I just want to make sure that there's the real number too. There's an additional spend of $8.7 billion.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, it's outlined in the table.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's correct, then, for the sake of the transcript?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, the tables are correct.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you. Can I turn to page 106 of Budget Paper No. 1? Obviously it's something that—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can I just go through, though—sorry, I was just looking for it. I couldn't find it. But, for 2026-27, I think it is important to go through what those investments are, because I know you don't have to deal with the pressures that we are dealing with, but we do. So there is $1.4 billion in payments for new PBS listings. It would be very difficult, I imagine, if you were in my position, Senator Hume, to say no to that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, you did last time you were in government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There is $1.3 billion in health terminating measures. So those are various programs that—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are they fiscal cliffs?

agency: Department of Finance
text: were funded for a period of time. There is $1.1 billion for Services Australia resourcing and $436 million to extend NDIA staffing. There's the Fuel and Fertiliser Security Facility. There is $2.2 billion for defence for their additional spending—and I note that you have promised to spend more than that—and $3.4 billion in hospitals, which is the investment through the national hospitals agreement. In all of those areas, I think you would be hard pressed—I note that none of those are on your list of cuts that you've announced in the last day or so.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, they're not. They would be funded. But they are choices of government, decisions of government—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, realistically—

agency: Department of Finance
text: and I'm happy for you to own them.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You're running the argument, presumably, that you would not be spending what we have outlined in table 3.3. I've just taken you through a list of what those things are, and I would challenge you to say any one of those—are you not going to spend $2.2 billion on defence or spend on new drugs or on keeping Services Australia ticking over? In which case, what's the criticism?

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you're anticipating questions that I'm asking. I'm just asking for clarification.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, yes. It's all very easy to run a political argument. It's harder actually to sit at the table and make decisions. There is no shortage of claims for funding through the budget, and I gave you the list there. You've agreed that none of those are areas that you wouldn't address yourselves.

agency: Department of Finance
text: All I am questioning is the claim of $178 billion in savings when actually you're spending more. And they're decisions of government. If they're decisions of government, fine, but own it. They're decisions of government; they're not savings.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There are $178 billion in savings and reprioritisation across our budgets, something that you did not do in any of yours. You didn't take any hard decisions. You just didn't do things. You didn't deal with the energy crisis. You didn't deal with the aged-care crisis. You didn't deal with the NDIS running away from you. On none of those issues did you actually do the hard work. What I'm saying is that we're doing the hard work. Yes, it involves spending and investing in certain areas. But in any of those areas—if it's medicines, if it's hospitals, if it's defence spending, if it's NDIS—tell me which ones you wouldn't do. Then let's have a real argument.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator, would this be a time to rotate the call?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll go to you, Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I want to go to back to the review of KPMG. Dr Watt's review made eight recommendations, most of which were for Finance. I'm particularly interested in recommendation 6, which made a list of recommended changes to the Commonwealth procurement framework. One of the clear takeaways, to me, was that Dr Watt recommended that the government have the power to ban unethical suppliers, and I currently have a private senator's bill before the parliament to do exactly that. Recommendation 6(a) was:

6. Finance should strengthen the Supplier Code of Conduct framework to:

a. provide strengthened sanctions, including the ability to restrict or prohibit suppliers from bidding for Commonwealth

Government contracts where appropriate

However, Finance merely noted most of the subrecommendations of No. 6 and indicated:

The Government will consider recommendation 6(a) to 6(f) and respond in due course.

Minister, when do you expect to provide a full response to these recommendations?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, we only got it last week, from memory. We'll work through it as quickly as we can. We're doing some work on the Supplier Code of Conduct now, which has been out for consultation and which I'm working with Minister Rishworth on, so it makes sense to have a look at the supplier code recommendations as part of that work.

agency: Department of Finance
text: First we had PwC misusing confidential information. Now we've got KPMG misusing confidential information, being dishonest about the use of it and treating a whistleblower appallingly. How much evidence do we need that procurement officials need to have the power to dodge and to ban those very poor contractors, as now recommended by your independent reviewer?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I talk to Dr Watt quite a bit about this, and also the fact that we only recently got the Supplier Code of Conduct in, and that came in post PwC, I think.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, that's correct.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The mechanism to deal with poor behaviour through government procurement wasn't really available. We did that work. I'm constantly engaging with the department on what tools we need to ensure the best behaviour and conduct possible for government work. That is partly why we're doing further work on strengthening the Supplier Code of Conduct to make very clear what we consider good practice to be—to clarify, because I think there has been some feedback from suppliers that some clarification on aspects of what constitutes good practice would be welcome. So we're doing that and we'll look at what other powers are needed. And, yes, both of those examples that you raised—and we've had a couple of others, I think—give us the opportunity to think through what else is needed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You've had other contractors who've been—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, I think there was another one that was raised here.

agency: Department of Finance
text: McNair yellowSquares.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. I think that was raised in another hearing.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think that's correct.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What's your inclination, then, in relation to strengthening your tools on this? Do we have to go through all of the big four in this excruciating experience before we actually give ourselves the opportunity to ban people who behave so poorly?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not necessarily. It's a big decision to put in place further penalties, and it would have to be something that—part of this gives us the opportunity to take that work and progress it through the normal government processes, so we are doing that work.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You say it's a big decision, but these—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Big in the sense that it's not a decision that I can make unilaterally. It's a more substantial decision than that, and we would have to take that through our own processes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, it's a decision of government. I guess most Australians, if they have been done down by one supplier and then the next one does the same, are going to be thinking very carefully about who they deal with in their household. People look at this and think about—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, I agree.

agency: Department of Finance
text: the many, many millions of dollars of contracts. How many times do we have to get burned before we give ourselves that very basic opportunity to ban someone who behaves so badly?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think the damage that has been done to both of those companies has been the hit to their public reputation, to be honest. That is also a factor in the changing of their behaviour, because they have had some very severe consequences from the public nature of their deficiencies. But we should have in place everything that we need as a government to make sure that we are upholding the highest standards of conduct from our suppliers. It's not just the big four that are our suppliers, though. We have hundreds of thousands of contracts, from tiny suppliers to very significant suppliers, and I have to consider all of that in the process.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The distinctive aspect of what we've been through as a country is that we've had one massive failure by PwC, who sell off their entire consulting business. They pay a big price. But then here we are two years later with another behemoth. We've got KPMG—$2 billion of business a year—and they did not learn the lesson that was provided to them free of charge in relation to PwC. So that kind of loss of reputation has not been instructive enough to get KPMG to keep its house in order, remembering many people say KPMG's errors are more significant than those we saw—which were appalling enough—by PwC.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't disagree with you, Senator Pocock. We've got the Watt review. We're looking at the supplier code. This will feed into that. I want to make sure we have all the powers available that we need. Plus, we've got to make sure the procurement system is running as best it can across the Public Service. Finance has a role there in terms of setting some of the guidance around how procurement should operate, but we've got a lot of work to do to make sure accountable authorities are doing the hard work as well.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I agree with that. I want to move on to the strategic commissioning framework, which we covered with other agencies earlier. The ANAO report on the strategic commissioning framework made a recommendation to the Department of Finance:

To support more efficient and consistent collection of data to inform effective workforce planning, strategic commissioning, ongoing oversight of Australian Public Service reform objectives, and public transparency …

Why has the Department of Finance's response to this recommendation been to note it, not to agree to it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: One of my officials will come up. But the principal reason is that it will be a decision of government if we want to change the obligations it goes to—all of annual reporting of all Commonwealth entities. We have a convention, and we've done it indeed with Dr Watt's review, that, when a recommendation is proposed that requires a decision of government, we note it. It does not mean we disagree. It means that there will need to be work done, and the government will need to balance the reporting burden that would be added—because financial statements are already a very comprehensive set of reports in the back of every annual report that you see—and what further purpose is served by that. So we're working with the Public Service Commission, and my colleagues down the end who are responsible for the rules that set out what goes in annual reports will determine if there's a way to give effect to what the ANAO has proposed. Anna, I don't know whether you want to add anything?

agency: Department of Finance
text: As the secretary has set out, the relevant reporting requirements are set out in an instrument that is made under the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act. That is why it would be a question for government if it were to change. Those standards are based around existing accounting standards which focus on a question of materiality and reporting, and so a change from that standard would require a decision of government, but we would, of course, examine those and provide advice. That is the reason that it is not for Finance to respond to that recommendation as accepting or declining it.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: The ANAO audit notes that previous reviews, including the Thodey review in 2019, identified the need for a whole-of-service workforce strategy and a more strategic approach to external providers. Why have we had these recurring concerns about data capability reliance on external labour? They've remained unresolved across successive reform processes, and we're still sitting here, really, looking for the right indicators to have a sense of what's going on. Why have we not seen progress in this area?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know that I would accept that we've seen no progress. I think there's been lots of progress. I think a feature of our system is devolved accountabilities. Accountable authorities are ultimately responsible for the actions, the procurement, the workforce decisions that they take. We try and set rules that help transparency, and the evidence of that is the annual reports that get tabled in the parliament each year. We're always trying to balance what standardised looks like versus creating a reporting burden that's not out of natural systems. And it changes over time. It's really been the work on strategic commissioning or the government's policy to reduce reliance on contractors and consultants, through the significant savings that I overheard were being discussed in the Public Service Commission's hearings. That has had accountable authorities thinking about how they best configure their organisation to deliver on the government's revised policy objectives.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It just strikes me, sitting here—the $20 billion in external consulting, labour hire and so on. That is a massive amount of money that hasn't changed in five years. It was that in the last year of the Morrison government. So this question of the level of devolution, the voluntary and flexible framework, the application at the local level—it's just not working to see a real reduction on the level that I thought the government was aiming for. Let me move on to possible—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We are at a point of rotation, if that's a useful break?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Excellent. Senator McDonald.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I have some questions for Comcover. I want to ask you about the live cattle export case, please. Specifically, how much has the Commonwealth spent on legal representation, expert evidence and administration since the proceedings commenced?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's been longstanding practice not to disclose the Commonwealth's litigation expenditure whilst a proceeding remains ongoing, for a couple of reasons. But, in particular, it could prejudice the Commonwealth's position. Let me add, though, there is an ongoing commitment to resolving outstanding matters. There are a number of issues still afoot, providing greater clarity of the members' loss. So I'll stop there.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm just looking through the timelines. In June 2011, the suspension; in 2014, the class action commenced; in 2020, the Commonwealth was found liable; in 2021-22, the compensation negotiations—sorry, it was in 2020 that Brett Cattle Company was awarded their compensation—in June 2025, the dispute over the scale of losses; and, in May 2026, the appeal dismissed. Where are we up to now? I mean, it's 15 years.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Thank you. You're absolutely right. It has been a very prolonged matter. I would note that class actions by their nature can tend to be quite prolonged. I would also note that there is a firm commitment from the Commonwealth to resolve the claim as soon as possible. There is certainly an acceptance from the Commonwealth that compensation is payable. I would note there are still matters before the court, so there are limits to what I can say. But let me flesh that out a little bit.

The remaining issues are how losses are to be allocated across the class members and the resulting compensation payable. I'm absolutely, I'm sure, right; I haven't checked all of the dates you just gave, but I take those at face value. There are some remaining steps. But I would note the most recent matters that have been in dispute go to the decision about the quantum of cattle that were impacted by the suspension. There was a 5 June 2025 decision that found that loss caused by the suspension was limited to the 88,000 cattle identified by Justice Rares, and since then there has been an appeal by the applicants—so that has been in play—which was dismissed earlier this year. I'd also note that the determination of those disputed issues has actually provided greater clarity for the assessment of the class members' loss. If I can just note that there has certainly been efforts to try and progress the matter from the Commonwealth's perspective. In terms of where we are, there is a process now on foot for appointment of referees to assist in working through effectively the mechanics of how quantum is calculated. I'll just pass to Ms Denley quickly on that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, as Mr Newnham said, the remaining issue is about how those exports are allocated among the members. The court ordered this be done through a referee process, and that's under way at the moment. At the moment parties are engaging on the appointment of a suitable referee, and that's not yet final. The timing of that depends on the court's management process. But the next case management hearing is next month, on Friday 13 November. So it's still progressing.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do you think it would be reasonable to expect that the referee would be appointed by next month?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's a matter between the parties. The parties are still having those conversations at the moment. It's all progressing in accordance with the court directions.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: Right. I keep going to funerals of people who have been waiting and waiting. I think it's now unconscionable. I appreciate the legal process. I don't resile from that, but, given that this was an Australian government action against Australian producers, it is horribly slow—torturously slow.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We've consistently sought to bring this to a conclusion, but people have rights under law to contest.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think the last time the government sought to bring it to conclusion was when they made an offer in 2022. I don't know about you, but four years doesn't feel urgent.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But there have been other things that have happened in that time, including an inability to agree on things and further court action being taken.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I understand all of that, but it still doesn't feel like a sense of urgency. As I said, there was another funeral just last month. It would be great if the government could act with more alacrity. I asked you about some legal costs. What about the total cost of administering and managing the litigation through Comcover and the relevant department separate from the compensation ultimately payable to claimants? Can you give me any information on that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do you mean the overall costs of Comcover?
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, for this class action.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think I could only repeat what Mr Newnham has already outlined in terms of costs.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. Following the May 2026 appeal decision, has the Commonwealth revised its settlement position in light of the latest judgement?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would go back to an earlier question. There was a public offer made in 2023 of $215 million. Since then, I note the previous points I've made about the areas for contention, which included the quantum of cattle in play. There has not been a revised offer. I would note that those issues have still been in contention. And I would perhaps just also point to the need for the Commonwealth to comply with the Legal Services Directions, and that includes ensuring that any settlement represents a reasonable and defensible use of public funds but also that we should seek to reach a fair and equitable resolution based on the court's findings, the available evidence and the model litigant obligations. In light of the recent findings in the Federal Court, we do feel that the position put previously has solid foundation. But I would repeat that there is now a process to work through, as Ms Denley said, the referee process, the quantum and the application within the class itself.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The only process that stands between the Commonwealth reaching a settlement is going through this referee process?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not sure I would characterise it quite that way—but partly. What I would say is the focus now is on that referee process, drawing from the single Federal Court judge decision and backed in by the full Federal Court earlier this year, which puts clear contours around the quantum of cattle involved in the loss and then a series of calculations to be made underneath that through the referee process to determine the allocation of loss within that member cohort.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't seek to reprosecute the case, but, as a butcher at the time, I can tell you that the impact on the cattle market and the price of beef right across Australia was devastating. It's always a mystery to me how the courts calculate these things. The Commonwealth is actively seeking to settle the remaining claims: would that be a fair characterisation?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can say that now and previously there has certainly been a strong appetite to resolve these matters. But, as I noted earlier, that's within the boundaries of our obligations under the Legal Services Directions, which include finding a resolution that's based on court decisions, the evidence available and our obligations as a model litigant.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is previous minister Joe Ludwig still a party to this action? Is he being defended?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The role of Comcover is to prosecute these claims. It's not a matter of individuals. This is something that Comcover is delivering.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: Would he be receiving taxpayer assistance still?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Mr Ludwig isn't a party to the claim. It's a claim that is against the Commonwealth. so, the Commonwealth, through the Department of Finance, Comcover, is managing the claim.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's my understanding that Mr Ludwig or an associated legal firm with Mr Ludwig has been receiving taxpayer legal support—is that correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not sure that I have an answer to that question, in terms of Brett Cattle. If you could provide more information, I could look into that. But, in terms of Brett Cattle, I can only repeat what I've said, which is that Comcover is managing it on behalf of the Commonwealth.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Business Enabling Services

agency: Department of Finance
text: On notice then, I ask you if Mr Ludwig has received financial assistance through Comcover or through the Commonwealth for legal support and/or advice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll take that on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There are some questions around whether or not Mr Ludwig still is involved in advising the case or the government's position. There's a concern that he has delayed the outcome between industry and government, which has, as we've already identified, been some 15 years.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't have any understanding of that or that that is the case, but I will take it on notice to be completely sure.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Thank you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I want to return to page 106 now of Budget Paper No. 1, a different table of truth, which is about off-balance-sheet spending. There was some commentary from veteran budget watcher Chris Richardson, who said the headline balance 'is now becoming the figure that deserves more attention than the underlying figure' because—I think this is the phrase he used—it allows politicians somewhere to hide their trash. I'm not entirely sure that the minister would agree that this is where she is hiding her trash—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would not agree with that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: but that's his line, not mine. I want to understand. If you add the hidden balance-sheet spending—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not hidden. You're asking about it, so I would argue it's not hidden. We report the headline cash balance in the same way the underlying cash balance has been reported for some time.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If you add the balance sheet to spending, is the headline cash deficit more than double the underlying cash deficit, at 2.1 per cent of the economy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's nowhere near as bad as it would have been if you'd been funding all those nuclear power stations off it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's not answering the question that I asked.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's reported as per the budget papers. I would just again point out that you were planning to fund all of those nuclear power stations off-budget, which would have deteriorated that line considerably.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We talk about how to answer questions in a succinct way—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's a double standard.

agency: Department of Finance
text: so you don't get—

agency: Department of Finance
text: You have criticisms of our off-budget funding, but your harebrained National Party scheme of funding nuclear power stations—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm literally just asking about your budget books.

agency: Department of Finance
text: would have impacted—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Let's not talk over each other. Let's let the minister finish and then let's go back to Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know what she's talking about. We're just talking about the budget books.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, maybe, if you were listening and not speaking over, you might be able to understand it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I was talking about your election commitments that you made at the last term.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Turning to the historical tables on page 428 and 429, can you then tell me if there has ever been a budget with a bigger hidden balance-sheet spending.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Page 428?

agency: Department of Finance
text: And page 429.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, the tables are there, Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, but I'm asking the question—

agency: Department of Finance
text: You're calling it 'hidden', but you're referring to tables that are published in the budget documents.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Forget the tables then. You can tell me straight. Has there ever been a budget with bigger hidden balance-sheet spending than yours?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The tables outline the expenditure and give you that historical perspective. I would also say that we are investing and have invested in a number of areas, whether it's in sovereign capability, in the National Reconstruction Fund, in Housing Australia to build more houses or in the energy transition. We believe using the balance sheet to support those important economic and community needs is an important part of the budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: This is the Housing Australia Future Fund that isn't building enough houses, the Rewiring the Nation policy that isn't making electricity prices cheaper, or the National Reconstruction Fund that is a billion dollars of corporate welfare and bureaucracy. Is that right?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I accept that you don't agree with them. I would say that, when you're in government, you created the Medical Research Future Fund, the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility, the Regional Investment Corporation, the National Housing and Finance Investment Corporation and the Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific. In addition to that, in your election commitments, you were going to fund a nuclear power policy, a critical gas infrastructure fund, a future generations fund, a regional Australia future fund and a housing infrastructure program, so I think coming in here and—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Asking a question about your work?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's legitimate, but just as legitimate is me pointing out that you had significant commitments that you were making to fund off-budget. There's a recognition that governments can use their balance sheet in order to deliver particular decisions, acknowledging that our decisions may have been different.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm going to ask the secretary the same question that I asked you because I still haven't got an answer. Secretary, has there ever been a budget with bigger hidden balance-sheet spending than this one?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Nothing's hidden, so I don't agree with the proposition and the question. It is outlined in the table that you've referred to.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Remove the word 'hidden'. Has there ever been a budget with bigger balance-sheet spending than this one?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have a look at the headline cash balance as a percentage of GDP. You can see, in that column, that there is a difference across the years, including in the years that you were in government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Has the net cash flow from investments ever been larger than the negative $33 billion in this budget in history?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's right that I answer these, because these are government decisions. Just to be clear, we have been very upfront about using our balance sheet appropriately to fund national priorities—just as you were in your election commitments, which were greater than ours, if you were being honest about them, to use the balance sheet to deliver those particular outcomes that you were after.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm really comfortable with you answering the questions, but you have to actually answer the questions that I'm asking.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I have. I have answered it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You didn't. I asked you: has net cash flow from investments ever been larger than the negative $33 billion in this budget?

agency: Department of Finance
text: You don't get to tell me how to answer.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Just a yes or no is a good start.

agency: Department of Finance
text: My answer to that question is that we have been clear about using the balance sheet to fund national priorities, whether it be in energy policy, housing, sovereign capability, support for innovation or projects that are run through the National Reconstruction Fund in a whole range of areas. It is entirely appropriate to use the balance sheet to fund those priorities.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You're absolutely right that it is your decision, and it is your decision to have record balance-sheet spending. It is your decision to do that, even knowing that it keeps inflation higher and interest rates higher. So I'm happy for you to own it. That is fine. In 2027-28 and 2028-29, it is consecutively negative $23 billion. Has it ever been $23 billion before in history?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, the historical tables are published there, Senator Hume. We are doing a lot. We've got a lot of issues and policies and programs that we are delivering, and we're using the balance sheet to do that—just as, as I read out, all of the commitments that you made in the recent election to do the same, and presumably you will make in the election in a year and a half's time. Because that's what you've done—the history is that you set up funds and use the balance sheet to deliver your election commitments. It's what you promised last time—and, frankly, it would be a lot more if you had won that election because you would be funding nuclear power stations.

agency: Department of Finance
text: In your two per cent real spending growth, is balance sheet spending included in that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not if you're referring to growth in payments.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. Thank you. I think that's what I'm referring to when I say it's hidden. Minister, in a supply constrained environment—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not hidden; it's published—in exactly the same way that happened under your government, when you were investing in all of those things—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Off-balance-sheet spending has risen dramatically, but that's not included in the spending growth that you were referring to earlier.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, it's reported in exactly the same way that it was when you were establishing the MRFF, the national Australia facility, the Regional Investment Corporation and all of those that you established in government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: In a supply constrained environment, when there is no productivity growth, and having driven government balance-sheet spending at record highs—and on-budget government is a 40-year high—do you not recognise that inflation is staying higher than it needs to be, for longer, and that interest rates are staying higher than they need to be, for longer?

agency: Department of Finance
text: In terms of the budget and the decisions we make, we have been very conscious of the role that the budget plays in demand across the economy, and that is why we have had a focus on savings and improving the budget bottom line in every budget update that we have handed down, including two surpluses, and halving the deficit on what we inherited. That is what contributes to supporting the work that the bank is doing, and we will continue to do it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll rotate the call.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's fine.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll go to Senator Pocock.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I have one last question, and it relates to consultants. We've been talking about the government's desire, which I don't doubt, to reduce expenditure on consulting and rebuild the public sector, and yet we're seeing the absolute value of spending on consultants continue to grow every year. Minister, I've asked you many times why you won't commit to a target for reducing spending, and you've answered that the PGPA Act prevents you from intervening in that way. What other options are available to the government and the minister when they need to influence the direction or operations of a department or agency?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, they've been reflected in the decisions that we've already taken, which are to reduce agency appropriation. That is the way that we influence that. I would like spending on consultants and contractors to be lower than it is. I'm not convinced that all agencies have done what we've asked them to do and respond. I acknowledge that some agencies—if I look somewhere, particular technical skills are being sought and are needed to supplement the work of agencies. That's fine, but we have invested in additional public servants to deal with that issue. So there is a level of frustration from me, and I have raised it with my ministerial colleagues—about ensuring that we are doing everything we can to reduce spending on consultants and contractors. It's expensive. We do a lot of it. This is appropriate. We never said we would not spend anything in this area, but I would like to see greater effort to reduce it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you considered something like a ministerial direction? Why wouldn't you consider something like that, which gives you a legally binding instruction or order issued by government to a department or agency? That's a tool available to you, is it not?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll take it on notice in terms of whether or not that's even an option. I would not think it is, because I am not the sworn minister for most of the agencies across the Public Service.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But the relevant ministers could all agree to adopt such a mechanism, could they not?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'd have to take advice on it. It's not something that I have given a thought to. I have been and I am talking with Finance about further steps that we can take to reduce the spending in this area.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Another option would be to build it into returns—KPIs—that affect salary. That's an option. Would you consider looking at that as well?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think that's already in place. Again, I'm not privy to all of the performance agreements that exist, but I am aware that procurement and delivery of programs—ensuring good procurement—can form part of those.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On notice, could you inform me of the use of any KPI or salary related measures that respond to the quantum of consulting expenditure. Thank you. Have you considered establishing a whole-of-government requirement via cabinet?

agency: Department of Finance
text: A whole-of-government what?

agency: Department of Finance
text: A whole-of-government response through the cabinet in relation to setting requirements for secretaries in relation to consulting.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would have to check. That's not really in my portfolio responsibilities. That would be a matter for the Prime Minister.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I note that we are now releasing Australian Naval Infrastructure.

agency: Department of Finance
text: They had to travel from Adelaide to be here.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I am aware. The committee does try to stress to senators who call witnesses to ensure that those witnesses are well utilised and called for good purpose.

Senator Mckenzie.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Good evening, Minister. I've got some questions about the Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2 and Finance's role in guidelines. Last night, we heard some astounding evidence in RRAT estimates, and I want to thank the infrastructure department secretary, Jim Betts, for his remarkable honesty. We heard about a $125 million program worth of projects under the Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2 being taken as decisions of government in the March 2025-26 budget. In PEFO 2025 they were reported as decisions taken but not yet announced. The secretary described in estimates yesterday these decisions of government as merely election commitments. There were no guidelines for these decisions. So the decisions were taken yet not announced, but there were no guidelines for these decisions to be taken under, because the guidelines were developed after the election. That is what he said.

The senior official responsible for delivering these grants said of the pre-election budget decisions, 'I'm not sure of the process to approve these projects.' Now the department secretary in Infrastructure was unable to answer questions about how the decisions were taken to list the projects in PEFO, and the projects in question are all listed on page 28 of PEFO and add up to $125 million. The secretary said he was unable to answer about how those decisions were taken, 'because those decisions were taken in a budget process at the time, and we may not even have visibility as to how those projects were generated.' I want to ask Finance what process was undertaken to assess the Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2 projects prior to decisions being taken to approve $125 million worth of funding in the 2025 budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know whether one of my officials can assist. I wasn't in the role, and so I don't know. I'm just reading that myself. I'm happy to take it on notice—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm happy to table PEFO if you need it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, I've just been given the publication.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can come back after dinner once you've had a chance to have a think about it. I really would like to reconcile Secretary Betts's evidence with how we get a FIFO listing projects that have had decisions taken without guidelines being in place.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Perhaps I could ask a question to help us with that inquiry. You've referred to both the processes for identifying things in PEFO and the issuing of guidelines. In relation to guidelines, Finance does have a role in reviewing guidelines for grants programs, which must be provided.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, thank goodness you do, because we had to amend MLCIP's guidelines thanks to your fancy footwork before they were published. When I say 'we', I mean the Commonwealth. I mean the government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: In relation to those guidelines, it would be quite usual for guidelines to be developed after a program is determined. Guidelines are issued to provide certainty to potential applicants as to eligibility assessment et cetera. It is quite normal for those guidelines to be issued after a decision has been made to establish a program, so I just want to clarify.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. If you go to page 28—I get that, prior to elections, there may be programs set up with an amount of money for which commitments can then go through an internal process on which the decisions are to be made. But here is a list of actual projects with money committed and decisions made, and the guidelines for this program weren't actually developed until post the election. That's a unique situation in my experience, and I've gone back and checked other PEFOs. I would appreciate accuracy because I was surprised by Secretary Betts's evidence.

agency: Department of Finance
text: A provision was made. It was published at PEFO as it has to be and identified as Treasury and Finance are required to do. The guidelines are then developed for the implementation of those decisions, so that is very normal to come afterwards. That's a provision that's been made. Then a grants program will be established in order to deliver it, and the guidelines are developed to do that. That would happen—and would only be able to happen—post election because you would have to be re-elected in order to utilise that provision and pay those grants. That is the way it operates.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I appreciate your evidence, but listing specific grants, not the entirety of the grants—when I read out part 5 on page 28 to Secretary Betts last night, because I thought the Commonwealth had run a round 2 of the Priority Community Infrastructure Program, he said it's a mistake in PEFO. I said, 'Well, have you rung Finance or Treasury to tell them it's a mistake?' and he said the name was changed. I just didn't have a paper trail for it, so I'm here to ask questions about it. That's all.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Let's review what he said. I think, in terms of establishing grant guidelines after in order to implement a decision, that's very normal.

agency: Department of Finance
text: For a program, absolutely.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I will find out—

agency: Department of Finance
text: But decisions were taken on these specific projects—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, but, like any decision that we take—

agency: Department of Finance
text: without—

agency: Department of Finance
text: it can be—yes. Then they go through—like we did, and like you did in the election campaign. Then, when you're administering those, you go through a value-for-money and due-diligence phase, which is set up through the grant guidelines, in the process that's done then. But let us review what—

agency: Department of Finance
text: These decisions were taken—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I haven't brought up—

agency: Department of Finance
text: on projects, not setting up a program, Minister. Typically, programs would be set up with the amount of money the ERC deems necessary. I'm happy to run through my questions, or would you prefer me to come back?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't mind, but we do need to have a look at whatever Jim has said, because I'm not across that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll come to that, if that suits the committee, once the government has reviewed Minister Betts—'Minister Betts'! He'll love that!

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
Minister, the AFR reported on 21 October:

Over the life of the Albanese government, unexpected spending revisions totalled $145.6 billion.

Secretary, I should ask you, probably: is this a figure that you understand and agree with?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know that I've seen that article. If you can make that available, I'll have a look at it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, if you've got it—

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I'll see if I can find it for you. It's from 21 October this year. I've got a link, but I haven't got a copy. I'll find it for you. I'll quote from the article:

Veteran budget watcher Chris Richardson said the public service was rapidly getting worse at forecasting the cost of government. "You want the public service to be able to produce, on average, unbiased forecasts. Nobody demands or expects perfection, but we're talking huge dollars, so it's worth understanding if there's something systematic going on," …

Secretary, these are fightin' words! Are you concerned about the accuracy and the quality of the budget estimates, given these systemic underestimates?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator, no—

agency: Department of Finance
text: You go, Richard.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I was going to say: no. If we could see the article, that would be helpful. I suspect that we may be talking about changes in expenses, and we can explain some of the things that will have driven those which don't go to the accuracy of our forecasting.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I will find you a copy of this article and I will come back to you with that. I want to ask you more questions, please, about the whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda that was outlined in the recent budget. The fact sheet said:

The Government is progressing 14 legislative reforms that will reduce regulatory burden in the financial sector by $780 million per year …

I want to know who is accountable for ensuring the delivery of each one of those 14 measures.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can I just confirm that the particular element of the regulatory burden reduction you are referring to is in the financial services sector—is that what you said?
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: As you are aware, the most recent budget included that statement, which identified a number of potential regulatory-burden reductions across a number of portfolios. It is those individual portfolios that are charged with delivering each of those, and they are itemised at the conclusion of the fact sheet. For those that relate to the financial services sector, it is the Treasury portfolio that has the lead on the implementation and delivery of those reforms.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: I do have this—

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you're saying it's Treasury that does the internal reporting arrangements to track the delivery—is that what you said?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Treasury is responsible for delivering the individual reforms. If I can just take a step back, you are referring to specifically to those items that relate to the financial services sector, not the regulatory ideas that we've previously talked about?
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text:
The whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda fact sheet says:

The Government is progressing 14 legislative reforms that will reduce regulatory burden in the financial sector by $780 million per year …

agency: Department of Finance
text: That is the Treasury who is responsible for leading those; that is correct.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Who is tracking the delivery of those items—Treasury or Finance?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Treasury is responsible for delivering those items, as a leader in regulatory reform and coordinating across government. We take a role in the coordination of regulatory reform, and so we certainly maintain some visibility of it, but delivering those reforms and advising on their execution is led by the Treasury.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: So delivery is the responsibility of the Treasury. I understand that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That is for ones that fall under their portfolio; there are others. But, if it may help—I thought we might go here—there's an October 2026 update, which I can table and give to you, which shows all of those issues where we asked the regulators to come forward with ideas. So this is a summary of all of those issues, which is slightly different. If you want that, I can table it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are the draft regulations for the first item on the list included there? That's for raising the monetary thresholds. They're out for consultation at the moment. Is that included on that list?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No; that list is the list of regulator ideas that we spoke about at the last estimates.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Well, I'd love to see them anyway.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, you'll still find it useful.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That will be good, if you could table it. Of the 14 measures, you were saying that Treasury are responsible for the delivery. Can I be really clear—Finance is responsible for tracking the delivery?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We keep a broad eye on delivery of regulatory reform writ large—that is correct.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: There were 14 legislative reforms that were mentioned in the fact sheet. There is one of them that's out for consultation at the moment. For each of the 13 measures—how do we know whether they've been implemented so far? Are you responsible for tracking that, or is Treasury?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That would be the Treasury. We mark the status at a high level. Those are in progress, and we know where they are up to. The detail of delivery and where individual pieces of consultation or implementation are up to would be best asked of the Treasury.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. I will ask those questions of Treasury. There was $10.2 billion in gross regulatory burden, which was discussed at the last estimates. We did have this conversation in Finance, certainly. I remember it very clearly because there was no real timeline as to when we could expect that figure to be achieved. But it was also subject to revision. Can I ask: have there been any revisions to that $10.2 billion since the budget?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And how much has been realised of the $10.2 billion so far?

agency: Department of Finance
text: As we set out at the last estimates, the implementation of each of those will take varying periods depending on the particular regulatory reforms that are being pursued. Some of those involve the passage of legislation through the parliament. Some of those have occurred since we last met. For example, the Regulatory Reform Omnibus Bill recently passed and received royal assent. Others, however, remain under development. To take an example, competition reforms involve engagement with the states and territories—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. Where is that up to?

agency: Department of Finance
text: and so, in order for those to be realised, there is further work that is required. The realisation of the $10.2 billion will be contingent on completion and implementation of all of the ideas within that fact sheet, a number of which remain in progress and another number of which have been delivered.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is there some sort of—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll report against it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There will be a report against it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes—as much as we can, because this is going to be an area of continued focus for us. For example, the EPBC assessment pathways are calculated at just over $3 billion of that $10 billion. If I'm correct, that comes in in a month or so through the National Environmental Standards. The legislation has passed but hasn't come into effect. Because we're focused on this and continuing to chip away at reg reform, we would also need to update this table. But I imagine we would do that in the budget next year.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The budget next year—so not MYEFO?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't think so, just for the reason that, for some of them, like the EPBC Act, we won't have an update, because it hasn't actually come in. It'll come in on, I think, 1 December.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I just don't think there has been enough time between May and November or December to effect any significant change. So I think it's probably more meaningful to do it in the budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. Can you just remind me this: when will the $10.2 billion be realised? It's 10.2 billion per year, obviously.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's $10.2 billion per annum once all of those reforms are in place and done. As Ms Harmer said, National Competition Policy, which, again, falls under the Treasury portfolio, is being led by CFFR and involves states and territories. So it's probably pretty hard to put a timetable around that. But we'll see what we can do to provide more meaningful information around it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Hume, we are coming up against the dinner break. Did you have a wrap-up, or are you happy to stop there? Excellent. We will now suspend for the dinner break, and we will return with Finance at 7.45.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Welcome back, everybody. We will continue on with Finance, and we will go to Senator McKenzie.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you so much, Chair. Who will I direct this line of questioning to, Minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've had a look at this over the break—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm sure you have. Who did you have a look at it with?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Just my team, and then a look at the transcript from yesterday. A couple of things. There are a couple of issues that have come up, but one of them is why they were reported in PEFO and listed in PEFO. Essentially that was to deal—I note it's a similar occurrence that happened in 2022-23 in the Final Budget Outcome and Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Outlook. We had made a responsible budget provision to fund election commitments. That was declared in PEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is that the $125 million?

agency: Department of Finance
text: For projects—sorry, let me just check. The list was at (v).

agency: Department of Finance
text: Page 28.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry I didn't add it up. It was whatever was listed in (v), the $125 million over two years.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I haven't checked Finance's numbers.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The measure is $125 million over two years from 2025-26. So a provision was made. The projects declared were the projects that had been announced by ALP candidates prior to caretaker. They'd been announced as part of the election campaign. The view that Treasury and Finance took was that because they had been announced, even though they were by candidates in the campaign, they had to be declared, and so they were declared in that way. When I look back, it seems a similar approach was taken for the community development grants, which were disclosed in the 2022 PEFO, and the list was provided there in the order of $116 million. So I presume you got the same advice we did.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think the difference, Minister, between the two is the CDG guidelines wouldn't have been undeveloped at the point of it being included in PEFO. My question goes to—it stays open, and the guidelines are clear. I think we can take that on notice. Someone can tell me, either in my office or your own. The guidelines for CDG are apparent. The concern with these projects being listed—I completely understand if they were announced by candidates and you needed to account for them in PEFO prior to caretaker, but, when I read this in PEFO, it suggests that they were decisions taken under the Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2, which, in the normal course of events of a government, would have a set of guidelines available and published for these projects to be assessed against. My question goes to the end of part (v), really, where the delivery of these grants will be subject to an assessment of value for money and compliance with the applicable requirements for the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Principles 2024. For me, it raised a question that the subject to assessment piece is actually an admission that these projects went through a budget process without going through an appropriate guideline process, and I wanted clarification about that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: They didn't. We made a sensible provision in the budget for commitments that would be made during the election campaign. That was the decision of government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But you didn't.
