agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, we did.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Because the $125 million over two years is, what, a quarter of the end bucket of election commitment money, which totalled over half a billion dollars in the subsequently named MLCIP.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There are two decisions there. We made a provision in the budget. The projects were identified by ALP candidates. Once we were re-elected, guidelines were established and applications were made against that closed grant program, as had been conducted under Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 1 post the 2022 election. At some point the decision was taken, for these projects and the ones that were announced post caretaker and through the campaign, to put them together in one—

agency: Department of Finance
text: When was that decision made?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know. That's not something we can answer. That would have been under Infrastructure's decision to run that grants project for these that had been named in PEFO and the ones that had been announced as part of the election campaign. Then grant guidelines would have been implemented. We've made some changes to my role of signing off different grant guidelines, but it is very normal for decisions to be taken in budget and then, as the implementing arm implements those decisions, for grant guidelines to be developed as part of that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Why were Labor candidates with no elected roles in your government announcing decisions that were taken as a government?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The decision by the government was to make a provision to fund commitments that we knew would be made.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But this isn't the total amount of money that was made.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The Treasury had a view, and Finance, had a view that the projects that were announced prior to caretaker needed to be declared. So they have been declared—there.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And they're raising questions about what process they went through.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No. Who's raising questions?

agency: Department of Finance
text: When you said that ALP candidates announced them, how did your government assess the worthiness of these projects that are listed in your PEFO? They weren't assessed by the infrastructure department. They weren't assessed by you—

agency: Department of Finance
text: They are, through the grants guidelines process, through the applications process—

agency: Department of Finance
text: They weren't assessed by Minister King. What process did these projects go through?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Just like the $1.6 billion that you announced for community infrastructure would have gone through the same process.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Tell me the process you went through, because this isn't the same process. The closed, non-competitive grant round of MLCIP isn't like other programs run by other governments, yours or ours. So my question is—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, it's the way we have been advised to implement election commitments.

agency: Department of Finance
text: How were these projects assessed for funding?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're not going to get very far unless you listen to the answers and then repose your questions. We might just try to take it in turns, as best we can, so everyone can hear what everyone is saying.

agency: Department of Finance
text:
The process that's followed is the one that's outlined:

The delivery of these grants will be subject to an assessment of value for money and compliance with the applicable requirements of the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Principles 2024.

That is what happened and, in every election commitment we made, that was stated at the bottom of any announcement we made.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What process—

agency: Department of Finance
text: On winning government—no, let me finish, because you've been interrupting me. On winning the election, we went about—Minister King, in particular, and her department—went about implementing the election commitments we had made in accordance with the advice we had and in accordance with the grant guidelines, rules and principles, which allow for the delivery of election commitments. In accordance with those rules—value-for-money assessments, ability to deliver—due diligence is done through that process.

agency: Department of Finance
text: This group of projects is a small proportion of the infrastructure projects that were announced and committed to by your government over the course of the election campaign. I understand, and am pursuing with the department of infrastructure, the process that the larger group of 220-odd projects is now going through. My question, Minister, to you as the minister responsible for one of the central agencies, is: what process did these projects go through to be part of the budget process? If some of your officials could assist, I'd appreciate that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've answered it three times. You're refusing to listen to me.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can hear you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The government decision was to make a sensible provision. That was the government decision.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You made these decisions in a budget.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator McKenzie—

agency: Department of Finance
text: You're not listening to my answer. We made a provision to fund election commitments that needed to be disclosed in accordance with the rules around pre-election fiscal outlook. So that gets done. Advice to the government was that any announcement made as part of the election campaign between that decision and the caretaker period had to be disclosed. That is what has happened, okay? So—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not asking you about the disclosure. I'm asking about the process by which these projects came about. An ALP candidate finds them and says, 'I want to fund 20 more classes.' What's that process?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's not something that Finance is responsible for.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But, Minister, are you responsible? Are you part of the team that makes that decision?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm telling you what I'm responsible for and what I'm appearing as: the Minister for Finance. I'm not appearing as an ALP candidate. As the Minister for Finance, we took a decision to make a provision for projects that were going to be funded against that provision. The ones that were made before caretaker were disclosed. In the event that we didn't win the election, presumably these would not have been your election commitments and you would not have funded them, but what we had announced before caretaker have been disclosed. On winning the election, we then went through a process, in accordance with the grant rules and principles, around due diligence around funding those projects. That is what the Infrastructure department has done. It is in accordance with the grant rules and principles. It is exactly what we have been advised to do to deliver election commitments, and I presume it is what you would have had to do for the $1.6 billion worth of commitments that you made during the election campaign.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Did the minister for infrastructure take these projects through the budget process?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can't say this any more times. The government made a sensible provision to fund election commitments. That is actually a responsible thing to do. It's disclosed. We then go through a process, once we've won the election, of implementing those decisions against the grant rules, principles and guidelines that are established, and that is exactly what has happened.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator McKenzie—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary, does PEFO include the Labor Party's electoral commitments?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator McKenzie, the chair is trying to get your attention.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I have a question for the secretary.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We are going around in a few circles here. I appreciate that you're not liking the answer, or it's not suiting where you're trying to go, but it is the answer the minister has given, and she's given it three time now.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Very good. Big claps there. Does PEFO include the Labor Party's election commitment?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Under V, they were commitments that have been made by ALP candidates in the election campaign.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That wasn't my question.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It is. You said, 'Are there ALP election commitments in PEFO?' That is disclosed in section V. That's exactly what they were, and I—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Did minister King take these projects through the budget process?

agency: Department of Finance
text: One, we don't disclose decisions of ERC, but I have been clear that the decision was made—

agency: Department of Finance
text: The decisions of ERC are actually clear in the budget. They're either in or not.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The decision that was made was to make a provision, which we did in the budget. I think it was in the 2025-26 budget. We made a provision; it was a DTBNYA. We knew we would be funding election commitments, so instead of not making a provision, we made a provision. In discussions in the lead up to PEFO, there was a view from Treasury and Finance that any election commitment that had been made prior to caretaker needed to be accounted for, and so it was.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Were the centrals concerned that ALP candidates and the ALP internal process was getting ahead of usual practice in elections?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No. It was about transparency, and it was about the fact that we were in government, commitments had been made, and the view was to be clear. These are documents that the secretaries of Finance and Treasury sign off on.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm wondering how the $16 million for the Bega Pool gets on the list.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If I can finish—it's a decision taken by the secretaries of those departments at the time about the content. And I know there is a lot of consideration about transparency and being very clear about what their view of the state of the budget is. Now, because of that—because there had been a number of commitments made since that decision was taken in the budget and caretaker—the decision was made to disclose those. I don't know how much clearer we can be.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've said three times myself that I appreciate the disclosure piece. I'm not talking about the disclosure, and I will repeat my question. I hope you can hear me when I ask, how does—for instance—the $16 million Bega Pool get on this list. Is it a failure of the infrastructure department or minister for not putting it through a process?

agency: Department of Finance
text: These are matters that are dealt with as part of normal election campaigns. How did you get to your $1.6 billion right across the country—over 200 more to deliver the project?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm here asking about a program—$125 million is not how much community infrastructure projects that you actually funded, you funded over half-a-billion dollars worth of projects.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You had $1.6 billion. How did you come to those?

agency: Department of Finance
text: When you talk about making a provision in the budget, you only made a quarter of the provision.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We didn't.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Given the infrastructure department told Senate Estimates it had no role in the identification of PCIP round 2 projects prior to the 2025 budget consideration, which department or minister did have a role in proposing these projects under this program.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It wouldn't be appropriate for the department. I mean, you would be in here slamming the table if the department of infrastructure dreamt up the projects they wanted Labor candidates to announce. You would be the first one.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So who was it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It was developed through the normal process of an election campaign. I don't know how your party does it, but these are matters that are dealt with through the party campaign. My job as finance minister was to make a sensible provision for some of those commitments. That's what we did. The Treasury and Finance secretary disclosed what had been announced before caretaker as part of PEFO. It then goes through the standard process that all election commitments have gone through, in accordance with the Commonwealth grant rules and guidelines.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The infrastructure department was unable to state when they became aware of the PCIP round 2 projects. Did the Department of Finance have visibility of the $125 million worth of projects proposed for funding under the Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2 prior to them being approved for funding in the 2025 budget?

agency: Department of Finance
text: This is not a matter for that, no. They were election commitments made by the Labor Party. We made a provision for which we would acquit them against, or some of them against, that was disclosed. Those commitments were made publicly, and I made sure that a full list was provided to the relevant secretaries. In very clear transparency, these are the commitments that have been made as part of the election campaign.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's post election though.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, it wasn't.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm just clarifying, because the secretary said—

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, it was so they could be fully disclosed. That's why.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On what dates did the Department of Finance provide briefings to the minister on the PCIP round 2 projects?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, they wouldn't have. It wouldn't have been appropriate, Senator Mckenzie.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Given the infrastructure department believes there were no guidelines supporting the selection of the $125 million of Priority Community Infrastructure Program round 2 projects that were approved for funding in the 2025 budget, is the Department of Finance aware of whether there were any guidelines?

agency: Department of Finance
text: So I've been through this. The guidelines were established alongside the implementation of the election commitments. That is very normal, very appropriate and in accordance with the grant rules and principles.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I can only reiterate what the minister said.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's very Bill Shorten of you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: They were done after the election. The grant guidelines were done after the election.

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, we know that. Here we've got a decision of government taken and disclosed appropriately, but, with these projects, the evidence seems to be that there were no guidelines for these projects to be assessed against.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Mckenzie, that is not unusual. That is how it happens now. If we take a decision, for example, to run a program in health—say, tobacco cessation. Let's take that. If we took a decision on that in the budget and said we were going to give it to a particular organisation—or it might be a competitive process, in which case it would be an open grant round—then we would announce it in the budget and then grant guidelines would be established in order to implement that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Agreed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So that is completely normal.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary, were you aware of these projects?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, Matt wasn't in the job then.

agency: Department of Finance
text: My predecessor was aware, and that's why the two secretaries—

agency: Department of Finance
text: The secretary was aware of the projects.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I disclosed them.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's why it's been disclosed in PEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I made sure there was a full list. In accordance with what happened for you in 2022-23, where the similar disclosure was made at PEFO—

agency: Department of Finance
text: They're not comparable. Please just stick to this.

agency: Department of Finance
text: They are. In terms of disclosure, they are, Senator Mckenzie.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The process for decision-making—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Treasury and Finance has a view—

agency: Department of Finance
text: The process for decision-making—

agency: Department of Finance
text: that election commitments announced before caretaker should be declared In PEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The minister is answering your question, Senator McKenzie.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm feeling berated.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm feeling like you're being quite rude, certainly towards me.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's a similar position to what was taken in 2022-23. You're saying it's different regarding guidelines. That's a separate issue. The disclosure of announcements of election commitments made before caretaker were disclosed in 2022-23. They were disclosed in 2025.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is the department aware of whether there was an official assessment process undertaken by any government agency prior to the decision being taken to fund the $125 million worth of PCIP round 2 projects—it sounds formal—in the 2025 budget?

agency: Department of Finance
text: So I can answer that. The reason it was round 2 was that our 2022 election commitments were round 1, so that was the decision taken—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It suggests they're a process, though.

agency: Department of Finance
text: to disclose round 2. After the election, the commitments that had been disclosed as part of subsection (v) of PEFO were brought together with the other commitments that were made post caretaker, and the grant round was delivered through that program, in accordance with the grant rules and guidelines. We have followed the rules every step of the way, no matter which way you try and come at this. We have followed the rules. We've taken advice. I met with the previous auditor-general about how you acquit election commitments in an appropriate way to make sure that we followed every single bit of advice. Minister King and I have done that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary, did the process undertaken for these PCIP round 2 grants funded in the 2025 budget comply with the requirements of the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act and the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Principles 2024?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Before the payments were made, they went through the normal value-for-money assessment in the grant guidelines, so yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's not my question. The payments, in most cases, haven't been made at all.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The PGPA is exercised once the grant guidelines have been finalised and payments are going to flow. Prior to that, it was a decision of candidates and what projects—the projects we knew at the time of PEFO are disclosed in part (v).

agency: Department of Finance
text: So it is your evidence to this committee that the process undertaken for the PCIP round 2 grants funded in the 25 budget does comply with both the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act and the Commonwealth Grant Rules and Principles 2024?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Secretary, it's a yes or a no.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Don't tell somehow how to answer.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I only found out about this program an hour ago. I would want to have a look at all the paperwork. You clearly are asserting that there is a problem—

agency: Department of Finance
text: There is no problem.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There is nothing that I've heard—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I want to be assured that there isn't a problem.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I will take it on notice and provide you that assurance.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you so much.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I want to turn to some questions about Snowy Hydro. Last night in Senate estimates, it was revealed that Snowy Hydro made a request to government for a new support package. It was confirmed by the CEO of Snowy, Mr Barnes, that this new support package would be required by the middle of next year and that it would cost anywhere between $5 billion and $10 billion. I want to ask: is Finance aware of this request that's coming to government?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, we're aware.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Did you find out last night, like the rest of us, or did you know about it beforehand?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We've been engaged with Snowy throughout. We support our minister as one of the shareholder ministers for Snowy Hydro.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you knew about that in advance, then. Does Finance understand the type of additional support that's being requested to be a loan or an equity investment?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Those decisions haven't been taken. I think Snowy would have a view, but we will be going through our processes to make those decisions.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Does Finance understand the quantum of additional support that's requested? My understanding is that it's between $5 billion and $10 billion, but is there something more specific that you can enlighten us on?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll be working with Snowy through the MYEFO process for the government to be able to make a decision on options of both quantum and what the financing might look like.

agency: Department of Finance
text: For the MYEFO process, are your—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll consider it as part of MYEFO—

agency: Department of Finance
text: As part of government—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It will come through our normal processes, as you would expect.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If that's the case, has the request turned into a submission to the minister or something that has allowed Finance to formally respond to the review of the liability yet?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The shareholders have had correspondence from Snowy, and we will be considering that and then taking, as you would expect, a normal submission process through MYEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: When was the request from Snowy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It was very recently. Obviously, we've been engaging with them as they've been going through this cost reassessment process, but it would have been around the time that the cost reassessment process was finalised.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It was the end of September that shareholder ministers received a letter from Snowy Hydro. That was around the time that Snowy's cost reassessment was provided.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Has Finance considered the amount of government funding required to prevent Snowy's credit rating—which I understand is BBB+ at the moment—being downgraded?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's one of the characteristics that we will think about as we provide advice to government for MYEFO.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think S&P have issued an advisory saying that they are, in essence, keeping an eye on how the government responds to the cost reassessment.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is that publicly available?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's publicly available.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You don't have a copy of it that you can table, by any chance?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I probably do, and we can get it for you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll provide you with a copy, because that has some—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's a 'no change' on their credit rating, but they're saying in light of the cost reassessment they'll keep an eye on how the government responds.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What does it mean for the Commonwealth's budget position if Snowy's credit rating is downgraded?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That would be a hypothetical question.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're not there, and—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's more than a hypothetical; it's a sensitivity analysis, isn't it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're going through the analysis with Snowy to be able to provide advice to government on a range of factors for what options for financing would look like.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yesterday the CEO of Snowy, Mr Barnes, confirmed that the net present value of the project won't be updated following the cost reassessment. Would an updated NPV help Finance to make its recommendations to the minister about the requested support package?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would come back to the fact that we will be looking at all of the analysis provided to us by Snowy, and we will be providing analysis for the government to consider.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That doesn't really answer the question that I asked, though, does it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Every aspect of it is being considered as part of all of the new information. The decisions the government needs to take in relation to this are all currently before government, and no further decisions have been taken.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Turning to the cost reassessment announcement, which had a revised cost to complete of $25 billion, how confident is Finance in the veracity of that assessment?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have commissioned an independent cost reassurance process from Turner & Townsend. That has not yet been finalised. That information will go in and inform advice to government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It was confirmed at estimates last night that the cost reassessment announcement was provided to DCCEEW on 30 September. I asked you what that date was and you confirmed that. Can you tell me—forgive me, I think I've just answered my own question. The letter was provided to Finance and to you, Minister, on 30 September, but why did we find out about it and that cost blowout only on that last business day before Senate estimates? Is there an obligation upon you to disclose that sooner?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think that's pretty soon.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's correct; there was a board meeting that Snowy Hydro had to go through, and they had to go through their own processes to sign off with the board. They then needed to be able to get something firm enough to put in their annual report.

agency: Department of Finance
text: When was the board meeting?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not in my material—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We got the materials, and Minister Bowen and I probably had a couple of weeks. I had briefings from Finance. We met with the board, and then the announcement was made. I think it all happened reasonably quickly, from my point of view, of getting the cost reassessment report, reading that and having the required meetings I needed to have. Minister Bowen and I met with the chair and CEO of the Snowy Hydro as well to discuss it. I think we wrote to the board or the chair as well on receipt of the cost reassessment prior to that. I think it's a pretty quick turnaround. I don't think there was anything about Senate estimates. The timing of Senate estimates was not a factor.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator, I have the timing of the board meeting for you, which was the 28 September.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's only the 27th today, isn't it? That makes sense. Can I ask, will you do a new net present value assessment?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We will see what information we get, particularly the independent costs assessment from Turner & Townsend to provide information to government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: When's that expected?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We would expect it shortly. They've been working with Snowy Hydro for a while. It's not something where they come in at the end, but it's not yet finalised.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are Turner & Townsend contracted to Snowy Hydro or are they contracted to Finance?

agency: Department of Finance
text: They're contracted through Finance.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Through Finance?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Through the Department of Finance, that's right.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Obviously, that contract is something, as you said, that's been ongoing for some time.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's been ongoing for a little while, but there's only so much they can do until the information, and the line-by-line cost reassessment, are provided by Snowy Hydro. They have been working with Snowy Hydro for a little while to get information, but they're not able to finalise their report until they have all of the relevant information from Snowy Hydro, which they are working through now.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You seem to have a natural sort of reluctance to say that there will be a new NPV completed, is there a reason for that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm just not sure, Senator. I don't want to mislead. I'm just not sure. We will get a lot of information, and we've got a lot of information, and we will provide that information to government to provide options.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There was a new project benefits analysis that was released just last week. That didn't include an updated NPV, which is surprising. Do you know what the net present value of this project is now?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Again, Senator, as I've just mentioned, we're going through all of the information, and we'll use the Turner & Townsend assessment to provide information to government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Since the receipt of the letter, has Snowy provided the minister or the minister's office with any additional information or additional submissions about that cost reassessment? I know you said that you've met with the board and you've spoken to them, but is there additional information that they've provided you since that original letter?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The cost reassessment report was part of that. The report which was provided to us.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I thought that it hadn't been completed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There's the Snowy's cost reassessment one. Finance is doing an assessment of that assessment.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Assessment of the assessment. Okay, I get it. I understand. Has there been any material on the potential sensitivities arising from that cost reassessment, which has been provided to you from Snowy directly? Maybe I should be asking you this: from a government perspective, what are the potential sensitivities that would be arising from your cost reassessment of their cost reassessment?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think we'd need the cost assurance material from Turner & Townsend, so—

agency: Department of Finance
text: We don't have that third-party artefact yet which enables us to see whether there are differences of view over what Snowy's own reassessment has done and answer that question. That is what we're waiting on, and then we will use that to provide advice to the government as part of the MYEFO decision-making period.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The minister, Mr Bowen, has said that the costs will be made public. Is that your understanding?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It will be a decision for government—

agency: Department of Finance
text: He's the government.

agency: Department of Finance
text: in conjunction with the board as to what is made public. It has been public. The cost reassessment, from Snowy Hydro's view, is $22.2 billion, with a $3 billion contingency amount. So that has been disclosed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister, in December 2024 you provided Snowy Hydro with a new statement of expectations. That revised statement followed the release of an updated business case which itself followed the 2023 project reset, which showed a $12 billion budget blowout. In view of this now $25 billion blowout, will you provide a new statement of expectations to Snowy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister Bowen and I will make some further decisions around how we respond to the cost escalation that we are seeing. I'm not sure if that will require a new statement of expectations, but I'm not ruling it out either. We haven't made those decisions yet.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Can I ask whether a third-party assurance on Snowy's own cost reassessment is—I agree with you that it's necessary. Is it normal? Is this something that has been done in the past specifically for Snowy, or is it something that is done for other GBEs?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not the first time that I'm aware that Finance has undertaken, or other departments have undertaken, an independent cost-assurance process. Most recently, I understand that the department of infrastructure undertook an independent cost-assurance process for Inland Rail, which assisted government to make decisions. So, for large megaprojects, it is not uncommon for an independent cost-assurance process to be undertaken.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Independent advice outside of cost is pretty routine. Finance is the commercial adviser to me across a whole number of GBEs and SIVs and things like that. So I think taking independent advice to verify and provide assurance to the government is not unusual.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister, I realise that you are one of two shareholder ministers for Snowy. The other shareholder minister has said publicly that, once Snowy Hydro has reassessed, he will release data. I think he said—what did he say? He would release the costs—release the report.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think it was on Sunrise he might have said that. It was a breakfast TV show, anyway. Is that something that he had discussed with you as the other shareholder minister and something you had agreed upon?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Good. So the report will be released?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We had discussed, I think, the process now, and we're mindful there's an OPD. But also, prior to that, we had discussed the need for as much information to be made available as could be. I understand there are some commercial-in-confidence sensitivities that we will have to consider as part of that, but we will do that to make sure we can provide as much information as possible.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. Thank you very much for that. That was very helpful. I want to go back to some questions about the whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda that I asked a little earlier.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Just while you're gathering your thoughts, Senator Hume, I will just note that we are still somewhat behind on the agenda, and, if any senator would like to place their questions on notice, that would be delightful. Back to you, Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I have one quick line of questioning here and then one more, and then I think that we will hopefully be nearly done with Finance.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You'll be done by 11.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, we'll be done by 11. On that whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda that we discussed a little bit earlier—thank you for that. We were talking about the 14 different elements of that. You said that you had high-level oversight of the regulatory reform agenda that was being implemented by Treasury. I just want to know whether you have a high-level update on the progress of each of those reforms. I know you said that Treasury implements, but, obviously, there is oversight from Finance, as far as regulatory reform goes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. We have visibility of the key elements that are outlined in that regulatory reform agenda, as the minister outlined earlier. The top item in that agenda is streamlining Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act assessment pathways. As the minister outlined, legislative amendments were made nearly 12 months ago, and another element of that kicks in later this year, which is expected to streamline timeframes for decisions under that legislation.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's the one that's out for consultation now, yes?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The EPBC?
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. That's out, isn't it; is that right?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think the element you were referring to earlier was in the Treasury portfolio, which is in—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, you're right; sorry. I'm getting all my regulatory reforms messed up.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Other elements—
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: The single national market?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, which one was that?
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: The second one is a single national market to create clear and consistent rules for Australian businesses, workers and consumers. Do you know where that one is?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are you referring to just the items that are within the Treasury portfolio or the whole regulatory reform agenda?
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: This is the Whole-of-government regulatory reform agenda: regulatory reform to unlock productivity and economic dynamism fact sheet.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think you're taking me to the individual items within the financial sector reform package. I don't have a breakdown of that in front of me. I do have that writ large, and I think, as I said, Treasury can give you more information that, writ large, the financial sector reform is in progress and that Treasury is undertaking consultation on a number of elements of those. Treasury would be able to give you more detail on the status of individual elements. We probably have them at a high level, because they have carriage of those particular reforms.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Again, that's the case throughout the entirety of the agenda. There are a number of items within the regulatory reform agenda. We have a high-level view, but the relevant portfolio that is delivering those reforms can provide you with more detail on those. There are a small number that are with us.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Alright. I have some questions about the Reserve Bank's credit card surcharge ban and whole-of-government procurement. As yours is the department obviously with the responsibility for whole-of-government procurement policies, I'm wondering if there is a whole-of-government policy for negotiating merchant fees with credit card providers.

agency: Department of Finance
text: To my knowledge, there is not a whole-of-government policy on merchant fees.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not that I'm aware of, Senator. The Treasury has responsibility for payment systems generally. Individual entities are responsible for their own banking and payment arrangements, and there is not a whole-of-Commonwealth position that I'm aware of in relation to the payment of fees.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would assume that the government would be in receipt of an awful lot of credit card payments. I'm not just talking about the ATO, obviously. There are licences and penalties and all sorts of things that get paid with credit cards. So I'm interested in why there hasn't been an effort to secure a better outcome, similar to travel or advertising or whatever it might be, given that, obviously, the government is one of the largest financial entities in the country. Is that something that has been considered?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think that is a question that might be better directed to the Treasury, given their responsibility for payment systems.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are they responsible for that? Are they responsible for the payment of penalties or fines or a licensing fee that might be imposed by another department?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Individual departments are responsible for their own cost recovery and charging arrangements and make administrative arrangements to give effect to those. Payment systems legislation and payment systems policy within the AAOs is within the Treasury portfolio, but individual entities make their own banking and payment arrangements to discharge their respective functions.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: I suppose so, but it is a whole-of-government issue. In the same way, I think the best example is probably travel or advertising. If there is a procurement policy that applies to every department and is negotiated by Finance, surely this would be up there with something that Finance could negotiate.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There's not such a policy that I'm aware of.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: The Assistant Treasurer said that he and the Treasurer had told the ATO to continue to engage with credit card companies to negotiate lower fees. You're telling me that individual departments have to negotiate individual arrangements. Do you have a list of the arrangements across governments? Is that something that finance would have?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Do you know if any departments have successfully negotiated lower fees?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think you'd have to ask each entity about what their arrangements are. Different entities have a different prevalence of accepting payments depending on the nature of their functions. You would need to ask those respective departments about the arrangements that they are making.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Home Affairs said that it removed surcharges under a government directive. Has the Department of Finance issued any guidance? Are you aware of any guidance that has been issued either from your from you guys, from the Treasury or from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet on how it needs to respond to the surcharge ban?

agency: Department of Finance
text: It's not something that Finance has had carriage of. It's a matter for Treasury.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What payments does Finance and its portfolios accept by card? Does it have fees, charges, licences or applications?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have very few services in that space. Some of my colleagues can assist with that.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Finance doesn't accept any payments by card.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's interesting. Has the department done any assessment on the impact on small businesses, on people in hardship, or on people who rely on credit cards for cash flow or who might lack other payment options? Is that something that Finance would do?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister, were you briefed on your department's approach to this prior to the announcement on 1 October?

agency: Department of Finance
text: There was certainly some discussion, and I think the Assistant Treasurer had written to ministers about the work that the Reserve Bank was doing. That had gone through the normal processes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would have thought that this would be an area that would be absolutely ripe for government procurement. It sounds obvious. Surcharges clearly are a massive issue, and there are elements right across government that require payments by credit card that people might not be able to use now. Is it something that you might consider in the future using your whole-of-government responsibilities and your procurement heft to be able to get a better deal?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No. This work has been led by the Treasury. It's got significant impacts at the ATO level, but for other agencies you'll have to direct questions to them.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thanks.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Collins?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you, Minister, for the letter about the defence estate. I have a few questions on that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sure. I'd forgotten about that little chestnut.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you been given a timeline of when Victoria Barracks, Sydney will be handed over to the Department of Finance?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No, not definitively. My understanding is that Defence is working to relocate people who are currently working there by the end of this year, but we haven't got a formal or final date.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It has been indicated to me that it might be in the next month or so. Is that not correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have not got a final date, but I do know that Defence is working towards being off that site as much as they can by the end of the year.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you made any preparations to take over the maintenance of Victoria Barracks Sydney?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That'll all be subject to those final discussions between Finance and Defence. For some of the work that I've been doing, I visited Victoria Barracks—first time I've ever been in there because it's not publicly accessible.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Sorry, it is.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not really. You can—

agency: Department of Finance
text: It is. You can go there every week. You can go there to do lawn bowls. You can go there for tours. You can go to the museum every single week or a couple of times a week. It is publicly accessible.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I went there last Thursday to have a look, as I'm trying to get around to the other 67 sites and trying to visit all of them. They are all quite different. There are some that have been vacant for a long time—old training facilities, all the way up to those that have significant heritage value like Victoria Barracks in Sydney and in Melbourne. They're quite varied locations and sites, but we're doing all the work that you would expect us to do. Defence is doing some of that. When they hand it over to Finance, as final decisions are made, there will be agreement about maintaining the sites in all of their varied forms.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I noted in your letter to me that you estimated that there was going to be $3 billion in remediation costs. Have you done any costings on Victoria Barracks Sydney as to the remediation?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We drew that figure from the report that had been done. I do have a figure in my head; I just want to make sure that it's right. We haven't verified a number, but that was a figure—we're very conscious of the ongoing costs associated with maintaining all of these sites, not one in particular but all of them, and how we best utilise that investment into defence operational capability.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The defence minister has put it as a $200 million bill for maintenance. They're all ongoing costs for Victoria—

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's the figure I had, which I think was from the independent report.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That was actually from the defence minister. The Security and Estate Group, who is overseeing the divestment process, has said to us a number of times, and they also confirmed on Thursday last week, that they don't manage a budget for upkeep site by site, so they don't actually have those figures per site. What happens is you have a maintenance program that's spread over the entire state. You get a contract for the entire state and all the estates in there. So I'm wondering if you're aware of where the defence minister got the $200 million figure for Victoria Barracks Sydney, because previously it was $50 million over five years. Now it's $200 million over 10 years.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'll see if there's anything I can help—that's the number I had in my head too. I'm trying to locate it for you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So the Department of Finance hasn't done any costings on anything or—

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Any costings on relocation?

agency: Department of Finance
text: No.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So relocating staff or—

agency: Department of Finance
text: There's relocating staff, there's relocating infrastructure, there's vehicles, there's armoury, there's—

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's being managed by Defence. We will not be doing any of that. We have a very specific role, which is when the properties are ready to be handed over to Finance they are done. We expect some due diligence—probably not all of it—to be done, and then it will come to Finance for the next decisions about the sale of those facilities.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What sort of due diligence will be done by the Department of Finance? What are you looking at there?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That due diligence would typically involve, and this would be site specific, doing the building reports, assessing conditions of the buildings, looking at the heritage and ecological overlay of the site—so doing the heritage assessments, looking at site valuations, looking at any contamination, estimating the cost of any remediation and so on.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. So you will be doing the costings on remediation and all that sort of stuff. That will happen with Victoria Barracks as soon as Defence has moved out—is that correct?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We will commence that due diligence process when Defence moves out.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Is KPMG doing the due diligence process? You're not actually doing it yourselves? KPMG has been engaged to do the due diligence?

agency: Department of Finance
text: As a strategic property adviser, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have engaged KPMG to manage the due diligence process, yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: How much is that contract for?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The KPMG contract as our strategic industry adviser is $16.7 million from March 2026 until 31 January 2028.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And that contract was entered into prior to the issues that have emerged around KPMG.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you received any expressions of interest for the purchase of Victoria Barracks Sydney?

agency: Department of Finance
text: On our website, we've got two avenues where people can express interest for all properties, including Victoria Barracks. We've got a 'feedback on future use' form, which is where people express interest with either concrete proposals or ideas for how to use the sites. We received 91 'feedback on future use' forms, and we have also received 18 general inquiries for Vic Barracks Sydney.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are any of the general inquiries actual potential buyers, or do they just have ideas on what they want to do with it?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Typically, the people wanted to know about the divestment process and so on.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you had any engagements with potential buyers?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not at this stage.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And neither have I.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. There were reports earlier in the year, when these were first announced, that somebody approached the Albanese government with a $5 billion proposal to buy all 67 sites. Are you aware of that? That was reported in—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, it didn't come to me.

agency: Department of Finance
text: You're not aware of it? That was in the AFR.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I know there are sensitivities about a number of the sites, but there are many of them where there is a lot of community support for different roles—housing, for example. There's a lot of interest from state governments. So we're working through that. We're going to be sensible and methodical. The issues around heritage and history are really important. They will be dealt with very carefully. I think there's some concern that I've seen raised about these buildings not existing any more. That's just not true. They are historically significant, but they are no longer required to position the Defence Force for the operational practicalities that they need going forward. So we are doing the careful and thoughtful work that's required, including me visiting all of the sites. I've done 15, maybe, and I'm trying to get around to all of them. I went to Penguin last week and met with some of the staff that work there. The mayor joined me. I talked with her about the community's issues. So I'm really trying very hard to get across what everybody's view is. There are a lot of mixed views, and I'm getting all of that feedback.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I just want to thank you for going to all the sites. I think you're the only Labor representative that has embarked upon that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think Peter Khalil's been going to a number of them.

agency: Department of Finance
text: He's been going to the community information sessions; I'm sure about that. I know he's been down to HMAS Penguin because, if it weren't for his visit down there, the whole thing would still be fully divested. We're still unsure about which part of HMAS Penguin will be sold off. I know you said in here that the capabilities would not be lost, but the only part you can sell down there is the angophora forest and the accommodation, and I just can't for the life of me understand why you would want to do that and why you'd want to have eight luxury apartments looking down upon the critical work that our Navy people are doing.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, that's why it's important to go and visit so that, instead of looking at a map, you can actually see how the site is positioned. I was able to see the forest. I understand that the Sydney Federation Trust is interested in managing the forest or having that as part of the area that they manage on that site, so all of those are reasonable requests for us to think through and work through.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you had any feedback on Defence Plaza Sydney? You're talking about being reasonable about this process, not trying to diminish Australia's capability. Forces command has been split up, part of it going to Randwick Barracks, which has been partially sold as well, and part of it's going to Defence Plaza, Sydney—an office block, very open plan. Have you visited there yet and taken a look at the spaces there and whether it's actually fit for purpose for the forces command going in?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I haven't because it doesn't fall within my responsibilities, which are related to divestment of the Defence estate. That's very much in the responsibility of the defence ministers. I did visit Randwick Barracks last week as well to have a look at that. There is a lot of unused land as part of that site.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Which is mostly contaminated.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Certainly, it was explained to me that there was some contamination on that site, but that's not unusual for Defence sites, frankly. I mean, many of them seem to have contamination that will have to be considered as part of the divestment process.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Collins, I'm going to rotate the call.

agency: Department of Finance
text: On that contamination point, where does the liability for that land? Will it be the Department of Finance, the Department of Defence? Will you be remediating the land before you sell it on, or does it come off the sale price? What do you do? How does that all work? I mean, nearly every Defence site is contaminated, as you say, except for Defence Plaza, which is a fancy new corporate block. Who pays for that?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We will do the due diligence and then we will give options and a divestment strategy to the government to make decisions about how we do that. That could range from the project cleans the site up or it's sold as is with that information disclosed. Each site will have a divestment approach or a plan that will be agreed by ministers.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And some of that's being managed now like the Fairbairn golf course out here in Canberra. Part of their argument to me to not sell that land is because of the contamination, but they still use it as a golf course, so people are using the land knowingly. But their argument is you can't dig down and start building and things like that—unsettling it. All of those things are being considered.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Will you come back to me, or should I just ask one final question: how is it going to work?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, you're over the agreed time. We are very, very, very far behind and we're trying to work on the priorities of your collective party.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I understand. I've been here all day. Respectfully, can I just ask one more question?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's an issue for you to take up with your party, not me.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I am happy for Jess to take my time.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you. Will there be conditions of sale? At Victoria Barracks in Sydney, they do use the helicopter pad for St Vincent's Hospital for heart and lung transfer. They use it all the time. Will there be a condition that they will still be able to access that there? For anything with heritage, when you sell these bases, the Commonwealth heritage protections actually get lifted. What are you going to do about protecting these places?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, for those buildings, there will definitely be conditions on the sale because of the heritage value of those sites.

agency: Department of Finance
text: And the parade grounds and the mess halls, what's going to happen?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Well, they're all heritage listed and protected—the parade grounds, the mess halls, all of them. In Victoria Barracks, Melbourne, I think there's a couple of buildings that aren't heritage listed but are just a couple of later additions. But almost the entire block has a heritage overlay, and I think it's the same for—

agency: Department of Finance
text: But you lose that when you sell it, right? Once it goes from Commonwealth to state, you're going to lose the Commonwealth protections.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Again, none of the decisions about who would be the purchaser have been taken but they will be protected.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Options are that you can put covenants over it, but that will go to depending on what the government decides as to what the sale process and the use of each property is.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But they will absolutely be protected. The heritage of those buildings is very significant, and they will be protected.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The buildings are one thing, but I just want to put on the record, just so you're aware of it, that many of these parade grounds have had the ashes of veterans, of serving members, spread across them. There's the wives of the personnel there that have died on base. They've got plaques. There are a few plaques. There are many, many plaques around the rose gardens and the rose bed around the officers' mess. There is so much history inside these messes. When they get moved across into Defence Plaza Sydney, there is going to be no mess for them in there anymore. There are no messes. There's virtually no gym. There's a gym for 10 people, and you're going to have hundreds and hundreds of people in there. The whole fabric of this is going to go. I just want you to know that. This is the impact. This needs to go into your due diligence, with all of this.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've certainly heard aspects of that, definitely, and I can only assure you that those aspects will be protected. The parade grounds and others have heritage overlay right now. I might be wrong on Sydney. I know the Victorian one has—

agency: Department of Finance
text: In Sydney, the parade ground is.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I know the parade ground is. But, in Melbourne, the entire site has a heritage overlay. Is that the same in Sydney?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. There are 12, and then a site.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Minister, is there any opportunity that we can save Victoria Barracks Sydney? Can anything be done? Please, please, please, can you do anything to save Victoria Barracks Sydney, at the very least?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The government has taken a decision to divest a number of Defence estate facilities, and both Victoria Barracks Sydney and Melbourne is included in that. But what I'm telling you is that I am meeting with people. We are doing the work. We are considering all the issues that are being raised.

agency: Department of Finance
text: If due diligence shows that it's not the right thing to do—I know the feedback has come back to you; I know the feedback is not good—if they say to you that you are diminishing capability, is there an opportunity to walk back on this?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The government's not reconsidering the decisions we've taken. If that Defence estate review, that independent audit, in fact, itself pointed out that these decisions had been kicked off for decades and had led to the issues now, which is Defence is spending money upgrading and maintaining facilities it no longer needs for a modern operational capability, then we have to deal with that. What I'm telling you is that the work that I'm doing is visiting the sites, talking to as many people as I can and being fully across the issues that are being raised. But we are not reconsidering the decision about whether or not to progress with divestment of these sites.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Senator Canavan.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I just want to go back to Snowy Hydro. Has the department been involved at all or had any oversight or been asked to provide an updated valuation of the Snowy 2.0 project since the most recent blow-out in costs?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We just covered a lot of this with Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We are waiting for an independent cost assessment that we engaged Turner & Townsend to do. In this current fiscal update, MYEFO, we will give some advice to government on that cost reassessment that Snowy Hydro has proposed, and what funding and in what form—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I know you've been overfunding. My question goes to the valuation of the asset on the books of the Commonwealth. Is this process doing that too?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think that will be part of that consideration.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We went over this with Snowy Hydro last night. I was a little surprised to hear from them that their claim is that their cost of capital has reduced since the last reset in 2023-24. Have you had a look at those conclusions of Snowy Hydro?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not that I'm aware of. We are working through all of the material that Snowy Hydro has provided to us. We will go through that. As the secretary has mentioned, we will provide advice on the quantum and the form of financing.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I just want to be clear that this is separate to the financing, because evaluation shouldn't be dependent on finance per se, particularly given you can potentially manipulate that valuation by different financing techniques. We want a proper economic valuation of what this means for the Commonwealth—for future taxpayers. My issue here is their conclusion that their cost of capital has reduced over the past two years, at a time when at least their risk-free rate in their WACC calculation should have significantly increased in the last two years given massive increases in long-term bond rates for the Commonwealth. Have you spoken to them about that conclusion which they have made?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I didn't see that in the testimony. We will review the Hansard. I'm happy to take it on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Independent of the Hansard, I would have thought the conversations would be ongoing, given the size of this cost blow-out. Have you had conversations with Snowy Hydro about their calculation of their cost of capital?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're having ongoing conversations with Snowy Hydro. To go into our analysis, I'm not aware that we've had that specific conversation, but I will take that away to see whether we've had that conversation and to run that to ground a bit.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. When you do the valuation for an asset like this, are you using a weighted average cost of capital—or the government bond rate? What's your discount rate for the net present value calculation?

agency: Department of Finance
text: As you mentioned, there are a range of methodologies, and we'll work through that.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Previously when you valued the Snowy 2.0 project, what has been the discount rate you've used?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't know what it was for Snowy Hydro. I know that it can be around 12 per cent, but I'm not sure what it was for Snowy. We can take that on notice for you, if you like.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay—so around 12 per cent. They said yesterday—

agency: Department of Finance
text: To be clear: I'm not saying that 12 per cent was connected to Snowy. I'll take that away and get back to you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think previously, in the initial costings around Snowy, it was about eight per cent. That's from recollection. They said yesterday or last night that their internal rate of return will be five to six per cent. That would be well under, then, their cost of capital, meaning it would be a negative net present value on the Commonwealth government's balance sheet. How is it currently costed? Is Snowy 2.0 listed at its cost on the balance sheet of the Commonwealth or is it discounted to cost?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would have to take that on notice and get back to you.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. Going back to my question, do you calculate a weighted average cost of capital for a project like this that is inherent to the risks of that project?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Again, I can take that on notice for you, Senator.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Okay. Is there a leverage ratio that you've previously used for Snowy 2.0? Maybe you've missed that you have some information there.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I think this is saying that there are various ways to calculate that, so we'll take that on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's my concern, because it seems to me sometimes to be a goal to seek to deliver a particular valuation that's less embarrassing here. That's why it's good to have transparency about all the assumptions. And, to correct the record, I did get alpha and beta mixed up last night. When you calculate a WACC here are you going to use a beta variable that's consistent with the risks of an electricity company like Snowy?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We'll take that on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We are waiting on advice from the cost assessment, and then we have some capital partners who are also working it. We're not avoiding your questions; we do not have the precise answers to them yet. That is part of the process we will work up to support government decision-making.

agency: Department of Finance
text: In terms of the decision to proceed with this project, has there been a reassessment of the net present value of the additional cost, from today, independent of the sunk costs that have been incurred to date?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Not at this point. That is part of our work to advise government on the—

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's right, and I think Snowy might have some commercial-in-confidence material on that, but we will—

agency: Department of Finance
text: But, hang on, if you haven't done an evaluation of whether or not there is a positive net present value in continuing the project, how has the government come to the conclusion to continue the project given the massive cost blow-out? That might be a question for the minister. I mean, have you seen, Minister—

agency: Department of Finance
text: There are other benefits of the pumped hydro program being completed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: But let's just be clear. The government hasn't received a calculation of at least—I take there are always social and other benefits, but have you received advice on the net present value of the additional costs and potential benefits of this project from today—independent of the sunk costs?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have received information from Snowy—essentially the work that Snowy Hydro has done—but, as Finance has said, they have undertaken some assurance level of that work. It's not finalised.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I might be missing some details. Has the government made a decision to proceed with Snowy 2.0, even based on the higher costs?

agency: Department of Finance
text:
I'm just having a look for the media release, because we did have some words in there. It said:

Completing Snowy 2.0 remains the responsible course. With tunnelling now 65 per cent complete … abandoning the project would undermine grid reliability, scrap 5,000 jobs and lead to higher bills.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes, that was my recollection. It sounds like the government has decided, yes, they're going to proceed.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Have you received an estimate of the net present value of this project for the costs and benefits going forward from today, from the date of that decision?

agency: Department of Finance
text: There is material that we have received from Snowy Hydro, from their board, that is commercial-in-confidence that I think Mr Barnes might have been referring to. We are going—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I'm not referring to that testimony. I'm more interested in, particularly, the finance department. Obviously, Snowy is conflicted to some degree. It would be very embarrassing if they have to stop the project. Presumably, the finance department has a role here to play?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. Shareholders have been given advice very clearly that it's in the best interests of taxpayers to finish the project rather than to leave it unfinished, including advice on the benefits of the project. Finance—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Has—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes. Based on the cost reassessment, Finance is testing some of that and providing that advice to government. That's why we haven't taken any decisions yet, as I explained to Senator Hume, about further injections into Snowy. You may have covered this last night: power station excavation is 90 per cent complete; drill and blast tunnels, 95 per cent complete; TBM tunnel, 65 per cent complete; and design completion, 96 per cent complete. I've been down, and I don't know if you've been down to have a look, but it's massive. The power station underground is almost complete.

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's all well and good. I have been there, but that's not quite relevant to my question. My question is: have you received advice, Minister, on what is the net present value of the project going forward? That is extremely relevant. From a Finance perspective, I would say that's a lot more relevant than going to inspect the power station.

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have all of that information.

agency: Department of Finance
text: So you have received that. Did that show a positive NPV?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: It showed a positive net present value going forward?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: What was the net present value?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We're now going through a process that is commercially sensitive. I've answered your question. We are also going through a process of what information from the cost reassessment report we can provide to the Senate publicly—those decisions. You've asked me: have shareholders been assured about the net present value and the benefits of the project? Yes, we have. Finance is undertaking some assurance of that advice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Did the positive net present value include social benefits or non-economic benefits, or was it a—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't have that information to hand. We can take it on notice and provide you with what we can.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Was a positive net present value figure provided to the minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: We have commercial-in-confidence information from Snowy.

agency: Department of Finance
text: The net present value is not—

agency: Department of Finance
text: I don't have the authority to provide Snowy Hydro's commercial—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Was a positive net present value figure provided to the minister?

agency: Department of Finance
text: The minister has said that it was.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I just answered that. I've answered that, but I'm saying that we're just going through a process of what information we can provide in order to give transparency on some of the advice that we've received but acknowledging that there are some commercial realities with which we're working at the moment, so some of that information may not be made public.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Given the minister has indicated and disclosed that a positive net present value figure was provided, I think it's fair and reasonable, Chair, to ask about the nature of that net present value calculation. All I'm asking is: was that net present value calculation based on just the economic benefits of the project to Snowy 2.0 and to the Commonwealth government, or did it include social and other factors in its calculation?

agency: Department of Finance
text: I've answered as best as I can for tonight. If there's more information that I can provide about that, I will. I just want to take some advice on it.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Are you taking that on notice rather than just taking advice?

agency: Department of Finance
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Excellent. Finance, I know this is going to really upset you, but we're going to let you go. Rather than moving on to Services Australia for three minutes—

agency: Department of Finance
text: Hang on—we've just got a correction.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Please go ahead.

agency: Department of Finance
text: I would just make a small correction to the evidence of my colleague earlier in answer to a question from Senator Hume. Senator Hume asked about charging by the Department of Finance. Finance does do only a very small amount of charging. We do accept credit cards in doing so; however, we have not applied a surcharge, so accordingly there is no change to our policies. I did just want to confirm that we do accept credit card, but it's very small number of payments given the nature of our responsibilities.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: So Finance absorbs the costs?

agency: Department of Finance
text: That's correct.
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Governance and Resource Management

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you very much for that correction.

agency: Department of Finance
text: There is just one more. It's not so much a correction, perhaps, as a clarification. Earlier, Senator McDonald was asking questions about the Brett Cattle matter, so I want to provide a little bit of clarity on our earlier answers regarding that. Former minister Ludwig is a respondent in the Brett Cattle matter. The Commonwealth controls the defence, including on behalf of Mr Ludwig. The Commonwealth does not and has not in the past taken instructions from Mr Ludwig.
