The Attorney-General's Department meets the costs of the defence of the proceedings against him, the defence of which the Commonwealth controls, and will take the remainder of the questions—there was a number from Senator McDonald—on notice.

agency: Department of Finance
text: Thank you very much. Any more? No? Excellent. Thank you so much for your time. We will now break and return with Services Australia.

agency: Services Australia
text: Welcome, everybody. I would like to welcome Mr David Hazlehurst, Chief Executive Officer of Services Australia. Would you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Services Australia
text: No, thank you.

agency: Services Australia
text: Excellent. We will go directly to questions and we'll start with Senator Hume.

agency: Services Australia
text: Mr Hazlehurst, I will try to make this as quick as possible so that we can get you out of here at a reasonable time. I wanted to ask, obviously, about the AI breach that occurred on 18 June. I want to understand why there were no internal notifications that alerted you to the unauthorised access to Services Australia's service in June, when the breach actually occurred.

agency: Services Australia
text: Thank you, Senator. I'll invite two colleagues, the Chief Information and Digital Officer and the Chief Information Security Officer.

agency: Services Australia
text: Your question was related to how the agency didn't get a notification when the OpenAI agent incident occurred back in June?
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: Yes.

agency: Services Australia
text: At the time when the incident occurred, even OpenAI was not aware of that incident.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: No, sorry. I think I'm not clear. Why didn't your systems pick up on the breach immediately?

agency: Services Australia
text: This is a public-facing website. The Medicare statistics reporting service portal is a public-facing website that has aggregate data in there that has no personal information. There is no accreditation or authentication that's required to access that system. No password is required, and it's generally accessed by vendors or researchers. The information that's in there, while we have protocols that sit on our websites that provide security at the back end, is an open resource for, as I said, researchers and vendors to access. So there wasn't a prompt at that point when the incident occurred. We received the notification once OpenAI also went through the process in understanding that they had had a misaligned agent that accessed the website in that way and moved beyond the front part of the portal into the back end. Should that misaligned agent have had, say, malicious intent, we would have seen a different response if it had tried to use credentials to access the back end and tried to move laterally through the system. That did not occur. Should it have done that, we would absolutely have received a prompt because of the cybersecurity protocols that sit within that environment.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: The way it was described, I think, at the time was that this AI agent had gone through the back door, but it found the back door open. Is that an accurate description?

agency: Services Australia
text: No. I'm sorry. I would not explain it in that way. I would say that it had a misaligned action that actually moved beyond the front-facing system into the back end of the system.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: But you didn't pick up on that entrance through the back end of the system?

agency: Services Australia
text: No, not at that time.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: So does that suggest that the security at the back end of the system was inadequate because the only way it was picked up was because OpenAI notified you after the fact?

agency: Services Australia
text: Can I provide a little bit of context? I think it's important to understand the nature of the affected system or the site. Again, as we mentioned, this incident related to that public-facing statistical reporting service. The activity didn't involve access to customer records. The agency maintains intensive and extensive monitoring, logging and security controls across its environment, with our highest-level protection focused on the systems that hold sensitive information and data. So, yes, it did misaligned activity and, yes, it accessed part of the system that it should not have been allowed to access, but it didn't move further than that.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: So it didn't need credentials. It didn't need passwords. That, to me, sounds like a lack of security at the back end. You said that, if it had malicious intent, you would have picked up on it, but it doesn't really matter what the malicious intent is or whether it had or didn't have malicious intent. It didn't need to breach security to get that data.

agency: Services Australia
text: The data was publicly available. It didn't need to try to access the back end to access the data. What it did was that it had activity where it was trying to seek further information, and it did move into part of the system that it should not have moved into. Our focus on monitoring matters is that we apply the greater scrutiny to systems that deliver critical services.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: I understand that, but can we be really clear: this was an unauthorised entity that accessed your system and you weren't aware. Is that correct?

agency: Services Australia
text: We weren't aware at that time.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: Yes, but you were made aware by OpenAI. Can I ask what Services Australia did after it was made aware? My understanding is that it took five days before you notified the Australian Signals Directorate. Is that right?

agency: Services Australia
text: Following receipt of the notification, the agency commenced technical validation activities. Just to set a little bit of context on that as well, this was a very unusual disclosure, so when we received the notification through that public disclosure mailbox, we then had to assess if it was—
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: The veracity of the disclosure.

agency: Services Australia
text: Exactly.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

agency: Services Australia
text: So why couldn't you inform ASD at the same time as testing the veracity of the disclosure?

agency: Services Australia
text: We had not seen an incident like this occur in this way. I will say, with hindsight—and certainly, we've implemented processes now that make a situation like this look different—we referred the matter for technical assessment. We needed to know whether the report was credible and what system or site was affected, because their email referenced a vulnerability. It also spoke to an AI model. We weren't aware that it was an agent, we weren't aware that there was misaligned activity at the time with the notification that came through, and we needed to understand whether a vulnerability actually existed and whether any unauthorised access had occurred. So, during that time, the matter was referred for technical assessment on 11 September. It was escalated to the cybersecurity operations centre on the 14th. I'll just mentioned that that timeframe in there is also because, at the time, this type of disclosure mailbox wasn't the way that normal cyber incidents would be reported to us, and if they had been escalated or come through in a different environment, we would've immediately been into our 24/7 cyber operations centre. But that wasn't the case. This mailbox was not monitored on a 24/7 basis; it was monitored nine to five during the week. So once it was confirmed and escalated to the cybersecurity operations centre on the 14th, the vulnerability was confirmed on the 15th. And once confirmed, we immediately took the service offline, declared a cybersecurity incident and notified the Australian Signals Directorate. Again, from that, we saw that their forensic analysis found no evidence that customer information, Medicare records, payment information, identity information or any sensitive personal data had been accessed, altered, or disclosed. So our existing security controls also prevented access to the other agency systems and datasets. That's the process that occurred to that point.
witness_position: Chief Information and Digital Officer, Technology and Digital Programs

text: What's the dollar figure for what the surcharges would be that you're now absorbing?

agency: Services Australia
text: For 2025-26, for the social security and welfare program the total for surcharges was $872,954.60. That was absorbed, historically. For the child support program, the total surcharge was $452,600.37.

agency: Services Australia
text: That's not a small amount. Have you sought the same sort of transitional arrangements that the ATO has sought from government?

agency: Services Australia
text: No.

agency: Services Australia
text: On that, with social security and welfare, which was the largest figure, we had not previously had any surcharge. People had always been able to use a credit card to repay a social security debt that they owed the government.
witness_position: Deputy Chief Executive Officer, Payments and Integrity

agency: Services Australia
text: Yes. The Assistant Treasurer said that the government became aware in July that the ATO could stop accepting cards. When did Services Australia or, I suppose, you, Minister, first consider the impact of the surcharge ban on Services Australia's operations?

agency: Services Australia
text: I think it's the same as the answer I gave in Finance. I think there was a letter to me, which would have been from the Assistant Treasurer. I would have to check the date of that, but that's kind of where we were given insight into the decisions the RBA was taking and some of the discussions that were being had.

agency: Services Australia
text: Based on the information that I have, on 21 January 2026 the Treasury requested information on the costs.

agency: Services Australia
text: Back in January?

agency: Services Australia
text: Yes.

agency: Services Australia
text: Obviously, potentially knowing this was coming, Services Australia must have had an assessment of the impact on people in hardship, people who rely on credit cards for cash flow. Was there a brief to the minister on this particular issue and what the impact would be if surcharge charging were removed? Was this something that you had a heightened awareness of and responded to, knowing that it might come?

agency: Services Australia
text: This was managed through the Treasury, so we provided input to the request but we were not involved in the policy discussions.

agency: Services Australia
text: Knowing that you were going to have to absorb that new cost, was that something about which you briefed your minister before 1 October?

agency: Services Australia
text: I'll hand to our CFO.

agency: Services Australia
text: I did not brief the minister on the actual requirement to absorb these fees. It was a decision by the organisation to make sure that we were providing the services that we do in the proper manner. I am not sure whether the minister was briefed from a program point of view, but from a budget management point of view I did not brief the minister, noting that within our $6.1 billion budget this is something that we felt we could absorb for the greater good.

agency: Services Australia
text: Mindful, Senator, that we were already absorbing the larger cost. We always have, in relation to social security. In relation to child support, these are the transfers of money between two parents, and so we felt that was a call we could make. We didn't brief the minister.

agency: Services Australia
text: Okay. Thank you.

agency: Services Australia
text: Thank you very much. We do appreciate the late-night fun and frolics in the Senate, so thank you for coming. We will now release you.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Welcome. I will just enter an apology for Dr Arndt, who is unable to attend today but is ably represented by Mr Will Hetherton, the chief corporate affairs officer, and Mr Richard Brandweiner, the chief investment officer. Would either of you care to make an opening statement?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You could table it, in the interest of time.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You could table it.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text:
I'm very happy to table it.

The statement read as follows—

In the 12 months to 30 June 2026, the Future Fund delivered an investment return of 14.8%, adding $37.4 billion to the portfolio. After one of the strongest returns in its history, tie value of the Future Fund now sits at a record $289.7 billion.

This exceptional result was achieved despite investors facing a challenging year marked by geopolitical conflict, market volatility and persistent inflation. We experienced strong performance across the portfolio, and benefited from an increased focus on active management, exposure to commodities, geographic diversification and low exposure to bonds.

The Fund's strong returns were also achieved whilst increasing our investment in the national priority areas of domestic housing, infrastructure and the energy transition. In line with our revised Investment Mandate, we have committed $3.5 billion to those three sectors since late 2024 and we now hold almost $20 billion of investment in domestic infrastructure in our portfolio. Our strengthened focus on investing in the national priority areas, while

prioritising strong returns and prudent risk management, is another way in which the Future Fund is contributing to Australia's economic prosperity.

We also recently marked a major milestone, with the Future Fund turning 20 this year. The Future Fund has evolved significantly Over the past Mo decades, but the foundations of its culture, focus on collaboration and first principles approach to global investing have been present since inception. Since the Future Fund's inception in 2006, investment returns have now added $229.2 billion to its value.

The value of the six other funds managed by the Future Fund Board of Guardians now sits at $66.3 billion, taking total funds managed by the Board to $356 billion.

Since our last appearance before this Committee, our Chief Executive Officer, Dr Raphael Arndt announced his decision to leave the Future Fund after almost two decades of service and six years as CEO. The recruitment process to appoint a new CEO is progressing well. This is a confidential process conducted in accordance with APS requirements so we have little to add today but we look forward to announcing the outcome in due course. Dr Arndt will be continuing in his role through to the end of 2026 to support a smooth transition of responsibilities.

I am joined by our Chief Investment Officer, Mr Richard Brandweiner, to answer any investment-related queries.

I welcome your questions.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Perhaps I can make two comments. Since we were last here, in the 12 months to June 2026, the fund delivered an investment return of 14.8 per cent, adding $37.4 billion to the portfolio and it now sits at just short of $290 billion. And also, since our last appearance, our chief executive, Raphael Arndt, announced his decision to leave the fund after almost two decades of service and six years as CEO. We wish him the very best with his move. The recruitment process to appoint a new CEO is progressing well. This is a confidential process conducted in accordance with APS requirements, so there's little that we can add today. But we do look forward to announcing the outcome in due course. And Dr Arndt will stay in his role through to the end of 2026. I'm joined by Chief Investment Officer Richard Brandweiner, who's been with the fund for three months, and we're happy to respond to your questions.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you. All our very best to Dr Arndt. We will miss him on these late-night escapades. So please pass on our very best and our thanks from the committee. We'll go to Senator Pocock.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thanks for being here at this late hour. I have a question about question on notice no. 648. The response reported that there are 11 APS employees who received a total annual remuneration package of over $1 million and all of them were employed by the Future Fund Management Agency. Is this still correct, or are there more or less employees with a total remuneration package of over $1 million?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I think that data related to the 2024-25 year. We have subsequently tabled our annual report, and the statutory remuneration table discloses, I think, 17 employees with remuneration, reported on that basis, of over $1 million.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So it's gone from 11 to 17 in a year.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: That's correct.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Can you provide on notice the years of service and the seniority of those 17 positions.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes, I can. Happily.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: What was the highest total remuneration of any employee in the Future Fund Management Agency?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: That will depend. We've provided two tables in our annual report this year. One is the statutory remuneration table on page 116 of the 2025-26 annual report. That reports a total remuneration for one employee of $2.2 million. However, that incorporates accruals of both deferred short-term performance bonuses as well as a long-term incentive that is not payable at this stage but is accrued nonetheless. The cash basis is also reported, and that's on page 115 of the annual report. It discloses there that the total cash remuneration of $1.7 million was paid to Dr Arndt.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you. Just going back to the $2.2 million package, including the short-term bonus and long-term incentive: can you tell us what proportion of the $2.2 million they represent?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Let me just see if I have that.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I can't disaggregate that. There is a line item for other long-term benefits, and that picks up both those short-term deferred performance-related payments and the accrued value of long-term incentives that have not yet been paid.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Okay. No other APS employee earns such excessive remuneration for their work. Why is it that the work of the Future Fund is so different and special as to attract such high pay?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text:
The approach to remuneration set by the board has been in place, I would say, since the fund was established. There have been some tweaks along the way, but it is largely the same approach. The Future Fund is quite distinct from other agencies and departments within the public service. Our job is to maximise risk adjusted returns. We operate in competitive global financial markets, both for investment opportunities and for talent. The board's remuneration strategy reflects that and is based on remuneration within the financial services sector.

The other point I think is really important to make is that short-term incentives and long-term incentives are tied directly to investment performance. A large part of the remuneration that is paid, and reported in quite a lot of detail in our annual report, is at risk and reflects the very strong performance of the fund, not only this year over 2025-26, as I mentioned in my opening comments, but also over three years and longer, during which the fund has generated about $84 billion for the Commonwealth.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: How many of the 17 employees earning over $1 million are women?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't know that number. The majority of the 17, I think, will be other highly paid staff who aren't called out individually within the reporting. If I look briefly at the KMP, where this is disclosed, I'd say that, in the table you're referring to—the statutory remuneration table—one female member of staff is paid over $1 million. We can take it on notice, but I'd also say that the gender balance within our senior investment team is good. What we're really talking about here is making sure that people who are performing strongly and contributing to the performance of the fund are remunerated appropriately. I would fully expect that that includes senior females.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: What's the gender pay gap in the Future Fund?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The gender pay gap for the Future Fund is disclosed in our gender pay gap statement, which is on our website. I would preface my comments by saying that the gender pay gap has improved, although it needs to improve further, and we're very committed to doing that. The median gender pay gap for 2025 is 18.3 per cent and the average gender pay gap is 21.8 per cent. I believe that the latest data coming through from our submission to WGEA is a good improvement on that, but I don't have the details at this stage.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You can understand, I imagine, why members of the public, and the rest of the APS, would be shocked that a public servant is earning such high remuneration and that there has been such an increase and such a sizeable group of them entirely within the Future Fund. Minister, do you have any comments to make on that pay rate given that the person who's in charge of health and ageing is earning half that $1.7 million that I think Dr Arndt earned? We've got people who do very hard jobs who are paid way, way less. What's your reflection on that?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: A couple of things—as Mr Hetherton said, it is quite a unique job that the staff of the Future Fund do. We have to pay competitive salaries for the industry that they are working in. I met with the chair of the Future Fund recently. He assured me that, on coming into the role, he has essentially undertaken an assessment of remuneration across the fund to ensure that it's appropriate. The Future Fund is now managing $356 billion in public assets for the public. If you look at comparable funds internationally, I was advised that this is in the middle to lower range of salaries for people undertaking this type of work for governments. It's easy for people to see the numbers and be concerned, but I think, if you see it in the context of the financial services industry that we are having to attract talent from—it's generating a return of 14 per cent in the last year alone, which has seen people get those short-term bonuses associated with those returns, including over multi-years—it is explainable.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I wonder if, then, you could provide on notice the international data and how the Future Fund has used such data to justify the rates of increase that it talks about benchmarking against? If you are benchmarking, could you provide that data?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I saw that the salaries in association with Canada—I think it was reported in the AFR recently that the chief executive of Canada's pension fund generally earns $5 million to $7 million a year. In the financial services industry, for specialist investment skills like this, we do have to pay a remuneration that is going to attract talented people to come and work in the public interest. I've met with staff of the Future Fund as well in my time in this role, and they are people that have made the choice to come and work for a public fund.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm reminded of a CEO of a very large company not so long ago who was paid many millions but whose children were cared for in child care, and he was delighted that their salary meant that they were doing it for love, not for money. Clearly, we've got people doing these positions, where money really does matter, and the people who do really tough caring roles are paid so much less. It is a real challenge in our wages system.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't disagree, but the market sets the remuneration packages for people with these types of specialist skills. It's essentially a sovereign wealth fund. We ask it to generate returns. The fund has been incredibly successful exceeding those returns, and we have to pay for talented staff to manage that. I agree—I understand all the arguments around it, but I have looked at this closely. We have to pay—and we're not paying rates comparable with commercial entities, I would say. That's the point. There is an element of the people I've met working at the Future Fund such that they accept that and do it because of the public purpose behind that.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I want to go the issue of—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Senator Pocock, I'm going to do 10-minute blocks.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Okay.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We'll go to Senator Hume.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I just want to ask about the recruitment process for Mr Arndt's replacement. When were the ads first published?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The position was advertised publicly on the Future Fund's career page and the APS Gazette on 27 August.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Have applications closed?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't know when the applications closed. I can take that on notice.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Can you tell me if there's been a recruitment firm engaged to support the search?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes. Spencer Stuart was engaged.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Spencer Stuart, yes. Is it purely domestic or is it an international search?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: It's a global search.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Mr Arndt's a stalwart of the institution. There has been a significant degree of turnover in the rest of the executive too, so I'm wondering if there's been any consideration given to whether there will be potentially more significant change or loss of corporate knowledge at the fund. I'm wondering if there's an appropriate transition plan in place for Mr Arndt's departure.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't think turnover has been at particularly high levels. I think in the annual report this year we report turnover at 16.6 per cent, which is well within the bounds that we would expect in the industry. In terms of the handover, Dr Arndt is with us through until the end of December and is ensuring that he's transmitting his knowledge and experience through the organisation. I would say that there is a significant depth of corporate knowledge within the organisation. The chief operating officer has been with us for 20 years. I've been with the organisation for 19 years. I think that the average tenure of our those on our investment committee is around 10 years, so there is significant depth of knowledge.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You said that it's expected that Mr Arndt's replacement will be announced in due course. Can you give us something a little bit more specific than that?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm afraid I can't.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Is the reason why you can't because you know and you can't tell me, or because it is in some way controversial or contravening some breach of privacy? Or is it because nobody knows?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The process is ongoing. I'm not directly involved in the process. I understand it's progressing well but I can't go further than that.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I just want to ask about some speculation on drawdown of the fund. There was an article in October, I think it was, that suggested that the Future Fund may be called upon because of the growing trillion dollars in Commonwealth debt and rapidly rising bond yields. For the record, has the Future Fund been asked by government to prepare any materials in preparation for an earlier drawdown of the Future Fund than the deferral currently committed to out to 2032-33?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Senator Pocock.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm just looking at page 117 of your report and the fees paid to board members. Mr Combet, as chair, was paid $274,713. Was that for a full year? When was Mr Combet appointed? He's been there for at least a year.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes, he has.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes, a full year. How is that board fee set? Is that relative to similar organisations, Minister? How do board fees get fixed?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The Remuneration Tribunal would set those.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: And would this rate be parallel—comparable—to other similar boards?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: What do you want us to compare it to?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: This is a chair of a board.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes. But the Future Fund is different to, say, the chair of a board doing a particular piece of work, say, in the health department.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: It's quite different to that. Or are you asking us to compare it to commercial funds under management of $365 billion?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No, not commercial. I am asking about similar other public sector bodies. You referred to the Remuneration Tribunal. Perhaps on notice—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: It would be at the higher end, I would imagine, of government boards. But I know the amount of work that is done for that, and for the experience and knowledge that Mr Combet—and Mr Costello before him—brought to the role. In fact, I met with Mr Combet last week, and we were going through just how much time he is spending on the Future Fund, which would make the hourly rate, I think, associated with that remuneration pretty low.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Could I have, on notice, a comparison of this chair's payment relative to similar other boards in the public sector?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't think there is a similar board. I don't know how you would do that. We could look at GBEs potentially.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Okay. Great, Thank you.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Because there are hundreds of boards. I just don't want to do—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm just curious. You're saying it's the upper end. I'd like to see the comparison. I want to go to rates of return and the places of investment. What specific human rights and international humanitarian law due diligence has the Future Fund undertaken in relation to its investments in Palantir and Elbit Systems?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Senator, we've covered this in the past. The individual decisions around particular companies in which we invest are taken by our external investment managers. Those managers make the decisions. They also research in line with their screens and assessment if they have them. Our role is to identify the overall risk settings for the portfolio and then implement strategies through external investment managers to deliver that. As I think you know, as you'll recall, we do comply with appropriate sanctions and we have a number of exclusions from the portfolio as well.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Do those sanctions go to investments in companies that are dealing in the West Bank?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The approach we take on sanctions is that we consider the conventions and treaties that Australia has signed in relation to economic activities. Sorry, I've confused myself. Could you just repeat your question for me?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm wondering what controls you have in place for your external investment managers in relation to companies that are doing business in the West Bank?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So we apply the treaties and conventions that Australia has ratified in relation to economic activities and we apply sanctions—clearly, Australian sanctions, but also US sanctions—across the portfolio. I'll leave it there.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So could you answer my question? Do they have any reach to companies trading or doing any business into the West Bank?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Those aren't sanctioned and they're not excluded from the portfolio.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So you have no control over what your investment managers are doing in that zone?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We look at the strategies that they will be applying and satisfy ourselves that they're the strategies that we are comfortable with and fit within our framework.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Do you do any independent human rights assessments in relation to any of the investments in the Future Fund?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We do. Richard, you might want to talk to this.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes, that's fine. I'm trying to get my head around this, Senator. I've only been there briefly. But, just to clarify what Mr Hetherton was saying, the whole exclusion process is based on the federal government sanctions, and that applies across the whole portfolio. Beyond that, we use a lot of passive exposure—so we invest in passive equities around the world. And a lot of the sorts of exposures you're talking about exist because they're in the index. However, we do have some managers that invest in some of the companies that you're talking about, and they do do their own screening and their own engagement with those companies. For example, you were asking about Palantir. One of our underlying managers has been working with them for some time on human rights performance. They've supported two shareholder proposals asking for human rights due diligence and impact assessments. We don't do stewardship on global stocks, but our underlying fund managers do, and they've been engaging with the company on that basis.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So that's one manager out of how many managers?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Well, the passive managers don't do that. These are managers that do smart beta investing, and the bulk of our exposure would be through that manager.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: So you've increased holdings in both Palantir and Elbit Systems in the first half of 2026. I want to know whether those additional purchases were made through passive index tracking arrangements or active investment decisions.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No, they weren't active investment decisions. In both of those cases, they were a function of additional inclusions of those stocks in different indices. With index providers, it's a dark art, and it's hard to know. I think, for example, Palantir went into the MSCI quality.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes. The change there was that the allocation to Palantir occurred because it was included in an MSCI index.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: What does MSCI mean?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: That's a global index provider.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You've given me an anecdote or an example of one manager that does engage with looking at what Palantir is doing in their investment decisions. Do you have an overview about what engagement and analysis across your investors is underway, in relation to both Palantir and Elbit Systems?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: When we choose a fund manager—this is my understanding—we evaluate their credentials in terms of engagement and stewardship. That's part of the way we would assess them. This particular manager is very strong in that respect. To be clear, we don't have many global equity managers, so this would be, by and large, the bulk of any sort of engagement.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I appreciate you answering my questions, but it's fair to say you do not know how the majority of your fund managers are dealing with Elbit Systems and Palantir. You've told me about one.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't think that would be correct. As Mr Brandweiner points out, as we appoint managers, we look at the strategies, arrangements and policies that they have in place, and then we have ongoing engagement with our managers, whether they are index tracking or more active managers, to understand how they're performing and how they're implementing any particular strategies or considerations within their portfolio.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Elbit Systems was previously excluded from the Future Fund's investment portfolio because of concerns related to prohibited weapons. When and why was that exclusion lifted?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I think perhaps a year or so ago we discussed this. Elbit Systems was excluded originally on the basis of involvement in the manufacture of cluster munitions. In 2023, our external advisers, based on their monitoring and research of the company, identified that that was no longer the case—that the company was no longer involved in those particular munitions, which are subject to an exclusion from the portfolio under our policy—and it therefore became investable again. That meant that our external investment managers were able to invest into it, and that's what they did. And that's how it came back into the portfolio.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Regarding oversight and transparency, what view do you have into the range and nature of the weapons being invested in by Elbit Systems and Palantir? What confidence do you have about what is in that basket of production by those two companies, who are attracting considerable interest around the globe for their activities, certainly in Gaza and the West Bank?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We rely on two external advisory services, who are expert in this space, and they are Moody's and Sustainalytics. They do the research in this space, and other areas match that against our portfolio on particular companies. We draw on their advice.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Moody's and Sustainalytics have a service which examines the weapons elements within the portfolios and provide you with—what sort of information?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: With an assessment as to whether the companies that they're looking at are operating in areas that would contravene our policy.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: How often do you receive those reports?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Every six months.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Has the Future Fund sought legal advice on the implications of the International Court of Justice's July 2024 advisory opinion for Australian public investments in companies operating in or supporting illegal Israeli settlements?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I think this came up in our last hearing. I think the answer was no.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Events have changed in these areas. Have you sought legal advice?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Has any assessment been undertaken of the fund's exposure to companies identified in the United Nations Human Rights Office database of businesses involved in settlement related activities?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Not that I'm aware of, but I'm happy to take that on notice.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Has the government considered whether public investment in such companies raises issues under Australia's obligations to aid or assist in maintaining an unlawful situation? Minister, this may be one for you. What's your view about public investment in companies that may be aiding or assisting in unlawful situations? Is this something that you would like the Future Fund, our sovereign fund, to be paying attention to?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The statement of expectations and relevant government decisions have to be taken into consideration by the Future Fund, and the expectation is that the Future Fund would follow those.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We're in a changing situation, aren't we? We've got 22,000 children who have been murdered in Gaza. We have a lot of Australians very concerned about that. They would be delighted to have a growing sovereign wealth fund, but many of them would be extremely uncomfortable with any engagement with firms that are profiting from the murder of children and adult civilians. Have you had any advice from DFAT or the Attorney-General's Department on these matters?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't believe so. I don't know whether the Treasurer and my departments have had any engagement. I can't recall any that would have come. We don't micromanage the Future Fund. We set the policies. We set the statement of expectations, and then the fund has a job to do, which is to provide a return on investments to build up the resources required to fund ongoing superannuation responsibilities across the—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Are you comfortable, though, with the sense that our superannuation funds are in part built on very significant increases in the profitability in the share price of companies that are clearly engaged in circumstances where human rights are definitely under attack, where we're losing a lot—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: That's the assertion from the Greens, and we—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: It's a fact—22,000 children lost. I'm not making that up.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No, but we're talking about how the Future Fund invests. We're not talking about broader matters. We're talking about the responsibilities the Future Fund has to provide a return on investment for the Australian community. We provide a statement of expectations. If there are government-wide sanctions in place, then the Future Fund is required to follow those. We expect that the Future Fund does what we ask of it and follows those government directions. In my experience, that is exactly what the Future Fund does.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Is it time to review that charter of investment to reflect the circumstances that are that the United Nations is drawing attention to?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We always keep these matters under review, and we are always in dialogue with the Future Fund itself, including in a meeting I had last week with the chair.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Can the Future Fund on notice please provide a list of its holdings in companies identified in the UN Human Rights Office database of businesses, as was recently updated, involved in activities related to Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including the value of each holding and whether any have been subject to a human rights risk assessment.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I will certainly take that on notice.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm going to plough on until you pull me up.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: You've got a couple of minutes.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Last estimates, I raised with you the High Court of New Zealand decision, where they declared that the New Zealand Superannuation Fund's $86 billion investment framework was unlawful. I asked you whether you had received legal advice about the legality of investments in settlement activity or military operations in Palestine. Your answer was that the government had not sought advice about whether its investments were consistent with international law and there'd been no analysis done of that court decision. I'm asking you, why not? Are you concerned that you could also be in breach?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I don't think I have anything further to update the committee on.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Could you provide, on notice, advice about whether your investments are consistent with international law.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm happy to see what we can provide. I think it would be a matter for the Attorney-General's Department, but I will see what we can do.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I see, in your investments in weapons, as of 30 June 2026: $114 million in Palantir, over $100 million in General Dynamics, $51 million in Northrop Grumman, $22 million in Thales, $21.7 million in Boeing and $13.8 million in Lockheed Martin. These are very sizeable amounts of investment in weapons production, are they not?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We're a very large portfolio, so the holdings we have in companies tend to be significant. The companies that you listed through there aren't covered by any of our exclusions or sanctions that are in place, and so they're an investible part of the portfolio for us.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I also note in your investment portfolio a very sizeable set of fossil fuel investments—$300 million in Santos and $672 million in Woodside. You talk, in your publications and certainly in your media releases, about greater climate transparency. Have you given any thought to the contribution that our sovereign wealth fund should be making in the Future Fund to reducing harmful investment in fossil fuels, which are warming our planet and threatening great risk to the children of the future?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: We give a significant amount of thought to managing risk within the investment portfolio, and that includes climate risk—absolutely it does. Our task is set out by the legislation, the Future Fund Act and other pieces of legislation, and by the investment mandate, which charges us with maximising returns with an acceptable but not excessive level of risk. That's why we do consider risks around climate, but it's not led us to a point where we believe that we should be excluding parts of the energy sector in particular.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thanks for your answers.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: And thanks very much for your investments in renewables.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: The minister makes a makes a good point. We've talked about this in various situations as well. We do invest extensively in, for example, Tilt Renewables, and we've talked about that. That, I think, makes us one of the largest investors, if not the second largest, in renewables in Australia.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you so much for joining us. I have no doubt there'll be more questions on notice. At this point, I would like to thank the Digital Transformation Agency for providing us with their opening statement and provide our congratulations from the committee to Mr Fechner, who's the new chief executive officer—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Continuing.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Continuing? Well, appointed, yes. I would also like to thank the ASC for waiting patiently—Mr Alex Walsh, the acting chief executive officer, and other officers of the ASC. I would like to say that the committee is sorry for not having been able to get to those agencies today as different members of the committee have different, competing priorities, but we will endeavour to change it up next time.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Sorry, Chair, can I just ask—is the committee resolving to spill over?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: No-one has asked for a spillover, but you can certainly provide us with a letter. We've come to the end—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm not a committee member, but I was hoping we'd get to those two.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: There are many options open to members of the committee. I've tried to negotiate throughout the day to get to all of the things. Unfortunately, that has not been successful.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm conscious of the fact that senators obviously still have questions, and if senators still have questions—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: If senators have questions, as you well know, they are well within their rights to seek. But we don't have anyone here asking. No-one has asked for a spillover, so we haven't set one, but you can certainly—

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: I'm asking for one.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Can we resolve into a committee, then, so that we're not wasting any more of these poor, unfortunate people's time?

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Yes.

agency: Future Fund Management Agency
text: Thank you. I would like to thank everybody—the witnesses, Hansard and Broadcasting—and declare this meeting of the Senate Finance and Public Administration Legislation Committee adjourned.
